Product Description: GE Monogram 48" vent hood
Incident Description:
I own a GE Monogram 48 inch kitchen range vent hood and noticed that the grease baffle filters provided with the hood do not cover the entire air intake opening of the hood. I contacted GE regarding my vent hood, model ZV48SSF1SS, in which is found three 12.75 inch x 15 inch x 1 inch (25mm) [REDACTED] baffle grease filters, rated for fire prevention, and which according to the parts diagram of the hood should have only have three filters. The parts diagram states that the filters are GE part #WB02X10877. GE confirmed that the part number is correct, but upon pressing them for the dimensions they stated 13.5 inch x 16.5 inch x 2.25 inch which is clearly not the size of the filters I have. I then looked up the part number at repairclinic.com where a nice image of the filter laid on a grid confirms that the filter is 12.75 inches x 15 inches. I also confirmed that an internal ledge within the vent hood will not allow a filter greater than 30mm in thickness. So GE does not know what filter fits my vent hood and GE was not aware that three filters with a width of 12.75 inch each can only cover 38.25 inches of the vent hood opening leaving 7 inches of the 45.25 inch wide opening uncovered by a grease filter. This leads me to believe that when GE contracted with [REDACTED] for 48 vent hood filters they either transmitted an erroneous specification or thought they could get away using a filter for a narrower hood in the 48 hood. 

As you know know grease baffle filters must cover the entire opening of a vent hood to keep grease out of the vent exhaust duct that passes through an attic before exiting a roof. When the filters do not cover the entire opening, there are manufacturers who may provide spacers to fill in the gaps. Notably GE does not provide spacers. Because the filters serve to prevent a fire from passing up the duct, a gap may allow fire to travel into a duct and ignite grease in the duct which of course will burn down a home. 

This was a major design error on the part of GE. [REDACTED] provided what GE requested. Had GE provided three 15 inches x 15 inches  x 1 inch filters, homes could have been spared from burning down. A GE rep told me that there were no recalls on the vent hood; however, the lack of recalls provides no certainty that fires did not occur and that lives have not been lost because the causes of a major fire are often difficult to determine given the destruction of responsible factors. With respect to fires and there causes, I speak from experience as a former US Navy engineering officer responsible for fire prevention and fire fighting aboard a guided missile destroyer.

Of course having uncovered these facts, I will have to take 3 measures. Firstly, I will be engaging a consumer products tort lawyer for his opinion on the viability of a civil lawsuit. Secondly, I will be engaging the US Consumer Products Safety Commission (you guys whom I hope will take my concerns seriously) which has regulatory tools to uncover what injuries may have occurred and force GE to provide remediation. Thirdly, I will be engaging my own insurance company, [REDACTED], which is very interested in mitigating fire risks.

UPDATE 7/29/2025:
Dear CPSC Clearing House,

I have communicated with the maker of the baffle grease filters intended to keep fires from entering vent hood ductwork and they have informed me that the orientation of the filters in the image I provided you was incorrect. Both the prior owner and myself who followed his practice had the baffles incorrectly horizontally oriented.  When I rotated the filters 90 degrees such that the baffles were vertically oriented the gaps disappeared. 

I now see that on p 15 of the hood installation manual, which I recently downloaded only because I was searching for an electrical parts diagram, the orientation of correctly installed filters is depicted. As noted above, I also realize that they were installed incorrectly by the former owner of my home. I simply followed his practice and never thought about the gap until I began to wonder why there was a gap. Because it is obvious that filters can be installed incorrectly and not fall onto the range, perhaps GE could have provided a warning in the manual stating that filters must be installed as seen in the picture and that no gap should be present between filters when they are installed correctly. I installed them incorrectly just as the former owner did and I would never have noticed my mistake but for my conversations with the maker of the filters [REDACTED]. It is a wonder that the prior owner of my home didnt burn the house down because he grilled meat on a gas range under the hood. Because purchasers of homes are also unlikely to be provided installation manuals on preexisting appliances, a permanent warning label on the hood and the filters would be a nice safety feature.

I have looked at manuals of current versions of the same GE hood and although they contain a diagram showing the vertical orientation of the baffles they do not contain warnings regarding incorrect filter baffle orientation and the necessity of not having gaps between filters caused by incorrect orientation of rectangular filters because the gaps create a risk of fires entering the vent ductwork. I am also concerned that the GE parts folks gave me the wrong dimensions of the filter after they confirmed that the filter part number was correct, and I am concerned that none of them could inform me that incorrect filter orientation was the cause of the gaps. It is only because I communicated with the USA rep of the Italian company which made the fire rated filters that I understood that the gap was due to an error by the prior owner and myself to properly install the filters. How not to do something is an important instruction that should accompany any instruction on how to do something. Unfortunately that type of instruction - which is necessary whenever it is physically possible to do something incorrectly - is rarely provided.  Image 2417 is an incorrect but physically possible  installation with gaps between filters apparent, and image 2422 is correct installation with no gaps. 

Thus, my only recommendation is that whenever fire is a risk, clearly worded warning labels with diagrams of correct and incorrect part orientations to advise users on proper installation be provided on or next to parts that can be improperly installed.

Product Description: Gas oven/stovetop standalone
Incident Description:
Electrocution and explosion hazard on General Electric Gas oven/stove model JGBS66EEK1ES. Gas oven/stove has Line and Neutral wires improperly installed at factory to the ignitor/spark module.  This miswire caused two dangerous conditions, that would have been mitigated, had the unit been properly assembled at factory. The violet Line wire was plugged into the Neutral position on the spark module, with the white Neutral wire plugged into the Line position on the module. The rear cover holding this module was removed for inspection and cleaning. The wire connected to the NEUTRAL position of the spark module became unplugged, resting inside the chassis. The cover was reinstalled without noting this loose wire, and an attempt was made to ignite the stove from the knob. This energized the disconnected Line wire, which contacted the oven chassis/ground. This created the first hazard, electrocution thru the body of the oven. As the oven was on a AFCI circuit breaker in the house, it did trip properly. The second hazard was that with this line wire disconnected, the spark module was inop, and turning the knob further allowed gas flow without ignition. 

If this spark module was wired properly, the wire that became disconnected by removing the rear cover, would have been a NEUTRAL wire, carrying no voltage. This would have prevented the electrocution hazard, and the spark module may have potentially remained functional, using the ground wire as a return path, preventing freeflowing gas without a spark. This may still have tripped the AFCI/GFCI breaker, which would alert the user to a problem. 

The positioning of the spark module allows for (if appropriately installed) NEUTRAL wire to catch on the panel below it on removal. 

This wiring reversal was verified by comparing it to the wiring diagram taped to the rear of the appliance, and voltage tests.

UPDATED ON 5/29/2024: [After correcting the problem identified in this report, (reversed neutral and Line wires) the gas stovetop has a more powerful ignition spark. Before the cover was initially removed for cleaning, and throughout the life of the unit, the burners would often fail to light until the knobs were turned almost past the ignite portion of the knob. I used to have to turn the knob back to the ignite range and it would often "flare up" on first ignite. Now the burner will light right away at the BEGINNING of the ignite portion of the knob. This is much safer as there is a lower gas flow and flame.

I did not contact the manufacturer as it is out of warranty, after business hours, and from past experience in contacting their support, they would not have been capable of recording a serious safety report. ]
Answer Explanation: No prior service or opening of unit.

Incident Description:
On New Years Eve 2011, I  used my five person George Foreman Grill at home to make dinner.  My mother, brother, and I used the grill to grill steaks.  We grilled them individually for safety  and to lock in the taste.  After letting it cool for a good hour while eating, my mother asked me to bring the grill from the counter to the sink to clean it.  The grill sat unplugged and was not hot. I picked it up and after approximately two seconds of it being  in my hands the ribbed metal grill lid slammed shut.  It closed on both of my thumbs with such force that I felt it had taken them clean off.  I was instructed to run them under hot water because my family believed that the grill  had burned me.  They were unable to understand my complaint due to the excessive screaming and crying that followed.  After it was discovered that I had no burns I was given an ice pack and was told to sit down and relax for a little bit. 

While I was sitting at our dining room table my mom had to throw the grill  away; not because it hurt me but because it broke.  When it slammed on my thumbs, the metal lid crushed with such force that the clamps that held it in place snapped  apart and the lid broke in half while my thumbs were still in it.  I sat for five minutes before I asked to go the emergency  room. Before we left I examined my thumbs and found a deep green/ purple blood blister had already formed under my right thumb nail.  The time between the lid closing on them and the blister formation was less then ten minutes.  By the time we arrived at the emergency room I was still screaming and crying from the pain. 

 I was seen right away  I had I two nurses, three x-ray technicians, and a doctor all attempt to move my thumbs but they were so injured from the weight of the metal lid that they would not move.  They remained locked in a bent position and were unable to straighten.  I had to have two separate sets of x-rays taken due to the excessive swelling and immobility.  In the x-ray room I had a technician examine a shot and asked me, damn, what did you say you did again?

The x-rays revealed that I had fractured my  left thumb in two places and crushed the bones and all the veins in my right.  I was given three pain killers, two prescriptions, and my  hands were wrapped with a splint all the way past my wrist. I was also instructed to meet with an orthopedic surgeon on Monday January 3rd to see what they thought.   The orthopedist rewrapped my wrists with new splints that now go all the way to my elbow to limit mobility.   I was also given two more prescriptions to assist  with the pain. In addition, I have also had an MRI on my right hand because it is believed that I have severe muscle and tissue damage. 

The results of my MRI  revealed that I had contusions consistent with my pain, tissue and muscle damage.  I have been seen by a different Orthopedic Surgeon as I was displeased with my initial Orthopedist.  My new doctor gave me yet another series of x-rays which revealed that my bones have healed. However, I am still suffering from muscle and tissue damage.  The doctor gave me two new prescriptions for medication and a prescription for occupational therapy three days a week for a month.  I have been attending therapy two days a week and have a received copies of my at home therapy regime.  Over the course of the four weeks that I have been attending these therapy sessions I have received two Edema Compression Gloves to help minimize the swelling, an air cast for my left hand and  Comfort Cool Therapeutic hand splints for both hands.  The air cast was worn 24 hours a days for a week and now is only to be worn at bed.  The hand splints are to be worn during the day.  At my therapy sessions I routinely have my hands cast in Paraffin, use putty, Digi- Flex Hand/ Finger Exercisers, Cando Wed Finger Flexion, Extension, and Wrist Exercisers, and various other exercises. At this point, I still have nerve damage in both thumbs to the point where everything I touch feels like sandpaper.  I still have difficulty extending and straightening both thumbs.

Due to this injury I have had to miss three full weeks of work, which is a bigger deal then just missing out on wages ( I am part-time  and paid hourly  and am not paid for  sick time).  I work at a middle school with autistic children as a support aid.   These children  rely  on my presence to assist them throughout the day.  I help them with taking  notes, homework, exams, and basic social interaction.  Approximately 90% of job is documentation, I also dictate for a few students who struggle with writing. Product Description: Commercial Electric brand Selectable White Tape Light 40 inch Model # LR433-5WX7PIR2-G1-1024
Incident Description:
Im reporting a product that needs to be recalled for fire safety hazard: Commercial Electric brand Selectable White Tape Light 40 inch Model # LR433-5WX7PIR2-G1-1024, (purchased from the Home Depot in Arlington, VA on 11/ 28/25)
On Tuesday 12/2/25 I plugged in the USB charging cable to charge the rechargeable controller. After a few hours, the red charging light indicator turned green, so I unplugged it from the outlet and connected the tape light to the controller. I began pressing the On/Off switch and toggling between the lighting mode and brightness options. I held the tape against the wall of my kids closets to determine what position to mount it. After a few minutes, I turned it off and a few seconds later, turned it back on again, but the lights wouldnt come on. I didnt think it could lose charge so quickly, so I plugged the controller back into the charger and saw the red indicator light came on again. I noticed the controller surface was very hot to the touch. I immediately unplugged it and noticed a bubble forming on the plastic front cover. I ran to put the hot melting controller into our stainless steel kitchen sink and watched it continue to melt a hole into the controller as it began smoldering with a steady stream of smoke and a putrid electrical smell. I took photos and videos, then wore an oven mitt to carry the device outside onto the driveway for fear that it would spark and explode in the house. It smoldered for about 30 minutes longer.
This product MUST be recalled and consumers notified of this serious fire hazard. If I had installed this in my kids closets, the clothing wouldve certainly caught fire and burned our house. It was a very scary experience and I will never purchase another product from Commercial Electric again. 
I plan to return the faulty product and the additional ones I bought, back to the Home Depot for refund and will let them know I filed a report with CPSC, but want to hold onto the burnt unit for whomever might need it for further investigative purposes. I will notify the Commercial Electric manufacturer about this too. 
Please let me know what will be done about this.

We cooked chicken skewers on the new grill unit using a layer of aluminum foil beneath the raw meat, by placing this foil on top of the grill grates, as we had done with our former Jenn-Air indoor grilling unit to avoid flare-ups from dripping fat or marinade.  This time, however, within ten or fifteen minutes, a fire had started inside the grilling cartridge.  We saw flames coming out from the portion of the grill grates that was not covered with aluminum foil.  (Again, this was an electric unit, not a gas unit, so there should have been no flames of any kind.)  There was also smoke with a chemical odor.

When we turned off the grill and removed the chicken skewers and foil, we discovered that the fire had melted the metal grill grates.  We later discovered that these new grill grates were not made of solid metal, but of a sculpted "Excalibur" nonstick material with aluminum rods inside for support.  This Excalibur material appears to have physically melted off the aluminum bars, turning pale gray and ash-like, and slumping into the grill basin, onto the electric heating element.  (Since the different parts of the grill have melted together, and due to the chemical odor, we have not tried to remove the cartridge from the cooktop for closer inspection.  This is my best effort to describe what I have seen.)  There is now a hole several inches wide in the center of the grill grates, where the bars used to be.

In trying to investigate this problem, which we reported to Jenn-Air on the same night it took place, I have discovered that the user manual for a similar Jenn-Air cooktop warns users not to use aluminum foil on the grill grates, apparently due to a fire risk.  Yet there is no such warning in the user manual of the grill cartridge we bought and used.  Furthermore, there is at least one report online by a customer who had an identical meltdown on his indoor Jenn-Air grill with Excalibur grill grates, and he did *not* use aluminum foil; he cooked steaks directly on the grill grates, and the steaks must have covered enough of the grilling surface to cause the rise in temperature, melting the grates.
Answer Explanation: The product remains untouched and unused since the incident.  We have contacted Jenn-Air, but they deny responsibility.

Incident Description:
I purchased two of these cabinets about 4 years ago. I recently placed 2 wine glasses on the top shelf of one of the cabinets and the entire shelf instantly failed in such a way that all of the wine glasses on that shelf (about 13-15 glasses) came crashing out of the cabinet towards me and down onto my floor. Normally, my small child is playing on this floor right where the glass fell, but luckily was not home at the time. The glasses shattered all over my floor, where my dog and I were standing. As this occurred, the edge of the shelf hit the top of my left eye socket and caused bruising and pain to the bone and surrounding tissue for over a week.

Method of shelf failure: The front edge of the shelf dropped past/inside the front 2 shelf supports, much like a trap door would open in a floor, allowing the shelf to fall forward.

I checked all 5 other shelves of these two cabinets and this failure mode does not occur with the other shelves because the shelves are sufficiently deep to ensure they remain on the front shelf supports.

I also noticed that the back of the shelving unit "gives" a little behind where the failing shelf sits. This could compound the problem.

Product Description: Product is a Horizon Fitness model T101-05 exercise treadmill.
Manufacturer / Importer / Private Labele: Johnson Health Tech of North America
Incident Description: This product is a trap hazard for children, especially toddlers or crawling children. When stored in the upright position as advertised and described in the manual, this product is at risk of trapping or otherwise harming a small child. The product is held upright by a single hydrolic piston. When touched, this piston releases and is gravity aided to convert the treadmill belt deck into the downward position for use. There is no locking mechanism to prevent this process and there is no safeguard to stop the descent of the belt deck. If a small child were to go under the belt deck and trigger the piston by simply touching it lightly, the belt deck would descend potentially trapping the child under the full weight of the belt deck (Which takes two people to lift). This could result in harm or even death. This issue may be resolved by employing a single strap around the console and the bottom of the belt deck to hold the belt deck into the upright position and prevent accidental triggering of the piston.

I had it in only for about 5 minutes when the range made a beeping noise. I went in and there was an error code in the display. There was no way for me to turn anything off or stop the "alarm". I immediately looked up the code and it stated it was a "Run Away Temperature" code. I ran and flipped the breaker to turn the oven off. I have gone on-line to see what the problem could be and everyplace I have looked said that the Frigidaire ranges were recalled for this reason except ours. Along with many other people who have not had this problem resolved.

I called yesterday to find out if by the slimmest chance ours was recalled because we can't afford a new range or spend the $500 (is what everyone on-line as said it would cost) to get this repaired. The gentleman who answered to phone said yes, there was a recall...YES!! No, after he transferred me to the Recall Department they informed me that it was not the oven but the cooktop. UGH!!! Oh, and Frigidaire is being so nice and sending me the cooktop replacement part that I don't need at the moment.  The appliance repair company (who Frigidaire referred me to) said that they just had someone else last week with this same problem. Come on Frigidaire...Obviously, the Runaway Temperature is a problem with our model Range as well as the others that it was recalled for. I have 4 young children and really miss cooking in my oven~especially with the holidays coming up!! Thanks.

Incident Description:
An apartment tenant was baking in her kitchen over. After opening the oven door she pulled out bottom rack prior to removing a cookie sheet. While doing this she was wearing a oven mitt made of cotton. This mitt extended two to three inches beyond her finger tips and must have inadvertently contacted the bottom electric heating element inside oven. The bottom element was within 5-inches of the racks front edge.

This contact went un-noticed and tenant re-hung her oven mitt in the pantry closet. Approximately 10-minutes later she was alerted by a smoke alarm sounding and discovered a fire inside the pantry closet.

The subsequent origin and cause investigation determined the first item ignited was the cotton oven mitt. No ignition sources were found inside the pantry closet. Based upon the tenants statement, reenactment and physical evidence remaining this investigator concluded the following:

- The oven mitt came into contact with the hot element inside the electric oven.

- This contact resulted in the ignition of the cotton mitt, just a smoldering ember that went unnoticed by the tenant.

- The smoldering oven mitt was hung in the pantry closet where it fully ignited and ignited other items inside the closet.

- The oven mitt was purchased around Christmas 2011 at an Anthropologie Store. (www.anthropologie.com) and based upon the tenants description was style #21235684.

- The kitchen range was a [REDACTED] electric range, Model # [REDACTED] and s/n [REDACTED].

It is the opinion of this investigator that two design deficiencies interacting resulted in this ignition.

1. The material selection of the oven mitt had no fire resistive qualities and should not have been in use near ignition sources or hot surfaces.

2. The design of the ovens bottom electric heating element extended forward too close to the front edge of the bottom oven rack and did not have adequate clearance for a hand to grasp the bottom rack to pull it forward.

One leaf clung to the louver and clearing it was with the swiping action of the free hand. The sharp edge of the louver sliced the tip of the thumb and the hook of the formed end of the louver gouged the end of the laceration with an avulsion. The maintenance was among the items the installation instructions state may be performed by the homeowner. The instructions, Lennox 506945-01, 7/2018, Homeowners Information cautions only to turn off the electrical power at disconnect before attempting to perform any service or maintenance. The maintenance operation followed the cautionary statement  electrical power was not involved.

2.	If that cant be done, protect against them.

In the case of the discharge air louver, there are 100 six-inch long metal fins projecting their sharp edges upward in a 20-inch diameter circular array (see revised attachment Lennox 13ACX Air Conditioner Discharge Air Louver Sharp Metal Edges Revision A). 600 inches is 300 times the 2-inch test sample described in UL 1439.       c. Hazard communication is to inform and remind those who install, operate, and maintain the air conditioner about potential hazards and how to avoid them. Operation and maintenance manuals communicate hazards with signal words such as Danger or Warning. Labels are part of a system of such communication, providing visual alert. 4. General

Sling had 2 silver rings and a padded shoulder.  The 2 silver rings are to help tighten and loosen the sling.  Sling was to sit on the shoulder and tuck underneath the arm. Fabric Care: Wash Cold, Hang dry.  With the sizes that I listed above.  No instructions nor warnings on both the packaging or on the sling itself.

I was able to look down and see his face.  During about a 4 hour time frame, I fed him, changed his diaper, family and some friends held him and went to some local stores.  However, as I was online at a local chain restaurant, I looked down and he was pale.  I immediately rushed him to the nearest ER where they ran all types of tests. He was in the hospital for 30 days due to lack of controlled body temperature but wasn't able to suck and placed him on seizure medication.  

My son is currently 3 years old and has been diagnosed with Cerebral Palsy.  He is not able to sit on his own, stand on his own, crawl, walk or talk.  He is receiving Physical Therapy, Occupational Therapy and Speech Therapy.  He is currently being seen by a neurologist, orthopedist as well as additional specialists.  

I hope that The Rosado Sling will not be used since it was a tragic incident that has caused my son's current injuries.

Incident Description:
I am writing to report a safety concern regarding the Hitachi G12SS 4-1/2 In. Angle Grinder.   

After sustaining a deep-cut on my right knuckle of my index finger using this machine (required stiches), I examined my actions and other contributing factors that led to this incident.  I believe that several of the items I identified were directly attributed to the tools design.  These items are listed below with a description:

1) Switch Position:   

The switch is positioned on top of the tool and all the way forward on the tools barrel.  The barrel is used as a handle to grip the tool.  The location of the switch, and its use by the thumb to operate, places the index fingers knuckle forward on the underside of the barrel in a bent position and directly adjacent to the horizontal blade which is located on the underside side. 
When switch is operated by the thumb, it is pushed forward.  The index finger is intended to be protected by the shroud on blade, provided that it is rotated in a position to do so.  If not, when the machine is turned on, it can jerk slightly, thus causing the blade to touch the knuckle on the index finger.  
I have another model of Hitachi angle grinder and have used other manufactures angle grinders.  the others, as well as many I have looked at, all position the switch elsewhere.

2) Barrel Shoulder:

The tool has a very short "shoulder" on the plastic housing near where the switch is located.  The shoulder is not sufficient to keep the operators fingers from being forward near the blade.  
3) Shroud Position:

There are no "stops" to keep the shroud from being rotated in a manner to allow the blade to be exposed to the operators lower index fingers knuckle.  

In addition, I will add that injured me instantly when I first turned on the machine.  This occurred while I had the shroud off.  I did not recognize that an action of gripping the tool in a normal position and turning it on would directly expose the index fingers knuckle to the blade.  I have also found that the shroud must be in specific position so as not to expose the finger.  Note, when holding the tool, the finger is on the underside and out of normal view.

Recently when I used this tool, I again found the design to be very concerning in regards to safety and am thus looking to dispose ot it, even though it has been only used a few times.   This use, and the fact that this tool and its design is still for sale, prompted me to submit this complaint.

Sincerely, [REDACTED]

Product Description: Halo SleepSack Swaddle - Newborn Size - Cream Color- Zip up SleepSack with removable Swaddle
Retailer: Given as a gift from Cox Hospital
Incident Description:
We have been using the Newborn Halo SleepSack Swaddle for our 11 lb daughter (size Newborn listed as 6-12lbs) since we brought her home from the hospital in August. This item is a zip up "sack" that has fabric that attaches in the back via velcro patches that you swaddle around the baby. The purpose of having the removable fabric is to be able to use the sleepsack from the newborn swaddling stage and then transitioning into just the sleepsack.
This morning I woke up horrified when I opened my eyes and saw my baby in the bassinet beside the bed with the removable piece of fabric around her neck and over her mouth and nose. She had wiggled enough to get her hands out and the velcro in the back apparently came lose and allowed the fabric to cover slip up around her neck and over her face. I immediately yanked the fabric off her face and was so relieved to see that she was safe. Once I knew she was safe, I took a quick picture of the fabric around her neck (but I had removed from her face) before picking her up because I knew immediately that I had to share this information to hopefully prevent what could be a fatal accident for another family. 
We are extremely cautions when it comes to our infant's sleeping specifics. She sleeps in a bassinet next to our bed. There is NEVER anything else in the bassinet and she is always zipped into a sleepsack. She is always swaddled in this sleepsack or the fleece version if it's colder. We always swaddle snuggly as recoomended and make sure she is using the correct item for her age/size. We have done everything right. We took every step possible to make sure she has a safe sleeping environment and this is something that should not EVER happen. It's apparent that we swaddled the sack correctly, because the front velcro never broke open. If it would have been a looser swaddle, then  the velcro would have become detached and not wrapped around her neck and covered her face. This item needs to be pulled from the market and replaced with a sleepsack that does NOT have a removable swaddle piece. I know the company is trying to market the item as "versatile" and appealing to the consumer by saying that it will transition with your baby. But it's not safe.

We bought our Samsung WA456DRHDSU/AA washing machine in December of 2012.  At first it ran so smoothly.
But then over time, It started to shake a little and make a worrisome banging sound during the spin cycle.  At first, it would shake and bang and then that noise would go away as the spin cycle continued. From about 2014 to 2016, we had no idea that we were putting ourselves, our children and grandchildren in danger, but we suspected that what the machine was doing wasn't a good thing.  In the summer of 2016, the machine started shaking and banging much louder and lasted a whole lot longer.  I would be afraid to go check it in case it was about to explode or something.  In September of 2016 it started shaking and banging so bad that an error message appeared on the machine and the machine shut down.   
We were not aware of a recall at that time, and therefore called an appliance repair company to check out what was wrong with our machine.  We were told it was the "shocks" and had those repaired at a cost of $250 to us.

Even though our machine has run better since that costly repair, we don't dare place heavier items in there or fill the machine more than halfway full.  This is unacceptable. We should be able to wash clothes, bedding, towels, etc as we have done for years and years.  Without worry.  We have always just placed things that needed washing in our old washing machines and washed them and didn't worry that the machine was going to go out of control.  Seems technology has made us go backwards, instead of forward.

Product Type: Washing Machines, Other or Not Specified (140)
Incident Description: I own Samsung Washing Machine Model WA422PRHDWR/AA purchased 3/5/2013.  On 6/14/2014 it experienced a sudden failure of an assembly associated with the drain pump.  On this model and several other Samsungs from the 2012 and 2013 time frame the drain pump was attached to the drum in a plastic housing.  It appears this was a serious design flaw since the plastic housing is subject to intense stress and failure is inevitable.  Samsung came to recognize the flaw in early 2013 and relocated the drain pump assembly to the frame both in newer models and as a retrofit to the original design.  In my case the pump broke loose in the final 3 minutes of the final spin so only a gallon or so of water spilled out.  I have read other accounts of similar failures earlier on the wash or rinse cycle that resulted in enough water spillage to cause damage to flooring, walls and fixtures in excess of $17000.  I believe the failure mode of this flawed design is dangerous to consumers.   Water and electricity don't mix, and when the pump breaks loose water in the drum goes in many unsafe directions, both within the washing machine and within the consumers laundry room.  In addition to reports of damage to property there was at least one consumer who found subsequent black mold after making repairs.  I feel lucky I had no water damage, but I'm sure there is significant danger associated with this flawed design which will fail suddenly and catastrophically.  Samsung issued 2 Service Bulletins soon after the flaw was recognized by them.  Those Service Bulletins (Number ASC20130509001 and ASC20130222001) are now very difficult to find on the internet, presumably because the risk managers at Samsung want to hide any smoking guns.  I know CPSC's primary interest is consumer safety, and at first blush this flawed and defective design often will only result in inconvenience and cost to the consumer like it did in my case.  When my pump broke there was no injury and loss of life.  However, I believe with the suddenness of these failures and the mixing of water and electrical and electronic components it is inevitable there eventually will be reports of death or injury if there haven't been already.  I ask that you look into this and note the many similar accounts to mine that can be found on the internet.  I ask that you make Samsung come clean about this dangerous problem and protect the public by performing a recall to safely retrofit the flawed design.

Incident Description:
User was cutting grass on an established lawn with the push power mower. Without notice the mower suddenly made a several loud noises as if it had struck a foreign object on the ground. Before shutting down, it appeared to eject an unknown object from beneath the mower, but nothing was immediately found. The female operator did observe blade damage as well as a damaged component in the blade area that had contacted the blade, but did not understand exactly what or how it had occurred. The mower was parked until I came to inspect it several days later.
Upon inspection I discovered that the mower was designed to allow the lower handle section to extend through holes in the deck. The lower handle bracket assembly is made of a composite material rather than metal. The adjusting/retaining wingnut appears to thread into the composite material rather than metal. In this case, the right wingnut had backed out which allowed the lower handle assemly to slide directly into the blade path. Correspondingly approx. 3 inches of the lower  tubelor handle section had been cut off and ejected. A search later located the part across the street in another yard where it came to rest in the driveway next to the foundation. Further inspection indicated the left wingnut would not tighten securely, suggesting the threads into the composite material were compormised. It appears to be a very poor and unsafe design by allowing the handle assembly to extend directly through the deck and into the area of blade operation. THe 3 inch steel projectile could have caused serious injury to operator or to by standers.
Answer Explanation: Contacted Lowe's and Troybilt. Took to specified shop (A-Z Rentals) Re: Case #[REDACTED] for repair/modify to prevent more failures. Lowe's still sells same design.

My wife and I purchased a new Samsung Electric Slide-In Range in October 2019.  It has worked fine, but we immediately noticed two (2) problems with this Range (Model No. NE58K9430SS/AA).
1.	The timer alarm is very soft. Unless you are standing very close to the oven you cannot hear the alarm.  If you are in the next room, you will not hear it.
2.	The front mounted knobs are VERY easy to accidentally turn on without knowing.  This has happened to us several times while cleaning up or moving from side-to-side looking for something in the overhead cabinets above or along side of the stove.  Luckily, since we are aware of the problem we watch.  However, we had an incident on February 3, 2020 that was nearly a catastrophic event.
 On February 3, 2020 we had a contractor in our home making revisions to our kitchen overhead lighting.  We had covered the stove top with a heavy towel to protect it from falling debris and paint.  It was about 4:30 PM and my wife and I were leaving for an appointment, leaving the contractor in the house with instructions to lock up when they were done.  Apparently someone bumped the leftmost knob (controls Left Rear Burner), and because the stove top was covered, the red glow of the burner was not visible.  A few minutes later the contractor noticed an odor and noticed the towel was smoking and immediately removed the towel and threw it in the sink and turned on the water.  We were lucky someone was in the house to notice the smoke and extinguish the fire.  Attached is a photo of the burnt towel.
In the aftermath, the burner had a heavy residue on it from the burnt towel material.  I have been able to remove the majority of the residue, but not all.  However the glass top is visibly dulled/scratched where I had rubbed to remove the burnt on residue.  So now I have a NEW range/stove with a scratched top because of your poor design.
THIS IS A SAFETY ISSUE!  I am sending a copy of this complaint to the United States Consumer Product Safety Commission.  Only quick thinking by my Contractor avoided a potentially catastrophic fire event.
I would appreciate a response to this complaint.

I'm reporting a serious safety concern involving a Maxi-Cosi Minla 6-in-1 High Chair (Model HC258HCR, Date Code 2024-01-12 RO-b). The high chair had never been altered or misused. We've only disassembled it a few times for cleaning (around three to five times total) since receiving it as a baby shower gift in May 2024. It was assembled correctly and placed on a flat, even kitchen floor at the time of the incident.

My husband and I were standing about five feet away, reading mail at the counter, when the chair unexpectedly gave way. Our son hit his head and nose as the chair tipped over, though the tray and harness kept him strapped in and prevented a more serious fall. He cried immediately, but thankfully, did not appear to suffer significant injuries. Still, it was terrifying, and it could have easily ended much worse.

After contacting Maxi-Cosis's customer care line on November 4, 2025, I spoke with a representative from their ITA department. She confirmed that this type of hinge or locking failure is rare, apologized sincerely, and offered several options: a replacement chair, a different Maxi-Cosi product, or a full refund. We have chosen to receive a replacement, which is being shipped to us. We will return the defective chair for inspection once it arrives.

I'm filing this report because a product designed for infants should never fail in a way that causes a complete tip or detachment while a child is secured in the seat. Even though our son wasn't seriously hurt, the situation posed a clear and dangerous safety risk that needs to be investigated to prevent it from happening to another family.

Company Comments:
(12/18/2012) Anchor Hocking, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Anchor Hocking to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20121121-8FFCD-2147461740, regarding a 3qt. glass casserole dish, which the consumer identified as being manufactured by Anchor Hocking. The consumer reported that the dish contained a casserole and was placed in the oven at 350° for less than an hour, when the dish shattered. Anchor Hocking is glad to hear that there were no injuries. We note that the consumer indicated that she has contacted Anchor Hocking, but has not produced the dish for inspection.  If she wishes to do so, Anchor Hockings Consumer Affairs Department can be reached at consumer@anchorhocking.com or 1-800-562-7511, ext. 2478.  

Based upon Anchor Hockings review of the proposed records, Anchor Hocking responds as follows:  

I. ANCHOR HOCKINGS CPSA SECTION 6(b) OBJECTIONS AND COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT.

A. Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed 

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim. Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Anchor Hocking products. Without having the opportunity to inspect the baking dish, Anchor Hocking is unable to determine whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Anchor Hocking product. 

In addition, because the dish has not been provided, Anchor Hocking cannot do an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse or other cause of the failure. Without an opportunity to review the facts and products involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.

B. Consumer Misuse

In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are:  hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; or using in a too-hot oven. Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance either supplier or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

C. Tempered Glass Bakeware

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish shattered. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumers report of the product shattering into many pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect.
To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warnings:

Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Tempered soda-lime-silicate is stronger and more durable, breaks into relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards when it does break, and is a more environmentally-friendly product. Tempered or heat-strengthened bakeware is similar, although not identical, to tempering of other glass products where safety is a concern such as automobile windows, sliding glass doors, shower doors, etc. The priority is to eliminate a severe cutting hazard if a break occurs. The alternative form of glass bakeware is made with borosilicate, which is significantly weaker against mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) and when it does break, it breaks into larger pieces of very sharp glass creating a significant risk of severe cuts, punctures, etc. Another failure mode is thermal shock, which results from a significant and immediate temperature change. Consistent scientific testing for decades has established that tempered soda-lime-silicate and borosilicate glass perform, at least, equivalent in thermal shock resistance. Indeed, Anchors testing, when the decision was made to change from borosilicate to tempered soda-lime-silicate in the 1980s, demonstrated a 40% improvement in thermal shock resistance for Anchors tempered soda-lime-silicate glass compared to annealed borosilicate silicate glass bakeware. 

Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals.  Anchor Hocking is proud that it has never had any of its products recalled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

Incident Description:
Dear Consumer Product Safety Commission,

I am writing to formally submit a safety complaint regarding a serious incident involving my Samsung FlexWash washer Serial Number WV60A9900AV/A5, purchased in March 2024. The issue I encountered has raised significant concerns about the safety of this product, posing a potential fire hazard that could endanger lives and property.

On September 20, 2024, my Samsung washer prompted me to perform a self-cleaning cycle. Following this prompt, I left my home for a couple of hours. When I returned, I was shocked to find that my smoke detector and fire alarm were blaring. I rushed to the laundry room to discover thick smoke pouring from the washer, accompanied by a strong burning odor. The machine was unresponsive, and I had to manually unplug it from the back to prevent a potential escalation into a fire.

This incident could have been catastrophic. Had I not returned home in time, the smoke could have turned into a fire, threatening my property and the lives of my family. I live with my wife, who is five months pregnant, and our bedrooms are located directly next to the laundry room. The risk posed by this defective product is unacceptable, and the safety of my home and family was in jeopardy.

After contacting Samsung Care, a technician inspected the washer and confirmed that the computer board was severely burned and charred. Despite the clear defect, my request for a refund or replacement was denied, and I was left with no choice but to accept a repair as my only option. The technician has now been to my home three times, and during the third visit, the replacement computer board they brought was also defective. The machine remains unusable, and I have lost all confidence in its safety.

Samsung has failed to provide any assurance that future repairs will prevent another potentially life-threatening incident. I am extremely frustrated with the companys handling of this situation, as I have been left without a functioning washer and with concerns about the safety of any future repairs.

Given the severity of this fire hazard, I feel that this product presents an ongoing danger to consumers, and I strongly urge the CPSC to investigate this matter. I believe that this washer could pose a serious risk of fire, especially if similar incidents are happening to other consumers who may not be as fortunate as I was in preventing a fire in time.

I also be able to provide the damaged computer board and the defective replacement part if needed . I am available to provide any further information you may need to conduct your investigation. Thank you for your attention to this matter, and I hope this will lead to appropriate action to protect consumers from this dangerous product.

Incident Description:
I turned my oven on 350 to preheat for baking.  Within 3 minutes the lower burner was flaming - flames were 5-6 inches high.  Turned off the oven.  Burner kept flaming.  Had to turn off the power to the range at the breaker.  Burner finally burnt itself out after breaking into multiple pieces. Had I not been standing in the kitchen at the time, this event would have had disastrous consequences. There was nothing in the oven and it was clean. I have had burner elements quit working but have never had one flame the way this one did in over 45 years. 

This range was purchased and installed in February of 2002.  It is a GE Spectra Self-Cleaning Radiant Range, model # JBP67WOD1WW; Serial #DD269836Q.  Online research shows this range has NOT been recalled by GE.  Online research also shows there have been many reports of spontaneous burning of the elements in these models.  I contacted GE about this rather than just replacing the burner myself due to the numerous reports about this model flaming.  They waived the service call charge and sent a technician out.  All he did was replace the burner to the tune of $198.26 - something I could have done for $53.  There were NO diagnostics performed nor was anything else about the range checked. When I asked if he was going to check anything else, the technician's comment was that since the burner turned on properly after he installed it, that meant there was nothing else wrong with the unit. Really?  What a ridiculous statement. Do I trust this stove?  No way.  I will never again leave the kitchen when it is in use for any reason.  It will also be replaced with another model as soon as possible - and it won't be a GE!

This range should have been recalled when these flaming issues first came to light.  At the very least, it needs to be recalled now.  This model is a fire hazard and GE knows it.  That is why they were so quick to respond to my complaint and so quick to waive the 'home call charge' and send a technician.  The fact that all he did was replace the burner at a very high cost to me is a travesty. I had the option to say no when he gave me the cost - however, I thought he was going to really check the range over and make sure there were no electrical shorts or any other problem.  Otherwise I would have said no thanks and gone and bought my replacement burner for $53 and installed it myself.  What a waste. 

Recall these range models before anyone else gets hurt or worse.
Answer Explanation: Mfg. arranged repair at my cost.

My wife was scared to death and shaking when I rushed inside. She was near to the range while incident happened. She had just walked two steps away towards the sink, and thankfully was not scalded by the blast of boiling water and steam that was ejected. The explosion left a black sooty film and spots in a 3' diameter area, all the way to the refrigerator. Thankfully there was only water, and not cooking oil in that pot.The fireball burned a hole in the bottom of the cooking pan too. Also thankfully, the circuit breaker tripped automatically. 

After cooling down, I removed the damaged coil. I also removed the control panel (with the four turn knobs on top) to inspect for further damage. In addition to the blown out area on the heating element/coil, the two wires that run from the control panel knob/switch to the coil had burnt areas on them (one place I could see copper wire poking out).

After cleaning up the mess, I started the circuit breaker again. I saw the burner light does not off even though all the burner switches are off. 
After the incident, I did little on-line research. I was able to find a CPSC report at
http://www.saferproducts.gov/ViewIncident/1201875
That report describes almost exactly what happened to us. Because of the similarity, I did use some of their text as a framework to compose our report here.

I also found CPSC Recall Alert #04-576 at :
http://www.cpsc.gov/cpscpub/prerel/prhtml04/04576.html?omni_key=Ranges_and_Wall_Ovens_Recall
Our model number JP6510C1AD and S/N ML737797 are not listed in the recall notice.

GE Consumer Relations Case# [REDACTED]) . The technician looked at the coil, wires and damaged pot. He told us that it is normal for burners to fail in this way. Honestly, I've known of coils/elements/burners failing over the years, but they normally just stop working, not explode without any warning whatsoever (and damage the control switches in the stove too). He mentioned something about repairs and I told him he was only here to inspect per GE's request, and not repair (at our cost for parts and labor). When I prompted him about the burner light that does not off even though all the burner switches are off, he mentioned something about a short in one of the switches.

Today we received an email from [REDACTED] at GE. She wanted to know how the how the technician's visit went. We have not responded to her yet, pending filing this report with you first.

In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are:  hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; or using in a too-hot oven. Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance either supplier or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

C.	Tempered Glass Bakeware

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish exploded into many small pieces. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumers report of the product shattering into many pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warnings:

Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals. After pre-heating the oven to 350 degrees for a few minutes, I put a pan of potatoes on the bottom shelf of my oven, then five minutes later put a pan of covered chicken cutlets onto the top shelf.  I set a timer for exactly 20 minutes and it beeped as I was emerging from the shower, luckily I covered up with a robe and slippers. I

I went into the kitchen to investigate and saw that the oven door was partially open and I was standing in shards of broken glass, some were imbedded into the soles of my slippers. I turned off the oven and looked inside, the glass pan that contained the
chicken had exploded into many pieces, glass was everywhere, in the food, all over the oven, in the broiler and scattered around the stove. I called my guests to let them know what had happened and that I couldn't host as planned.

I wore thick clothes, a rain slicker, goggles and gloves and still cut my thumb trying to remove the glass. Some of the glass is melted into the oven in large chunks and shards of glass are everywhere, I soon realized that the oven was beyond repair.  I saved the glass and took a number of pictures. I have contacted Anchor Hocking, they denied responsibility and informed me that I must turn over the evidence to be investigated them and they will not pay the cost of independent evaluation. (4/28/2011) Anchor Hocking, LLC: Anchor Hockings comments regarding Report No: 20110318-DA844-1172130

The report to the CPSC involved a glass baking dish, manufactured by Anchor Hocking.  The consumer reported that on March 18, 2011, she had been using the dish to bake chicken cutlets in the oven at 350 degrees for 20 minutes, when she opened the oven to uncover the dish, closed the oven, and left the kitchen.  The consumer then heard a loud noise.  When the consumer returned to the kitchen she discovered that the dish had shattered into many pieces inside the oven.  The consumer reported that she cut her thumb when she cleaned up the glass, although the consumer did not indicate that she sought medical treatment.

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect the product at issue in this report.  Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Anchor Hocking products.  Without having the opportunity to inspect the glass baking dish, Anchor Hocking is unable to determine whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Anchor Hocking product.

In addition, because the glass baking dish has not been provided, Anchor Hocking cannot do an inspection as to the cause of the failure.  Without an opportunity to review the facts and products involved in the report, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.  In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide.  Examples of this type of mishandling are: hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; or using in a too-hot oven.  Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance misuse or mishandling caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish exploded into many pieces.  There is an explanation for this method of failure.  Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening.  Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury.  The consumers report of a product shattering into many small pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warning:  Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns.  Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Tempered soda-lime-silicate is stronger and more durable, breaks into relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards when it does break, and is a more environmentally-friendly product.  Tempered or heat-strengthened bakeware is similar, although not identical, to tempering of other glass products where safety is a concern such as automobile windows, sliding glass doors, shower doors, etc.  The priority is to eliminate a severe cutting hazard if a break occurs.  The alternative form of glass bakeware is made with borosilicate, which is significantly weaker against mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) and when it does break, it breaks into larger pieces of very sharp glass creating a significant risk of severe cuts, punctures, etc.  Another failure mode is thermal shock, which results from a significant and immediate temperature change.  Consistent scientific testing for decades has established that tempered soda-lime-silicate and borosilicate glass perform, at least, equivalent in thermal shock resistance.  Indeed, Anchors testing, when the decision was made to change from borosilicate to tempered soda-lime-silicate in the 1980s, demonstrated a 40% improvement in thermal shock resistance for Anchors tempered soda-lime-silicate glass compared to annealed borosilicate silicate glass bakeware.  

Glass bakeware is not without limitations.  While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break.  Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking.  Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin.  Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority.  Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority.  Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals.  

Surprisingly, however, even with the obvious and known limitations that glass can break, the number of injuries associated with the use of glass bakeware is remarkably small.  Approximately 700 million pieces of U.S.-manufactured tempered soda-lime-silicate glass bakeware have been sold in the U.S. in the last 10 years.  Each piece of bakeware is used multiple times per year, yet the National Electronic Injury Surveillance Survey (NEISS), which is used by product safety experts to assess the risk of consumer products, shows that there have been zero to three unsubstantiated claims per year of glass bakeware shattering or exploding.  Glass bakeware is an extraordinarily safe product when used in accordance with safety and usage instructions.

Furthermore, the majority of these integrated lid/blade mechanisms tend to be black in color and camouflage their presence on a counter or inside a dark cabinet.  

I implore the CPSC and manufacturers (e.g. Ninja) to implement simple safeguards to reduce the likelihood of injury. Incident Description:
I, [REDACTED], purchased a pair of Shimano clipless pedal (Model PDM 520), [REDACTED]Mountain Bike Shoes, and cleats (Model SM SH51) that were installed on my mountain bike on 06/29/2019. The retailer who sold the clipless pedal system is Orange Cycle whose address location is [REDACTED]. A team member of Orange Cycle consulted me about the option to buy the clip-less pedal system, but there was no mention of any danger or learning curve that was necessary. 

The team member for Orange Cycle installed the clipless pedal system on my [REDACTED] Mountain Bike, Serial Number: [REDACTED]. The Shimano clipless pedal is designed to be used with a shoe that has a cleat which fits into the pedal. I purchased the compatible bicycle shoes manufactured by [REDACTED] and the cleats were attached to the shoe by the bike mechanic. Shimano, advertised, distributed and sold the pedals and cleats (clip-less pedal system) through a string of distributors. 

I was under the impression the clip-less pedal system was installed on my mountain bike in a proper manner. I was not aware of any product defects or any recalls regarding any of Shimanos products. The bike mechanic for Orange Cycle did not have me ride the bike to check to see if the bolt located on the pedal was too tight. According to a representative of [REDACTED] bike shops have a bike mount that is used to have customers practice safely detaching from the clipless pedals during the purchase process. This technique is used to ensure safety while training to ride on the bike with the clipless pedals. The mechanic can adjust the bolt to either tighten or loosen the mechanism used to remove your foot from the bikes new clip-less pedal system. 

I sincerely regret to inform you that after putting on the mountain bike shoes for the first time which were attached to the clipless pedals,  I sustained an injury to my lumbar area and left leg after falling off my mountain bike hitting a concrete floor. An X-ray was taken and found that I suffered a fractured tailbone. I have been suffering from low back pain, pain in my hips, and radiculopathy in the lower extremities. As a result of these injuries I have had to seek medical care at the [REDACTED]. I have not been able to work and have been suffering from a lot of pain. As part of my treatment I have been receiving physical therapy at [REDACTED] Hospital Outpatient Rehabilitation Center including acupuncture at [REDACTED] to relieve pain in my back and left leg and now right leg. I have not been able to recover and have continued my physical therapy treatment at [REDACTED] Medicine and Rehab Center which began on May 01, 2020.

 The team member for Orange Cycle, failed to properly inform me on how to disengage from the clipless pedals. Furthermore, there was no safety warning labels inside of the product container for the clipless pedals system because the retailer never gave me the box back or any manual that I would have expected on the date of purchase. I searched the Shimano website on October 15, 2019 and noticed there were no product safety labels or instructions on how to safely disengage from a set of clipless pedals. Nor was any mention of a learning curve that was needed to safely detach from the clip-less pedals. 

Shimano had a legal duty to warn its customers of the inherent danger from using clipless pedals. By not providing adequate training, warning labels, and or not properly installing the clipless pedals lead to an injury of my left leg as a result of hitting a concrete floor located in [REDACTED] on 06/30/2019. The proximate cause of my injuries and damages are the result of improper techniques used by Orange Cycle and Shimanos failure to disclose the dangers of riding a bike for the first time with clipless pedals. Those damages include medical bills, out-of-pocket expenses, lost wages, and pain and suffering.

STATEMENT OF FACTS
On Sunday, June 30, 2019 at approximately 5:03 PM. I went for a bike ride and latched on my clipless pedals for the first time and lost my balance landing on my left leg because I did not know nor was instructed on how to properly disengage my shoes from the clipless pedals. Both my shoes were latched on to the clipless pedals. As I got back up from falling, I did not notice anything at the time until I got home and started to feel pain symptoms in my lumbar spine and lower legs. I continued to struggle with pain and contacted my primary care physician about my low back pain and that I was limping as I strike my left foot on the floor causing me to walk with an abnormal walking pattern. There is also pain in my buttocks. I continued to suffer from pain that included the left hip and leg pain that radiated down the legs on August 18, 2019. On September 18, 2019, an X-ray of the sacrum and the coccyx area revealed a fracture that had healed, which was only seen in lateral projection. 

INJURIES AND TREATMENT
I was informed I suffered a tailbone fracture.  I continue to feel pain in the lumbar spine that radiates to my hamstrings, quadriceps, and the lower extremities. I am required to take pain medication that include [REDACTED], [REDACTED] ointment, [REDACTED] cream, [REDACTED] gel, and [REDACTED]. I have been receiving medical care at the [REDACTED] Hospital Outpatient Rehabilitation Center since March 2019 and have continued to receive acupuncture at [REDACTED] since August of 2019. The types of medical treatment are meant to assist me with chronic back pain that radiates to the lower extremities including cervical pain.

At the date of loss my rate of pay was $25.00 per hour. The amount of my lost wages directly attributable to my injuries, treatment, and recovery have not been fully determined. However, an estimate of $51,400 of lost wages have been accounted for since July 01, 2019, to May 14, 2020. 

PAIN AND SUFFERING
The events surrounding my injuries and subsequent treatment and recovery have been physically and psychologically devastating. I never asked for any of this to happen. Your insureds negligence in failing to place sufficient warnings regarding possible injuries from the use of clip-less pedals that were too tightly installed and had no training manual or brochure changed my life.
Before my injuries I lived a full life, free of pain and discomfort. Since my injuries Ive experienced serious pain and discomfort, anxiety, guilt and depression. All these are directly attributable to Shimano and retailer Orlando Cycles negligence.

Without income during the treatment and recovery period I was forced to borrow money from friends and family. This was entirely embarrassing to me. I am requesting your assistance with a  settlement offer of $500,000. Product Description: Bunk Bed that can also be used as two twin beds on the ground.
Incident Description:
Summary: No injury.  Manufacturing error could lead to serious injury.  Two Twin beds that can be mounted as a bunk bed.  Construction error makes it likely that the upper bunk is not secured.

Purchasing Details:
   We purchased a bunk bed from American Furniture Warehouse Firestone store [REDACTED]  on Sunday Nov 11th, 2012.  We picked up the bunk bed on Wednesday Nov 14th, 2012 and assembled it that evening.

Design Details:
   The bunk bed design enables the beds to be used as individual beds, or in a bunk configuration.  To secure the upper bunk, the instructions describe placing a 3 and 9/16" long x 17/32" wide hollow metal pin in a hole pre-drilled at the factory in each corner post of the lower bed and upper beds.  The upper bed is then placed on to the metal pin, securing it against lateral movement and ensuring that some vertical motion will keep the upper bunk on the pin.
   As we prepared to stack the beds, it became readily apparent that the pre-drilled holes did not fit the metal pins.  The pre-dilled holes were a touch over 2 and 1/2" deep and 3/8" wide.
   The width is precisely what is needed for 1" by 3/8" wooden dowels provided with the bed set for other joints.  The 1" dowel can go all the way down into the pre-drilled hole.

Problem with the design:
   As the metal pins do not fit in the pre-drilled holes, most installers would likely place a wooden dowel in to each hole of the lower bunk, and then mount the upper bunk.  However, this course of action would most likely push the wooden dowel in to the lower bunk, leaving the upper bunk susceptible to horizontal shear forces and vertical motion.  In best scenario, only a 1/2" length of the wooden dowel is securing the bunk against vertical motion.  Further, if there is vertical motion, this could move the dowel lower, resulting in no stabilization for horizontal motion.  

Likely outcome:
   If the bunk is not secured properly, the upper bunk could fall off causing serious injury.

Notice:
   We notified American Furtniture Warehouse on Nov 15th.  They offered to send a technician on Nov 20th.  We decided to manufacture our own pins.  I purchased a 4 foot by 3/8" diameter steel dowel, and I cut this in to 5" long segments.  These fit perfectly.  Our bunk bed is now secured.  I am concerned about other units of this product in the warehouse or installed recently as these were not likely secured properly.
Answer Explanation: Bed is intact.  This submission is about a likely problem.  It can be inspected if needed.  I have photos but the upload was not working.

wired model (120v)
Incident Description:
A Nest Protect Smoke + Carbon monoxide detector (the wired version) installed in our home had a false alarm, repeatedly warning of smoke where the was none.  I had to remove the device from the ceiling and remove the batteries from the device to end the alarm messages.

We had bought the device less than three months earlier.  Our home is about six years old, and we have never had another smoke alarm fail in this house.

After this unit failed, I called the manufacturer, which offered to replace the device.  A replacement arrived within a week.

This is the THIRD Nest Protect that has failed in our home, out of a total of six that we installed.  A total of four of the six have now failed.  We are very concerned about the failure rate -- 66% -- especially since the product is a fundamental home safety device.  While Nest has offered to replace each one without cost to us, I no longer trust the product and feel that a replacement of a flawed product is little better than keeping one that has already failed.  In fact, the fourth unit that failed in our home was a replacement for one of the first two that failed.

Of the four failures in our home, two were false alarms, and two were faulty sensors.  I have no doubt that we are far less safe with these units than we were with our old smoke and CO alarms - largely because I feel that I would not wholly trust a true alarm alerting me to a fire.  After the third unit failed, we asked Nest to refund our purchase price for all six devices, and they refused.  After our fourth failure, we asked again and they have promised to refund our money for all six devices.

We will now have to purchase new devices (from a company that is not Nest) to replace each of these.

My concern is that Nest rushed these products to market before the holidays, when they had not yet been fully tested.  If the overall failure rate is even a fraction of what it has been in our home, I feel strongly that these devices need to be recalled until the problems are resolved.

I have filed a separate incident report for each of our four failed devices.  This the fourth of four reports.

There are many reports of similar incidents online -- including many on Nest's own customer forum.
