Incident Description:
My wife noticed that our washing machine had brown and white flakes floating the the wash water and deposited on clothes after cycle was finished. We ran a self-cleaning cycle and the water in the washer had a significant amount of scum floating in the water during this cycle. Knowing that we had mold or mildew in our washer and that we are washing our 8-month old daughter's clothes, we could not use the washer until this is issue was resolved. We have run self-cleaning cycles per the owners manual since we bought this washer, always dry the tub and detergent tray following use and leave the door on the washer open at all times when it is not running. 

A simple online search returns hundreds of results on Samsung's online forum showing that this is a well-known and ongoing problem with certain models of these washing machines. I disassembled the washer by removing the washplate and basket. Removing the drum revealed gray/brown scum lining the inner plastic drum, the base plate of the basket, and the bottom of the washplate. We cleaned all parts with bleach and reassembled. 

After running three self-cleaning cycles, the wash water was still filled with scum. After additional research online I found several accounts that the washplate (Samsung Washer Washplate #SAM-DC97-18154A) may still have mold inside of it. The washplate on these washers is a plastic base with a metal overlay crimped onto the base. There is a small gap between the plastic and metal where water gets trapped and mold forms. Since the metal plate is not removable, there is no easy way for a consumer to clean or maintain the washer effectively. A self-clean cycle will not remove the buildup between these two pieces. 

It appears that the washplate is poorly designed (see attached photos). Simply gluing the two pieces together would eliminate ingress of water. A one piece design could also solve this issue. After removing the basket it also appears that the baseplate of the basket could have been designed to shed water so that another place for mold to grow was eliminated. Samsung has been receiving complaints online about this product for years and it is seems that the typical action is to recommend a service tech visit which is costly and cannot solve the problem in the long-term. 

This is a known problem to consumers and should be known to Samsung by now. It is my opinion that this issue stems from several design flaws that can render the appliance useless and/or unsafe. Many consumers do not have the time or ability to fully disassemble their washer to clean it and may not have the time or money to chase down a solution with Samsung. Consumers should not have to pay for costly repairs or do it themselves based on a poorly designed product.

Product name: OSI QUAD Advanced Sealant        
Manufacturer: Henkel Corporation/OSI      
Product Type: Solvent-based construction sealant/caulk         
Color Used: White, most commonly, sold in many colors

Packaging: Individually packaged plastic cartridges, compatible with standard caulk guns, labeling indicates "QUAD Advanced", "All Weather", "for Exterior use" and "For Professional Use Only"

Incident Description:
1. Introduction and Summary of Safety Concern
This complaint concerns the improper indoor application and misleading marketing of OSI QUAD
Advanced, a solvent-based construction sealant manufactured by Henkel and distributed through
major retailers including Lowe's, [REDACTED]. The product was applied inside my
home during a Lowe's window installation project, despite being intended solely for exterior use. The
chemical exposure required subsequent product removal. Manufacturer documentation and
misleading retail advertisements present a serious risk to consumer safety, especially when
installations occur indoors.
2. Background and Incident Summary
In 2022, I hired Lowe's to perform a full window replacement at my residence. The installation was
subcontracted to a third party, and solvent-based OSI QUAD Advanced was used to fill large interior
gaps around 24 windows without my knowledge or consent. I later learned that Lowe's
subcontractor had reportedly used this sealant indoors on every window installation he performed
for the company. This was confirmed to me in a phone call with Lowe's Installation Support. Shortly
after the installation, I contacted the manufacturer, Henkel, regarding the strong odor in my home.
Henkel later confirmed in writing that OSI QUAD Advanced is not approved for interior use and must
be fully removed if applied indoors, as covering it with other sealants will not mitigate the chemical
exposure.
Lowe's initially denied responsibility but eventually removed most of the product after inspection.
Nearly two years later, I discovered that multiple retailers had advertised the product as suitable for
both "interior and exterior windows"-a claim directly contradicted by the manufacturer's safety
guidance. Lowe's later admitted this in writing and quietly revised its website.
3. Timeline of Events
- August-November 2022: Lowe's subcontractor applied OSI QUAD Advanced indoors on 24
windows.
- January 3-10, 2023: Improper use confirmed by Lowe's during inspection and documented by a
representative.
- January 19-20, 2023: Lowe's representative personally removed most of the interior sealant.
- April 17, 2025: I alerted Lowe's to misleading online advertising of the product.
- May 5, 2025: Lowe's responded in writing, confirmed the sealant was not for interior use, and
blamed the subcontractor.
- May 2-6, 2025: Lowe's revised its website to remove misleading "interior/exterior" usage claims.
4. Safety Issues
According to the Henkel-issued Safety Data Sheet (SDS) for OSI QUAD Advanced, the product
contains hazardous volatile organic compounds (VOCs) not suitable for interior application. Lowe's
application of the sealant indoors, without consent or warning, introduced unsafe chemical
exposure. I experienced headaches and dizziness following the installation and have preexisting
autoimmune conditions affecting red blood cell production, which may heighten my sensitivity to
such exposures.
Moreover, the sealant was applied in thick layers across wide 1"+ interior gaps in 24 windows,
significantly increasing the volume of chemical material present indoors. No interior-safe alternative
was offered. Despite Henkel's SDS clearly stating the product is intended for exterior use only,
multiple retailers marketed it as appropriate for "interior/exterior windows," potentially misleading
both consumers and installers.
5. Manufacturer Responsibility and Retail Advertising
Henkel's product labeling and SDS documentation directly contradict the advertising language used
on multiple retailer websites. The manufacturer failed to promptly correct this misinformation or
prevent mass distribution of the sealant under misleading use cases. Henkel's emails to me confirm
that the sealant is not approved for indoor use and that complete removal is necessary if used
improperly.
6. Shared Accountability
Lowe's approved the materials list for this installation and created the scope of work. Their
subcontractor's repeated use of OSI QUAD indoors-including in my home-was confirmed by Lowe's
own customer service personnel. Henkel manufactured the product and failed to correct years-long
retailer misstatements. National retailers advertised it falsely. These actions jointly enabled
widespread indoor misuse.
7. Public Risk and Exposure
The false advertising of OSI QUAD Advanced as suitable for "interior/exterior windows" persisted for
years and remains live on retailer websites like [REDACTED]. This occurred during a
time when millions of Americans were spending extended time indoors due to COVID-19 lockdowns
and holidays. Many families may have been unknowingly exposed to VOCs and solvent emissions
in enclosed spaces, particularly if installers followed similar practices.
8. Relief Requested from the CPSC
I respectfully request that the Consumer Product Safety Commission:
- A. Investigate the chemical safety of OSI QUAD Advanced, particularly when used indoors.
- B. Review Henkel's product labeling and oversight of retailer advertising to determine whether
corrections or recalls are necessary.
- C. Identify the extent of public exposure caused by widespread indoor misuse.
- D. Mandate revised labeling, safety alerts, and retailer disclosures for any remaining inventory.
- E. Issue guidance for contractors and installers regarding proper product use and safer
alternatives.
9. Supporting Evidence and Documentation
I am prepared to submit the following materials upon request:
- Manufacturer emails confirming indoor use is prohibited and requires full removal.
- Archived screenshots of misleading retailer listings.
- Email admissions from Lowe's acknowledging misuse.
- Photos showing installation damage and improperly applied OSI QUAD.
- Timeline and inspection summaries documenting the issue and its correction.

Incident Description:
We blended cooked food and water in the "baby bullet" food processor. While feeding our 13-month old son, we noticed he was having difficulty chewing. He finally let us look into his mouth and we noticed a piece of rubber that was approximately an inch long. (It was the gasket to the food processor that sits at the base below the threading where the cup screws into the blade.) We matched that piece with the remaining gasket that had broken and found that there is still a one-inch piece missing. The remaining gasket was still firmly seated in the bottom of the base. We believe the missing piece was swallowed by our child. Fortunately, he did not choke on it necessitating an ambulance to help in a lethal situation. Our pediatrician indicated that since this material is plastic, it will not appear on an x-ray. We can only watch our son and wait to see if he has any side effects or if the piece will pass through his intestines. 

Before using the processor, I had removed the gasket to clean it since food was trapped underneath it. Replacement gaskets were included with the box. Again to reiiterate, I firmly inserted the gasket back into the bottom after washing it. 

The "baby bullet user manual and cookbook" indicates to inspect the gasket before using. It does not instruct on whether or not the gasket needs to be replaced at set intervals nor does it give instructions on how to replace it. This would be helpful information since food does get trapped below it regularly causing bacteria to build if not removed and washed.

This product needs to be taken out of distribution immediately. This information needs to be reported to the news agencies.

Please respond to us as soon as possible.

Thanks

circuitry of the power strip. No injuries were reported. Property damage to the power
strip and carpeting was reported.

The product appears to have been manufactured by T&B. T&B manufactured
and sold multiple outlet centers and surge suppressors under the Electric brand name until
September 28, 1995. At that time, this business was divested to Intelectron.

The photograph of the disassembled unit confirms a mechanical connection
(screws) between the casing components. That type of design had not been used since in
or about 1990. This particular surge suppressor was at least twenty (20) years old.

appears that the unit witnessed an electrical surge. In a product twenty plus years of age,
it would be surprising if any electrical surge protection capabilities remain available.
Quite amazingly, this particular surge protector, despite its age, nonetheless stopped the
electrical surge for the consumer. The electrical surge appears to have been well in
excess of the product's rating with the surge suppressor consuming itself rather than
allowing the surge to pass on to connected equipment.

There is no evidence of product defect.

Incident Description:
Smelled electrical burning coming from the area around our Bosch dishwasher. Looked in the cabinet adjacent to it to try and locate the source. Located Bosch Junction box for the dishwasher. That is where the smell was coming from. The wires going into the box were black from heat and had soot on them. Called Bosch. They told us to call Service Care and they would pay for the diagnostic charge. Service care came out and opened the box. It was badly burned inside. Could have caught our house on fire. Service care said it would be an additional 251.00 to repair and Bosch would not pay it that we would have to. Sent email to Bosch with a picture of the box. Bosch said it was due to a faulty installation. Called Sears where we bought the unit and paid for them to install it. They sent the installer out who had done the installation.
He said the following in writing:
Upon inspection I found a burnt connection where the common wire connects inside the junction box. When I removed the wires on the factory installed side of the box the metal connector block for the hot wire was loose and slid out of the plastic block. When I disconnected the wires from the house side they were all tight. There was obviously a breach of the plastic between the hot and common wire inside the block where the connection was made. this could only be a fault of the factory or parts from the factory. The photos taken show the faulty connection between the hot and common connection block that happened over a period of time. A hole was burned between the hot and common wire in the plastic wall inside the connection block. It was the result of the metal block that connects the hot wire not being secure in the plastic block.

I sent this information to Bosch as well. To date I have not received a response from them. My wife called them on August 9th. They said it was a faulty installation by the installation person. There are many instances of this same thing happening to others. We are still trying to pursue this with Bosch and Sears (installer).

Company Comments:
(9/30/2013) Anchor Hocking, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Anchor Hocking to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20130923-080DC-2147451625, regarding a 9 x 13 glass pan, which the consumer identified as being manufactured by Anchor Hocking and sold by Wal-Mart.  The consumer reports the glass dish from Anchor blew up all over my son and table and the floor.  She further reports that the shards were not hot or warm to the touch.  Anchor Hocking is glad to hear no one was injured.  Anchor Hocking notes that the consumer has not contacted Anchor Hocking or submitted the dish for inspection to date, but has indicated she intends to do so.  If the consumer wishes to do so, Anchor Hockings Consumer Affairs Department can be reached at consumer@anchorhocking.com or 1-800-562-7511 ext. 2478.  

Based upon Anchor Hockings review of the proposed records, Anchor Hocking responds as follows:  

I. ANCHOR HOCKINGS CPSA SECTION 6(b) OBJECTIONS AND COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT.

A.	Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed 

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim.  Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Anchor Hocking products. Without having the opportunity to inspect the dish, Anchor Hocking is unable to identify whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Anchor Hocking product. 

In addition, because the dish was not provided, Anchor Hocking cannot perform an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse, or other cause of failure.  Without an opportunity to review the product involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.

B.	Consumer Misuse

In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide.  Examples of this type of mishandling are:  hitting a hard surface, causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using the dish on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; or adding liquid to a hot dish. In this case, the dish was place on top of another dish, which can cause impact damage to a glass dish, resulting in breakage.  Anchor Hocking urges its consumers to carefully read and follow all of its care and use instructions.

C.	Tempered Glass Bakeware

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish exploded. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumers report of the product shattering into many pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warnings:

Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Tempered soda-lime-silicate is stronger and more durable, breaks into relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards when it does break, and is a more environmentally-friendly product. Tempered or heat-strengthened bakeware is similar, although not identical, to tempering of other glass products where safety is a concern such as automobile windows, sliding glass doors, shower doors, etc. The priority is to eliminate a severe cutting hazard if a break occurs. The alternative form of glass bakeware is made with borosilicate, which is significantly weaker against mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) and when it does break, it breaks into larger pieces of very sharp glass creating a significant risk of severe cuts, punctures, etc. Another failure mode is thermal shock, which results from a significant and immediate temperature change. Consistent scientific testing for decades has established that tempered soda-lime-silicate and borosilicate glass perform, at least, equivalent in thermal shock resistance. Indeed, Anchors testing, when the decision was made to change from borosilicate to tempered soda-lime-silicate in the 1980s, demonstrated a 40% improvement in thermal shock resistance for Anchors tempered soda-lime-silicate glass compared to annealed borosilicate silicate glass bakeware. 

Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals.  Anchor Hocking is proud that it has never had any of its products recalled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

Removing the original cylinder, I noted that it was heavy and should have had plenty of fuel, but I replaced the cylinder anyway.
  The second cylinder did not change the operation of the grill, the flame was still low and not producing much heat.  I knelt down and opened the front cabinet of the grill.  Suspecting a regulator or hose issue at this point I quickly looked at the regulator to see if it was possibly venting fuel, and reached to move the hose that goes from the regulator to the grill to see if it was kinked.   The flames and heat grew inside the compartment and I was hesitant to try to turn off the tank because the tank valve handle was extremely hot at this point.  Expecting that the excess flow valve on the tank would shut off the gas flow if the tank was disconnected, I removed my outer shirt and wrapped it around my hand and arm.  Reaching for the quick connector on the tank, I unscrewed the grill to tank connection, sustaining 2nd degree burns on my right arm.
  At this point the tank valve apparently failed and the tank caught on fire from the unrestricted LP exiting the valve.  Due to extreme heat and flames, and burns I had already sustained, I threw the burning tank off of my deck into the yard.

Also enclosed is my receipt and the product booklet with warranty. Although this item is still under warranty, the terms indicate that Krups would repair or replace the item. Since this item is a huge safety hazard, I am not interested in another one of these.

Defective design, This coffee maker overflows the carafe spilling scalding hot fluid onto the counter or table. For families with small children who reach onto the counter, this is particularly dangerous. From my inspection, it appears that either the plastic lid to the carafe or the cone filter chamber is the culprit. The lid has a small trap door and very small entry holes for the water. I am a foodie and purchase high end appliances, cutlery, kitchen devices and am well versed in how to use them. The cause of the chronic overflow problem is definitely not:

When this second spillover happened, I performed an extra deep vinegar soak and clean of all parts to make sure this would not happen again. It functioned fine for two mornings, then three days later the overflow occurred again. 

(2) The grind or type of coffee. We grind our coffee by hand where it is not too course, not too fine as we have for the past 4 years. We primarily use [REDACTED] Decaf or Breakfast blend. This was the coffee in use during the overflow incidents.

(3) The type of filter. We use the same filters we have always used. Two previous coffeemakers over the years have used the same cone type which we get at the grocery store nearby. I enclosed a few of those so that you can see for yourself
should you decide to test this. 

(4) The centering of the carafe. I have made 100% certain the carafe is centered directly under the cone (in fa~ there is a crevice that guides the carafe to keep it centered) and that the lid is correctly tightened on top with the thumb tab aligned
correctly.

(5) The water level. I have made 100% certain that I only fill the coffee maker up to the 10 cup level.

Incident Description:
My son bought on-line a Dan Wesson replica 6 inch revolver from AirRattle.com. The gun is manufactured by ActionSportGames. The gun is intended to be as lifelike as possible. It is all metal, except for a black plastic handle. We did not authorize this purchase.

When we found the gun, the orange muzzle tip was missing.  We found it in his room, and it seems that it was not permanently attached to the muzzle of the gun, as required by 15 CFR 1150.

This gun is intended by the manufacturer to be very lifelike. In fact, the manufacturer has received a license from Dan Wesson Firearms to replicate the real gun in this BB gun. 

Without this orange tip, it could easily be mistaken for a real gun and result in the accidental shooting of children or others by law enforcement members or armed members of the public who feel threatened by a child with this BB gun.

This product is defective, inherently unsafe, and not in compliance with 15 CFR 1150.

These doors are made to the strict standards of ANSI Z97.1 and CPSC regulations for architectural glass found at 16 CFR part 1201. The tempering process creates stresses on the glass that allow the glass to withstand greater than normal forces on its surface. Tempered glass, although extremely strong, can break if an end or corner is scratched, damaged, or impacted  these types of things can occur when the glass shower door unit is not installed as directed in the instructions provided with the product at the time of sale. It is uncommon for tempered glass to break, but when it happens, the glass does not splinter into jagged shards; rather, it breaks into small granular chunks to minimize risk to nearby people and property.

Product Description: Full sized under cabinet dishwasher.
Incident Description:
The left rail of the dishwasher's upper rack broke as I was sliding the rack our to load additional dishes. This caused the left side to suddenly drop several inches. Had the strain on the remaining right rail caused it to fail simultaneously, the entire rack would have fallen ~3 feet to the floor. Most of the time a top rack's load includes glasses. Had the rack fallen these glasses could have shattered spreading broken glass shards that could easily have injured adults and children in the kitchen. 

Upon inspection of the failed rail it was noted that the rail consisted of two pieces that had been tack welded together. Tack welding destroys the protective coating on the steel. Bare steel is subject to corrosion. These tack welds had then, predictably, rusted and failed. 

The manufacturer initially declined to replace the rail. The dishwasher had been in service for 16 months and exceeded the warranty period. With pushing the manufacturer agreed to pay for the part but not the labor. Additional pushing eventually led to the manufacturer replacing the part and covering labor. 

The concern is that this is an inherently very poor design. This failure so early in the product life would seem to support that notion. This is a part number used across several brands and many models; all ticking time bombs.
Answer Explanation: The manufacturer did replace the part with the same poorly designed and hazardous part.

Product Description: wireless headphones
Product Type: Stereo or Hi-fi Components or Accessories (546)
Incident Description:
Bose QC35 Wireless Headphones radomly turn-on and connect to Cell Phone.  This sounds like a simple technical inconvenience, but it has the effect of silently disabling the audio to/from your cell phone.  When this occurs, you can still initiate a call (e.g. to 911), but then you are unable to hear the dispatcher, and they are unable to hear you.  (Basically, your phone audio is now connected to your QC35 headphones, which may be in a distant room, and you have no idea this is happening.) This is a dangerous defect.
, in that it randomly, but silently, prevents you from completing phone calls, including requests for emergency services (911).  Online forums show that Bose is aware of this issue, and until recently they would replace units with this defect, at the consumers request. There are no longer offering replacements.  But, the random and dangerous nature of this problem warrants a recall.

Report Updated 8/23/24:

This defect allows the QC35 product to silently and randomly disable the audio of a previously-paired cell phone.  If you are a caregiver who relies on a cell phone to reach emergency services (as I am), then you may be unable to communicate with emergency services, yet you will have no idea why.  This can dangerously delay the response time of emergency services, or prevent an emergency response altogether..

Once you are aware of this defect/behavior (which takes some troubleshooting that is beyond the grasp of most users), then you can dispose of the defective device.  But, Bose has made no attempt to notify users of this defect and associated risk.  It seems that it is just a matter of time before a user experiences this outage at a moment when they are engaged in , or attempting to initiate,  a life-or-death call.

Product Description: Redi Shade - Original Pleated Paper Shade
Product Type: Window Shades, Venetian Blinds or Indoor Shutters (638)
Incident Description:
The product is called "Redi Shade - Original Pleated Paper Shade". It is a window shade made from paper, with an adhesive at one end that mounts to the top of the window shade. It comes with 2 clips that hold the pleats together to allow the height of the shade to be adjusted.

The problem is that the ends of the paper shade are razor sharp, and the paper is just sufficiently strong enough that it readily gives deep paper cuts. I got two paper cuts while installing the shades.  Additionally, the act of attaching the two enclosed clips is exactly the action that will most likely give the paper cut. That is because the shade had no external structural support, so it flops down when held in one hand. The other hand is forced to run a finger along the bottom of the shade to collect the pleats together so that the appropriate number of them can be clipped. But running the finger along the bottom of the shade is EXACTLY the action that will cause the paper cut.

One solution is to make the edges of the paper shade less sharp. A second solution is to warn the consumer that the paper edge should be made dull with some sort of instrument. I used a small piece of wood with a notch, and I ran it across the bottom edge 2-3 times to make it dull.

Product Description: Side by Side Refrigerator with bottom freezer and icemaker unit.
Incident Description: We bought a condo which included a Bosch Side by Side, built in refrigerator and ice maker.  The prior owner bought the unit new and never occupied it, so the refrigerator was turned on, but never used in day-to-day service.  The problem I am reporting is that the ceramic water line to the ice maker has disintegrated, causing minute ceramic debris particles to flow into the water that is becoming ice.  The ice is unusable and unsafe.  The line is surrounded by foam insulation from the manufacturer, so it is not accessible and cannot be replaced.  The disintegration of the line is a defect that was not caused by misuse.  There is no access to the line and no situation of operating use of the line that could cause line to fracture and disintegrate the way it did.  The problem was discovered by an independent repair technician.  The problem was masked by other defects in the freezer, which included a disconnected (severed) wire that should have powered a fan in the freezer.  Because the fan did not work, the ice maker never functioned because there is a temperature controller that prevents operation of the ice maker when the ambient temperature in the freezer exceeds a preset temperature.  A BSH approved servicer attempted to repair the fan problem and after several unsuccessful repair attempts, declared the unit to be not serviceable.  I sought a replacement of the refrigerator.  Bosch advised me that the unit was out of warranty, but they would offer me $1,484.85 against the purchase of a new $9,899 replacement unit.  Since the replacement unit cost and installation far exceeds BSH offer, I sought an independent repair.  That repair person was able to fix the wiring issue and restore normal fan function, but then discovered that the ceramic water line was disintegrating and that it could not be replaced and represented a safety hazard as pieces broke off and flowed into the ice.  We have not used the ice and so have not been injured, but anyone with this refrigerator and this problem would not know that foreign bodies are flowing into the ice and so this is a danger to consumers.  I have other Bosch products, and have a Bosch refrigerator in another dwelling, and typically Bosch makes a quality product.  I am confounded by how this issue happened and why this refrigerator presented with problems that neither repair person had seen in their careers.
Company Comments: (12/5/2024) BSH HOME APPLIANCES CORPORATION: BSH Home Appliances Corporation takes product safety issues very seriously. Customers are encouraged to provide additional information about incidents to Customer Service by calling 1-800-944-2904.

Incident Description:
My daughter suffered a deep laceration to her foot after the blade assembly from a Ninja BL660 fell out while pouring. 

We were using the blender for only the second time, and had removed the lid to check the consistency of our smoothie. She has an one inch laceration that required 5 stitches at the ER. The cut was very deep and almost went through the entire foot. 

I feel we were very lucky that she did not suffer a more serious laceration. Given her standing position, the weight, sharpness and fall trajectory of the blade assembly, the injury could have been much worse. She could easily have suffered a laceration to her arm or leg which could have resulted in a laceration to the radial or femoral artery. 

There is a warning on the lid, but it is a small 1 inch square sticker, light grey sticker on dark grey plastic. The lid does lock in place, but I don't think it's unusual to remove the lid from a blender. There should be some form of friction or locking mechanism, the blade assembly should not slip out as easily as it does.

As far as we could determine we did nothing unusual to the door (reports from others were similar) that could have caused the breakage. While Kenmore is the brand we have, other brands were named by internet reports.
Those of us who reported the shattered glass on Kenmore stove oven doors to Sears brought no offer to repair the stove or pay for a replacement part.  Most of the folks (including me) who called Sears got similar responses such as the warranty has run out and our stoves and parts are made by various manufacturers. 
I am not so concerned about the repair cost even though Sears would be better served standing behind their products when a safety issue occurs.  
Someone could really be injured.

Incident Description:

On the first occasion when I needed to change the bulb (very recently, because I used a CFL), I attempted to unscrew the bulb from the socket.  I then found that whatever was supposed to hold the socket in place was not really there.  Thus, when I twisted the bulb, it twisted not just the base of the bulb but the socket it was in and the multi-stranded wires that fed the socket.  The twisting force in the multi-stranded wires leading to the socket caused the weak insulation to strip off.   Some of the now-exposed strands from supply and return lines were then able to arc/short directly.  That part of the unit exploded in a shower of sparks.  Fortunately, an AFCI breaker cut the power on the circuit pretty quickly.  

I also took some close-up photos of where the twisting caused insulation to be removed, the most illustrative of which are attached, or provide the product itself. 

The design and manufacturing of this unit appears to have been very unsafe, with the item posing a serious fire hazard.   This report is not a post-mortem investigation following a serious fire or personal injury/death, but it is easy to see how such an outcome could have resulted, and may be the outcome in other cases (past or future).   I encourage you to take corrective action in order to protect other customers from these negative outcomes.

Product Description: 1 1/2 cu ft black countertop microwave
Incident Description:
This incident occured at my mother's home on December 9th, 2011.  She had a large countertop microwave which sits in a built in wall unit.   I, Her daughter, was visiting her for dinner, we had started cooking and my mother placed a microwaveable baking potato into her microwave.   This potato was purchased at her local grocery, individually wrapped in a plastic for the specific purpose to be placed in a microwave.  My mother placed the potato into the microwave and set the cooking time as indicated on the potato's label.  
After a short time I, her daughter, smelled an odor, thinking it was just the odor of the plastic baking in the microwave.  A few more minutes went by when I glanced over to the microwave I noticed smoke lifting off of the top of the microwave which had a strong electrical odor.  The microwave outside walls were too hot to touch and at that time I pulled the plug from the wall, noticing that the plug and the wall were not hot, which indicated to me there was not a problem with the outlet or cord.
I needed to get this microwave out of the house.  Since the microwave was too hot to touch I ran to the basement to get something to cover it with, I found a blanket.  I covered the microwave with the blanket and carried it to the garage to get the strong odors out of the house.  In thinking again I needed to get this out of the house completely and asked my mother to open the garage door.  As she was doing that she is telling me she sees fire inside the microwave as I was holding it.  I carried it outside and placed it in the her gravel driveway.  The moment I set it down and removed the blanket the microwave burst into flames.  Once I realized it was faraway from the house and posed no problem to the house or us we returned to the kitchen to find a small fire burning into the shelf.  That was easily put out with a wet dish cloth, but it did burn down about 1/4 inch into the shelf.  
I then took a pitcher of water outside and slowly doused the flames.  The microwave was left outside and is still outside.
Evaluating the situation it scared both of us.  If I a 60 year old healthy daughter had not been there and this happened when my 83 year old mother was alone she would have a terrible incident on her hands and had her home on fire.  This microwave was too heavy for her to move.

Yesterday morning upon entering daughter's room, I asked why it was so cold. She responded by using her remote at her bedside to initiate DeLonghi Heater, purchased last fall at a local retailer.
The unit turned on with fan and heat. I commented to her that her mouth did not appear as swollen as she'd just had braces applied 2 days before, a rather unpleasent experiance. We then both exclaimed,"What's that SMELL!?"!  Because the heater had just been turned on, I turned to look down and saw smoke billowing out  from the bottom rear left of the unit and less smoke wafting out the top of the unit, the whole time the unit continued operating as if all systems were "go". I quickly unplugged the unit and we both left the room to be able to breathe. It was that kind of toxic stench that was billowing into my daughter's room from this "Delonghi SAFEHEAT" heater.
It was that unavoidable memory of sheer anguish, of their limp, lifeless bodies in my arms, that motivates me almost exactly 35 years later, to put my many other priorities aside (and 2 weeks before Xmas, there's plenty I need to be doing, believe me). 
For it maybe, that some good can come from the horrible death my kittens must have experianced so many years ago. I know how blessed I am to still have my child, braces and all, here with me today. Over the course of the weeks since this purchase, I have noticed the odor of paint thinner in my basement whenever I went near the area where this paint thinner is stored. I have repetitively sniffed around my basement to determine the source of this odor as I am worried about causing explosive fumes to build up in my basement. I have an opened and partially used container of the same product as well as this new unopened container.

Each time I would notice the odor I would sniff for the source. But it was not the previously opened container of paint thinner that was emitting the odor each time I but the new unopened container. I even tried placing the new container of paint thinner in a different part of my basement and each time I find the odor of paint thinner is strongest next to the unopend container of paint thinner.  I have this container of paint thinner now sitting on my desk at my computer as I write this report to you. When I put my nose next to the container I can distinctly notice the outside of the container smells of paint thinner. Yet the container of paint thinner still has its intact seal under the cap.

Also, the plastic container has started to collapse inward as if some of the product has been removed and the container was squeezed to let the air out and then resealed again. But I assure you this container has never been opened. Any loss of liquid contents of this container must have occurred as a result of the out-gassing of the product through the walls of the plastic container after the container was filled and sealed at the factory. I would guess the perhaps about a half of cup of paint thinner has out-gassed so far from this sealed one gallon container of paint thinner judging from how much the container walls are sucked in.

I have also recently visited the same Menard's store where I purchased this product, and when I have gone by the paint department shelves containing this same product, I can also distinctly notice a fairly strong paint thinner odor in that area of the store. I even reported it to the paint department employee and had them come over to notice the odor but they didn't seem very concerned.

I am strongly concerned that the plastic that these containers are made out of is slightly gas permeable. I believe the paint thinner is slowly out-gassing through the walls of the container and evaporating but the air or nitrogen in the air space is not able to get through the container walls. Thus, the container is slowly collapsing inward as the paint thinner out-gasses through the container wall.

I believe that this is a safety hazard and should be investigated. Containers that are made to contain flammable solvents must be made of a plastic that is totally gas impermeable. I worry that millions of gallons of paint thinner are being sold all over the world in containers like this that are not totally impermeable to flammable solvents. Please respond to my concern and address this issue ASAP as I am sure that more of this product is sitting on store shelves all across the US waiting for purchase.  I will keep this container of paint thinner for a few weeks but must eventually return it if you do not contact me. The next time I buy paint thinner, I will purchase it in a tight sealing metal can.

Incident Description:
On November 16, 2016, my client, 15 year-old [REDACTED], invited two friends to his home in [REDACTED].  [REDACTED] wanted to show off his "new sword."  The sword is known as the "Anime Reinos De Rasos Charlotte Cuulhourne Sword."  It measures 41 inches in length, and features a 440 stainless steel blade with a length of 27 inches.  The sword was given to [REDACTED]'s aunt, [REDACTED], at an employee awards banquet in October, 2012.  [REDACTED]'s boss, [REDACTED], purchased approximately 28 units of the sword from a company called Top Swords, LLC, headquartered in Dallas, Georgia.  Having no use for a samurai sword, [REDACTED] gave it to her brother, [REDACTED].  The sword went into storage for approximately four years before resurfacing in the [REDACTED]s' home last fall.

On the day in question, [REDACTED] and his friends took the sword outside and were taking turns attempting to chop plastic water bottles tossed into the air.  [REDACTED] tossed a water bottle for his friend, fifteen year-old, [REDACTED], who took a mighty swing.  As [REDACTED] swung the sword, the blade disengaged from the handle, flew as much as twenty feet through the air, and impaled [REDACTED] through the forehead.  The incident was captured on cell phone video.

[REDACTED] was rushed by EMS to University of Louisville Hospital.  He was diagnosed with a penetrating traumatic brain injury with brain compression, malignant edema, intraventricular hemorrhage, subdural hemorrhage and bilateral anterior cerebral territory infarct.  [REDACTED] was intubated and ventilated, underwent a bicoronal craniectomy, endured placement of an extraventricular drain, received a tracheostomy, had a PEG tube placed, and spent approximately six weeks in a coma before being discharged to a rehabilitation hospital.  He underwent a second surgery yesterday to replace the top of his cranium which had been removed to allow for brain swelling.  [REDACTED]'s medical expenses are now in excess of $1,000,000.00.

Investigation revealed that the sword in question was not a "full tang" sword, i.e., the blade did not extend through the handle, nor was it a "rat tail tang" sword in which the blade extends well into the handle but tapers substantially.  The blade of this particular sword extended only 7 centimeters into the handle of the sword.  Furthermore, the blade was not secured by bolts or rivets running through the handle and the blade, but by what appears to be rubber cement.  The sword was clearly not intended as a battle sword but there is no way for anyone to know that.  There are no warnings on the sword itself.  There are no warnings on the packaging.  There are no warnings on Top Swords, LLC's website.  The sword by design, manufacture, marketing and labeling is inherently dangerous and defective.

Additionally, my investigation has revealed that cheap samurai sword blade disengagements are not unheard of.  The following is a YouTube link to a compilation of videos showing similar sword failures: https://youtu.be/Bh5H2Lw-CPs.   

We are pursuing a product liability claim on [REDACTED]'s behalf but I believe immediate government intervention is necessary to prohibit the importation of swords--and there are many--such as the one that catastrophically injured my minor client.  I am happy to provide additional documentation, photographs, etc. to assist the Consumer Product Safety Commission in any way I can.

[REDACTED]

A 13 year old female decided to wash her PE clothes. She may have had damp hands and grabbed her PE clothes and put them in the washing machine. She then grabbed a Costco Kirkland Signature Ultra Clean Laundry Detergent Pac (LDP) and held it in her hand, while she decided to grab more clothes from the hamper next to the dryer to fill the machine. She put those clothes in the washer and then went to drop the LDP into the machine, however it was stuck to her hand. 

She could not pull her fingers apart, as the plastic coating melted and began to dissolve on her skin. She tried to pull her thumb and index finger apart with a little more force, about 2 feet from her face. All of a sudden, the LDP exploded and burst.

Less than half the detergent from the PAC covered her face, mouth, eyes, hair and clothes. More was found on the door, on the floor, and blue drops of detergent were in the empty laundry basket a couple feet away.

The LDP must have had a lot of pressure to spray that distance and with such force.

She dropped the LDP and ran in the house immediately to the kitchen sink and began to rinse out her mouth and eyes. The right eye had the biggest hit.

This is where I found her, frantically rinsing the suds out of her eye, from her hair and mouth.

We rinsed at the sink for a few minutes, as she screamed from the pain.

I called the poison control number on the bottle and then proceeded to get in the shower to keep a slow trickle of water running through her eye.

Poison Control advised me to keep running water through her eye for 10 to 15 minutes. They then told me to have her close her eye for 20 minutes and rest.

We did this, and she was in constant pain, both in the shower and while resting. 

She was able to see out of her eye, although she saw a halo effect, had blurred vision and felt like she was looking through fog.

At 2:44 pm, I placed a call to her pediatrician and left a message for the advice nurse.

At the same time, I called my RN relative and asked her advice. She recommended we go to urgent care right away. 

At 3 pm we were on the road.

At 3:09 pm, As we were driving to urgent care, the advice nurse returned our call and said that we did the right thing and should continue proceeding to urgent care.

3:15 PM  We arrived at Urgent Care in Mountain View  to a packed waiting room

3:17 PM - We were called in for care after a very short wait. We learned that chemical burns to the eye are considered quite dangerous and high on the urgency priority list.

She was seen by several doctors and nurses and the main doctor was in constant communication with an Opthalmologist.  Her eye injury is severe and she has been in constant pain.

Her PH level in her eye was 8.5 and the appropriate level is 7.0.

They tested her eye several times - probably 4-5 times or more.

Her eye was rinsed with saline solution 4 separate times, 3.6 liters total to drop the base level back to normal.

The doctor used a dye test where she dyed both her eyes an orange color and then shined an ultraviolet light on both eyes so that she could see the chemical burn locations. The light showed several significant spots on her right eye, especially on the pupil itself, along the bottom and top right corner.

Her eye pressure tested in a normal range. Her right eye was 13 and her left eye was 16. Normal is 20 or less.

They put a patch on her eye to protect it and to keep her hands away from accidentally scratching her eye.

She is taking pain meds, pain eye drops, antibiotic eye drops, and using natural tears as often as possible to help the eye heal.

At 8 pm, we left urgent care, almost 5 hours after we arrived.

The problem with the laundry [REDACTED] is that the chemicals are super concentrated and do not rinse off the eye very well. This is a huge danger!!

Day 2 - Saw the opthalmologist. The ph level of the eye was high again, signifying that there was still detergent in the eye. The Doctor rinsed her eye again with saline and was able to bring the ph level back down again. She is able to see out of her eye, which is a good sign and there is constant redness which means the eye is fighting to heal itself. Will go back again tomorrow for another check up.

Product Description: Rowenta Clothing Iron
Incident Description:
Text of consumer's letter dated April 15, 2013 to Rowenta USA, with cc to Pennsylvania Bureau of Consumer Protection and Chairman, President and CEO, Kohl's:

I purchased a Rowenta iron at Kohl's Department Store in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania on April 28, 2012 (copy of receipt enclosed). When I was ironing recently, the iron cord shorted at the base of the iron and the electric spark from the iron hit me at the back of my right forearm. This caused a severe burn on my arm (picture of burn and iron enclosed). I immediately disconnected the iron. Then I washed the burn and rinsed it with cold water. The burn continued to sting and itch for several weeks and at times it would start bleeding again. However, this could have been a much more serious injury. I was very fortunate that the electric spark did not hit me in the face or eye; this could have been a very serious tragedy.

On March 23rd, I returned the iron to Kohl's for a full refund (copy of return receipt enclosed). I explained the above to the Kohl's customer service representative, but she made no comment. In the meantime, I've treated the burn daily with an antiseptic liquid until this morning when the scab finally fell off.

I am writing this letter to alert you because obviously this should never have happened. It's obvious that the cord was defective and there is a serious problem with your company's quality control procedures. Otherwise, this iron would not have passed inspection or been sold to an unsuspecting customer. I've bought irons from other companies, i.e., [REDACTED] and [REDACTED], but this never happened with these brands.

I started buying Rowenta irons several years ago after I saw one demonstrated on QVC. I continued to buy them because they produce more steam than other brands and they have vertical steam and burst of steam. For the past several years I've been buying the Rowenta brand at Kohl's; however, it's been my experience that the irons don't even last for a year. Usually, the way I can tell it's time to get a new one is when the iron starts leaking brown water from the vents. This is the first time I've had one that had an electric spark. This is very dangerous!

You need to look into this matter immediately. You need to ensure that Rowenta is producing safe products. This could happen again and the next time, the outcome could be tragic! maybe these irons need to be taken off the market until this problem is resolved. Please let me know what you decide. Thank you. I can be reached at [REDACTED].

I am also sending a copy of this letter plus enclosures to the Consumer Protection Agency. I don't want this--or something worse--to happen to anyone else!

P.S. I called your customer service number (1-800-769-3682) on April 15, 2013 at approximately 11:30 a.m. eastern standard time. I spoke with [REDACTED] and explained the above problem to him. I also asked him to provide me with the name and address of the President of Rowenta so that I could send this letter to him/her. (l could not locate this information on the Internet.) [REDACTED] advised me that he did not have this information. He told me that he would pass the message to you and that you would call me back within 24-48 hours, i.e., April 16-17th. It is now April 21st. You never called back. I can only assume, therefore, that you do not care about the safety of the Rowenta irons. Also, I can only assume that you are not going to provide me with the name and address of your President and, therefore, do not want your President to be made aware of this problem. My only hope is that the Consumer Protection Agency will investigate this matter thoroughly so that no other customer is injured.
(Primary) Victim Severity: Injury, First Aid Received by Non-Medical Professional
Company Comments:
(7/11/2013) Groupe SEB USA: After reviewing the attached April 15, 2013 letter from the consumer regarding a Rowenta Iron purchased at Kohls we wish to note the following:

The consumer did not return the iron to Rowenta for examination, and thus we were unable to examine it to evaluate what occurred or why.  And we have no information regarding the consumers manner of using the iron or storing it.  We note that the insulation on electrical cords, or the metal conductor itself, can become damaged by wear, flexing or age.  As the CPSC staff found years ago, this can occur in the electrical wiring of small appliances that receive lots of hand manipulation in normal use, particularly near the location where the electrical wiring enters the appliance or -- when there is a reinforced section (bend relief) where the cord enters the appliance -- where the electrical wiring enters the bend relief.  The electric cords of products such as irons, hair curlers, and hair dryers occasionally experience such flexure deterioration because of heavy use involving the user repeatedly turning, twisting, and bending them and positioning these products at various angles.  Using and/or wrapping the power cord for storage flexes the power cord at this point and can break or wear the insulation and/or conductor.

Rowenta Irons are listed by Underwriters Laboratories (UL) and incorporate bend relief bushings with sleeves to reduce flexure of the power cords.  UL conducts cycle testing to evaluate the ability of the power cords to withstand flexure.  Notwithstanding this testing, features such as bushings and sleeves only reduce, but do not eliminate, incidents of flexure deterioration.  Given the very large number of irons Rowenta has distributed that are still in service, the number of flexure deteriorations of which it receives notice is extremely small.  

Thus the consumers statement that his iron cord was defective has no basis.

The consumers statement that the irons do not last for a year is either inaccurate or reflects very rough use of the iron or failure to properly handle the iron cords, as Rowenta irons are well-made and typically used by careful consumers for a number of years.

The consumers letter stated that he called Rowenta and we never called back.  That is not accurate.  In fact, Rowenta did call the consumer back, asked that the iron be submitted for evaluation (but the consumer no longer had the iron), and replaced the iron as a matter of courtesy within about two weeks of the consumers call.  The consumer was satisfied with Rowentas response.

I must say that it is beyond our comprehension that GE would put such an item on the market as an acceptable product.

Because of the danger myself and my family were subjected to unnecessarily, I would like to see this product removed from the market, and the GE Reveal bulbs be returned.

Sincerely,

Incident Description:

Initially it appeared as normal steam that emanates from the unit as it dries dishes.  The control panel displayed no indicators normally illuminated.  Without any additional indication, the smoke thickened and filled the kitchen and soon thereafter the entire house filled with smoke.  TR was awakened at 1:18am by LS.  TR manually tripped the circuit breaker at the house's electrical panel, and the smoke slowly halted its escape from the dishwasher.  

The unit was opened on January 25 to determine the source of the smoke before attempting to restart operations.  The control board appears to have burned through its connectors, so no restart was attempted.  The unit is presumed to be non-functional.

Incident Description:
This is for the NordicTrack 50 Lb iSelect Adjustable Dumbbells (Model #: NTSAW23020.0    Serial #: PP830F1000052).  This is a weight-adjustable dumbbell set use for weight exercises, such as arm exercises, chest and back rows, squats, etc.  By turning a knob after the dumbbells are placed on the base, the motorized mechanism is able to add/remove weight plates to the dumbbell, thereby making the weight adjustable.  The key moving part is a sliding lock on the dumbbell that slides in and out.  The farther the lock slides out, the more weight plates it locks onto the dumbbell.  After about two months of usage, the sliding lock started to get misaligned.  After turning the knob to set it to a desired weight, the sliding lock would move to its position, but the misalignment causes the sliding lock to fail to latch onto the last weight plate.  As a result, after picking up the dumbbell, the last weight plate falls off on its own - sometimes immediately, sometimes after I start to use the dumbbells in an exercise.  The weight plates have fallen onto my body, so far with no serious injury (scratches and bruises), but if the dumbbell were to be positioned above my face or head for an exercise and the weight were to fall off, it could easily break a nose, injure an eye, break a jaw or cause a concussion.  The weight plates have also damaged my floor from falling onto the hardwood.  If the weight plate were to fall off while standing upright, it could easily break a toe as well.  Most recently, the entire sliding lock has come loose from the dumbbell and all the weights have fallen off. 

There is a serious product design and/or manufacturing flaw with this product that ICON customer support has so far failed to acknowledge or resolve, despite repeated attempts to get their attention and escalate (case #:[REDACTED]).  If you go to the [REDACTED] product page, you will see numerous reviews that complain of the same type of issue.  I urge you to please investigate this product immediately before more consumers get injured from this product.

Incident Description:
My stove is a JennAir JDR8895AAW, a gas cooktop/dual electric oven.  There is a washer on the cooktop that allows water to drip onto the self-igniter switch for the right rear burner control.

This morning, a small fire started at that switch.  Fortunately, my home circuit breaker shut off the power, and the fire quickly stopped.

Investigating underneath the cooktop, I see that a wire from the ignition harness had somehow broken loose, and had made contact with the cooktop, sparking the fire.

The fire itself was in the plastic that surrounds the gas control knob, scorching and possibly melting part of the control assembly.

I have turned off the gas, and unplugged the appliance.  However, anyone that allows any water onto the cooktop, whether from overflowing cooking or from cleaning the stovetop, will have this same problem.

Incident Description:
I baked granola bars in a Anchor Hocking 8x8 baking pan for 20 minutes at 350.  I preheated the oven and used a timer to stay at 20 minutes.  When I removed the pan from the oven I placed it on a heat pot holder.  About ten minutes later the pan exploded shattering glass over a ten foot area.  I was not in the kitchen when it exploded so no one was injured but would have been if close to the pan when it exploded.

Company Comments:
(1/11/2013) Anchor Hocking, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Anchor Hocking to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20121221-35E06-2147460783, regarding an 8x8 glass baking pan, which the consumer identified as being manufactured by Anchor Hocking.  The consumer reported that he baked granola bars in the baking pan for 20 minutes at 350 degrees.  He then removed the pan and placed it on a heat pot holder and ten minutes later the product shattered.  Anchor Hocking is glad to hear that there were no injuries.  We note that the consumer has not contacted Anchor Hocking or submitted the pan for inspection.  If he wishes to do so, Anchor Hockings Consumer Affairs Department can be reached at consumer@anchorhocking.com or 1-800-562-7511 ext. 2478.  Based upon Anchor Hockings review of the proposed records, Anchor Hocking responds as follows:  

I. ANCHOR HOCKINGS CPSA SECTION 6(b) OBJECTIONS AND COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT.

A.	Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed 

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim.  Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Anchor Hocking products. Without having the opportunity to inspect the pan, Anchor Hocking is unable to identify whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Anchor Hocking product. 

In addition, because the pan was not provided, Anchor Hocking cannot perform an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse, or other cause of failure.  Without an opportunity to review the product involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.

B.	Consumer Misuse

In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are:  hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; or using in a too-hot oven. Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance either supplier or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

C.	Tempered Glass Bakeware

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish shattered. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumers report of the product shattering into many pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warnings:

Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Tempered soda-lime-silicate is stronger and more durable, breaks into relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards when it does break, and is a more environmentally-friendly product. Tempered or heat-strengthened bakeware is similar, although not identical, to tempering of other glass products where safety is a concern such as automobile windows, sliding glass doors, shower doors, etc. The priority is to eliminate a severe cutting hazard if a break occurs. The alternative form of glass bakeware is made with borosilicate, which is significantly weaker against mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) and when it does break, it breaks into larger pieces of very sharp glass creating a significant risk of severe cuts, punctures, etc. Another failure mode is thermal shock, which results from a significant and immediate temperature change. Consistent scientific testing for decades has established that tempered soda-lime-silicate and borosilicate glass perform, at least, equivalent in thermal shock resistance. Indeed, Anchors testing, when the decision was made to change from borosilicate to tempered soda-lime-silicate in the 1980s, demonstrated a 40% improvement in thermal shock resistance for Anchors tempered soda-lime-silicate glass compared to annealed borosilicate silicate glass bakeware. 

Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals.  Anchor Hocking is proud that it has never had any of its products recalled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

Product Description:
The Fisher-Price Linkimals Cool Beats Penguin Baby & Toddler Learning Toy with Music & Lights is an interactive, battery-operated electronic toy marketed for infants 9 months and older.
The toy is shaped like a penguin (approximately 8 inches tall  6 inches wide  4 inches deep) with a hard molded plastic body, a rigid yellow plastic beak, and solid plastic feet that extend outward.
When activated, the toy plays music and flashes LED lights while moving its flippers up and down.  The products design uses heavy, non-compressible plastic with sharp angular edges around the beak and feet  components positioned at head height for a cruising infant.
It is sold as a developmental learning toy that encourages movement, dancing, and motor-skill development.
Product Type: Dolls, Plush Toys, and Action Figures (1394)
Model Name or Number: Linkimals Cool Beats Penguin  Model #: HML42
Incident Description:
On May 9, 2023, my son had just turned ten months old. That same day, while playing in a fully padded, age-appropriate play area under my supervision, he suffered a life-threatening traumatic brain injury caused by the Fisher-Price Linkimals Cool Beats Penguin Baby & Toddler Learning Toy with Music & Lights.

Because of his height and early mobility, traditional pack-and-play yards were unstable. We created a safe, low-to-the-ground play space with extra padding so he could safely practice standing and cruising. The Cool Beats Penguin toy was clearly labeled for ages 9 months and up, giving me every reason to believe it was safe for his developmental stage.

Shortly after returning home from shopping, I placed my son in his play yard with this toy. While cruising and taking steps, he lost his balance and fell onto the toy, striking his head against the toys hard plastic beak or foot. Within seconds, he began convulsing. My ten-month-old baby was having a seizure.

We immediately called 911 and rushed him to the emergency room. After imaging, doctors discovered bleeding in his brain and rushed him into emergency surgery (craniotomy) to relieve pressure and remove the clot. They later confirmed the impact was consistent with blunt-force trauma from a hard object.

This toy is marketed for infants just learning to sit, crawl, and stand  yet its construction includes sharp-angled, rigid plastic components that act like impact weapons in the hands or under the weight of a baby. There were no warnings, disclaimers, or visible cautions alerting parents to the risk of skull injury or blunt-force trauma. The age labeling and marketing gave a false sense of safety that nearly cost my child his life.

Fisher-Price has a long history of product recalls tied to infant injuries and deaths. It is unconscionable that a toy designed for babies would be engineered with hard plastic edges at head level for a cruising infant. This is not an isolated parental oversight  it is a design flaw that violates basic safety expectations for toys marketed to infants under one year old.

Because of this product, my son endured emergency brain surgery before his first birthday. No family should ever have to live that nightmare. I am submitting this report to request a full safety investigation into the Fisher-Price Linkimals Cool Beats Penguin toy and to urge the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission to assess whether this product meets infant-toy impact-safety standards.

A 10-month-old should not have to survive a craniotomy because of a toy labeled safe for babies.

Product Description: Steamfast steam cleaner
Incident Description:
On Sunday morning April 8, 2012 I was using a Steamfast SF-275 (serial number C2275-247262) canister steam cleaner.  After around 10 minutes of use, the steam started coming out very slowly then stopped.  At this point I was done cleaning so I turned off the unit off. 

I checked for pressure in the unit by squeezing the trigger for the cleaning nozzle.  Nothing came out so I assumed the unit was not under pressure.  I decided to remove the hose and unscrewed the knob attaching the hose to the main unit, suddenly without warning the hose blew off and sprayed steam and hot water on my forearm, wrist and thumb.  

I immediately put my arm under cold running water but every time I removed it from the cold water, the pain was unbearable, so I had to return it to the water.  I got an ice pack wrapped in a towel but the texture of the towel was also very painful on the arm.  I ended up keeping my arm in a bucket of ice water for the entire day until I decided to go to the Palo Alto Medical Center Urgent Care facility.  The doctor dressed the wound with and gave me codeine pain medication.  

Since there is no warning label about removing the hose, I thought there must be a one way valve on the main body of the SF275 to prevent the discharge of steam from the unit when the hose is removed, and because the hose is attached with a simple unsecured knurled knob, it seemed like a user friendly device, not a accident waiting to happen. Even though I was careful in checking for steam pressure by squeezing the trigger for the nozzle I needlessly suffered 1st degree burns on my arm.

If the SF-275 a 2 cent warning label or a $3 check valve on the output port this accident never would have happened.
Answer Explanation: They told me I was at fault.
Company Comments: (11/20/2012) Vornado Air LLC: This is in response to Report #20121030-DEBA1-2147462373.  Vornado Air LLC did have contact with this consumer regarding the SF-275 steam cleaner. We explained to [REDACTED] that as stated in the owners manual:  Allow unit to cool completely (at least 30 minutes).  Remove all accessories from unit.  [REDACTED] indicated in his letter that he waited around 10 minutes, squeezed the trigger of the cleaning nozzle, when nothing came out, he assumed no pressure and removed the hose from the canister.  By doing so, and not the recommended 30 minutes, steam was emitted, which can cause harm.

Haven't used the oven/broiler since.
I have photos of the permanently warped control pad that I can send.  The unit is available for inspection.  Thank God I was home, my wife would not have been able to move the hot stove to un-plug it or shut off the gas.  If we were broiling something that took longer and left the room we could have had a house fire.

Product Description: Riding lawn mower
Product Sub Category: Lawn Mowers, Leaf Blowers and Lawn Vacuums
Incident Description:
The consumer stated that last fall he stored his riding lawn mower, with a full tank of gas. The consumer stated that on 4/16/2012 he went to turn it on and the motor would not move. After several tries the consumer used jumper cables to connect it to the lawn mowers battery, to boost battery power on the lawn mower. 
The consumer stated that while using the jumper cables the wires that connect to the starter of the lawn mowers motor were burning hot and were emitting smoke. The consumer stopped and let the motor cool for approximately 15 minutes. The consumer stated that he tried it again and used the jumper cables to try to turn on the motor. He stated that it would turn but it was still not working properly. After several tries by using the jumper cables the motor started to turn over.  After a few more tries it started to run.  However at a low speed and running real rough.  It emitted a big cloud of smoke. 

The consumer stated that the motor was running and emitting smoke. The consumer came out from the shed where he kept the mower because he could not see with all the smoke. The consumer stated that he left the motor running for approximately 5-7 minutes and smoke was coming out of the shed. He stated that after these 5-7 minutes the motor started to function properly and the smoke dissipated rapidly. 

The consumer unhooked the jumper cables of the mower and left the mower running for approximately 3-4 minutes. He stated that he walked back in the shed and he took the mower out and cut the entire yard that approximately took 45 minutes.

The consumer stated that the lawn mower ran out of gas after using the lawn mower. He stated that it is unusual, because it usually does not take that a whole tank. The consumer stated that he went to fill the gas tank, when he opened the hood in the front he realized that there was gas all over the bottom area of the motor and the bottom frame.  The tank holds 1.5 gal.

The consumer stated that he filled the gas tank, turned it on for approximately 1-2 minutes to make sure it was running properly.  The consumer stated that he sprayed off a mixture of soap to the areas that were covered with gasoline and oil. He washed the lawn mower to remove all of the gasoline and oil. 

The consumer let the mower sit for a couple of days and on 05/04/2012 he turned on the lawn mower and the motor would not turn. The consumer stated that he looked inside and the gas tank was down to a quart of gasoline left inside. The consumer stated that the gas tank was leaking and he was unsure from where or where it was going. 

The consumer unscrewed the spark plug and over a quart of gasoline pour over the engine and the ground. The consumer stated that he tried to turn on the engine and it sprayed gas everywhere out of the spark plug hole. 

The consumer stated that after analyzing the lawn mower the consumer realized that gasoline was leaking into the engine. The consumer stated that he unplugged the plug from the oil tank and at least 2 quarts of oil and gas mixture was released into an oil pan that the consumer placed underneath the mower. 

If the spark plug wire was close enough to the lawn mower frame or any metal to cause a spark, it would of cause a massive fire or explosion.
The consumer believes that this matter should be investigated.  The carburetor float valve was stuck "open".
Answer Explanation: The consumer will be contacting the manufacturer to file a complaint.
