Product Description: Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames, a chemical designed to change the color of fire.
Incident Description:
CARY, NCA Cary mom is calling for safer labels, tamper proof packaging and warnings after her son ingested harmful chemicals, mistaking it for candy. 

[REDACTED] rang in the New Year a few hours early on Dec. 31. He and his young cousins celebrated the start of 2023 at the age-appropriate time of 8 p.m. and finished the night with games and prizes. 

We were doing these games and earning prizes and one of our family members bought some [REDACTED], [REDACTED] explained.

The 9-year-old grabbed a packet, but the [REDACTED] werent doing what they normally do. 

I ate it and got no flavor; they are supposed to pop in your mouth. When I didnt get flavor, I just put more in my mouth and thats when it started to burn, he said. 

[REDACTED] mother [REDACTED] noticed her son was in distress and when she took a close look at [REDACTED] candy wrapper, she realized that it wasnt candy at all. 

Instead, [REDACTED] had eaten Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames, a chemical designed to change the color of fire.

The package for Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames is like [REDACTED] in size and shape and the contents inside are similar too. However, instead of sugar Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames is made of dangerous chemicals.  

It contains chloride, polyvinyl and copper, [REDACTED] explained. We called Poison Control, and they immediately called a physician who consulted with toxicology.

[REDACTED] received an urgent call back from the toxicologist telling her to quickly get to the hospital. 

Doctors admitted [REDACTED] to [REDACTED] where he spent the night, after lab results indicated he had been poisoned. 

The liver specific lab results were all elevated, so it showed that there was some toxicity in his body, [REDACTED] said. 

After a night in the hospital, [REDACTED] levels returned to normal, but [REDACTED] was left frustrated and concerned over what she believed was the toxic chemicals kid friendly packaging.

It had a cartoon dragon blowing out flames, its called Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames. There was nothing alarming on the front package that would make a child or even in all fairness an adult say woah what is that. It doesnt need to be alluring to children, [REDACTED] said.

In fact, the adult who accidentally bought the Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames told [REDACTED] that it was in a bin with the [REDACTED] candy at the store, she never realized it was any different.  

According to the Federal Hazardous Substances Act, hazardous household products must have precautionary labeling to help consumers safely store and use products. It must also contain the words danger, caution, or warning, depending on the severity of the product. In addition, it must also include the principal type of hazard the product presents. For example, harmful if swallowed, causes burns, etc.

Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames is sold on [REDACTED]. The package sold there has a harmful if swallowed, label on the front, but [REDACTED] chemical package did not. Only when you flip the package over do you see warnings like caution, irritant and harmful if swallowed. 

The packaging has fooled others before. In 2018, Minnesota Poison Control put out a warning after several kids were sickened by the very same product. [REDACTED] says the time for change is now.

I dont want it to take a child dying from this for something to be done, [REDACTED] said. 

[REDACTED] has reached out to manufacturer of Luckys Mystical Dragon Flames multiple times and has not heard back.

(1/17/2014) Anchor Hocking, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Anchor Hocking to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20140106-734B3-2147448420, regarding a 9 x13 blue glass casserole pan, which the consumer identified as being manufactured by Anchor Hocking. The consumer reported that the baking dish shattered after it was taken out of the oven and placed on a non-heated cooktop. Anchor Hocking is glad to hear that there were no injuries. We note that the consumer has not yet contacted Anchor Hocking or submitted the dish for inspection. If she wishes to do so, Anchor Hockings Consumer Affairs Department can be reached at consumer@anchorhocking.com or 1-800-562-7511 ext. 2478. Based upon Anchor Hockings review of the proposed records, Anchor Hocking responds as follows:  

I. ANCHOR HOCKINGS 16 C.F.R. 1102.12 COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT.

A.	Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed 

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim.  Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Anchor Hocking products. Without having the opportunity to inspect the dish, Anchor Hocking is unable to identify whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Anchor Hocking product. 

In addition, because the dish was not provided, Anchor Hocking cannot perform an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse, or other cause of failure.  Without an opportunity to review the product involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.

B.	Consumer Misuse

In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are:  hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; or using in a too-hot oven. Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance either supplier or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

C.	Tempered Glass Bakeware

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish blew up. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumers report of the product shattering into many pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warnings:

Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Tempered soda-lime-silicate is stronger and more durable, breaks into relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards when it does break, and is a more environmentally-friendly product. Tempered or heat-strengthened bakeware is similar, although not identical, to tempering of other glass products where safety is a concern such as automobile windows, sliding glass doors, shower doors, etc. The priority is to eliminate a severe cutting hazard if a break occurs. The alternative form of glass bakeware is made with borosilicate, which is significantly weaker against mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) and when it does break, it breaks into larger pieces of very sharp glass creating a significant risk of severe cuts, punctures, etc. Another failure mode is thermal shock, which results from a significant and immediate temperature change. Consistent scientific testing for decades has established that tempered soda-lime-silicate and borosilicate glass perform, at least, equivalent in thermal shock resistance. Indeed, Anchors testing, when the decision was made to change from borosilicate to tempered soda-lime-silicate in the 1980s, demonstrated a 40% improvement in thermal shock resistance for Anchors tempered soda-lime-silicate glass compared to annealed borosilicate silicate glass bakeware. 

Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals. Incident Description:
I'd like to share my experience with Rheem/ Raypak pool heaters. I purchased a Rheem 206 heater for my pool on the Thursday before Memorial Day. It was installed exactly as specified, and worked flawlessly until the Saturday before Fathers Day. That day, the pilot had gone out, so I had to relight it, which was nothing to be concerned about. Fathers Day morning, after just just 3 1/2 weeks of use, I awoke to find the heater burned to a crisp! Happy Fathers Day to me!

Following the warranty instructions, I contacted [REDACTED], the local Rheem service rep. Their tech wrote it up as "beyond repair, burned up badly." He disassembled it enough to conclude the pressure switch failed, allowing it to burn after the pump shut down for the night. He contacted the Rheem regional rep by phone (right in front of me), telling him it was a "good install" and an obvious part failure.

Since that time, I have been completely turned down by Corporate and refused warranty service. They questioned every aspect of the process. They wrongly concluded the gas valve was broken during installation, and the unit was tampered with to get it to work the 3 weeks that it did! The corporate warranty person, sitting at a desk in California, disagrees with the field tech here in Michigan, even after the tech explained his 28 years of experience and sent pictures of the undamaged gas valve, (which is about the only part left intact on the whole thing!) 

Given the complete denial of responsibility for the fire hazard, I believe this product should be thoroughly investigated. As a highly trained firefighter and fire investigator, I can assure you that this thermal event did not originate in, or have any involvement with, the gas valve. It was installed in exactly the condition it was sold. From the included pictures, you will see the fire hazard. A report was filed by the Livonia Fire Department on the day of the event. 

I wonder how many other units have caught fire and have not been investigated by a very arrogant corporation.

(3/16/2018) Weil-McLain: NOTE:  Weil-McLain previously responded to CPSC Investigation Report No. [REDACTED] regarding this same incident.  We are providing our response to that Investigation Report in our comments below.  Please note that our comments below reference materials and information provided with the Investigation Report that were not included with this Incident Report.

Consumer initially contacted Weil-McLain on 10/3/2017 seeking replacement of the heat exchanger cover and gasket for a Weil-McLain Ultra-230 boiler that had been installed on 12/11/2009 by the prior owner of the Consumers residence.  Consumer informed Weil-McLain that he was neither the initial retail purchaser of the boiler, nor was Consumer able to provide Weil-McLain with any indication that the subject boiler had been properly maintained by a qualified service technician, the Consumer himself or the prior owner of the boiler.  Among other things, the Limited Warranty applicable to the subject boiler excludes: 

	Products that are no longer owned by the first retail purchaser (Warranty, paragraph 2); and

	Products that fail or malfunction as a result of improper or negligent care or maintenance (Warranty, paragraph 8).    

On 10/03/2017, Weil-McLain denied Consumers warranty claim based upon the information provided by Consumer himself and the above-referenced exclusions in the Limited Warranty (paragraphs 2 and 8).

Routine maintenance specified in the Manual for the subject Ultra-230 boiler would have prevented the condition experienced by this Consumer.    

The Boiler Manual for the subject boiler provides specific instructions for Annual Startup and General Maintenance that was required to be done on the boiler (starting at page 92 of the Manual). The vertical bar to the left of the Column outlining the instructions for the Service Technician contains a legend reading ANNUAL START-UP (See Firstyear special inspection).  The First-Year Special Inspection instructions, which appear on the next page of the Manual (page 93) provide detailed instructions relating specifically to the heat exchanger cover plate and the associated gasket.  This maintenance is to be performed within 12 months of the installation of the boiler.  Thereafter, the same inspection procedure is to be included as part of the routine service done at the annual start up at the beginning of each heating season.  In the event that the heat exchanger needs to be cleaned, page 111 contains additional instructions for the service technician to follow; these instructions also include the removal, inspection and replacement of the heat exchanger cover plate and its associated gasket. 

The foregoing requirement for annual inspections of the cover plate would have prevented the condition experienced by this Consumer.  In this instance, it appears that neither this Consumer nor the prior owner of the residence had arranged for a qualified service technician to annually inspect or service the heat exchanger cover plate or its associated gasket - or the boiler generally.  This permitted the deterioration of the gasket for the heat exchanger cover to deteriorate undetected.  As the deterioration of the gasket continued over the course of years, it eventually allowed hot combustion gas to leak from the inside of the heat exchanger, between the cover plate and the body of the heat exchanger and consume the gasket (which is why the photos show a missing section of the gasket material).  The continued leakage of hot combustion gas due to the gasket failure would also have eventually warped the heat exchanger cover plate as shown in the photos. 

We note that the Consumer reported that he arranged for the local gas utility company to inspect the boiler when the Consumer purchased the residence from the prior owner.  Consumer reports that the gas company inspection occurred on 10/26/2014, and that no issues were noted at that time.  Typically, a gas utility will check for gas leaks, but would most likely not have performed maintenance on the boiler or have removed the heat exchanger cover plate, inspected the cover plate and associated gasket and then replaced them.  Even if the gas company had performed the above procedures, approximately 3 years passed from the October 2014 inspection until the reported incident of October 2017.  During that time, none of the recommended annual inspections and maintenance of the heat exchanger cover plate and associated gasket were performed by a qualified service technician.

Incident Description:
As with other identical stories already summarized on the Consumer Product Safety Commission web page, we purchased a top of the line Tempurpedic Rhapsody Memory Foam King Mattress (approx $3999.00 - tax) and adjustable bases ($2800.00 + tax) plus 69.99 delivery from Mattress Firm.  The mattress felt great at the showroom store (very supportive - no odor), but when the mattress was delivered and removed from the plastic bag, my family's nightmare began.  A very strong chemical odor started filling our bedroom.  Since the store instructed us to expect such an odor (referred to as off gassing and alleged to be non-toxic) and that it would dissipate within 2-3 days, my family stuck it out and lived with the chemical odor for several days.  As instructed by the store, we also walked on the bed daily to progress the off gassing.  During this time, my family all slept in alternative locations (son's room, guest room, gameroom couch) while maintaining an ozone air purification machine, bowls of vinegar, and a window fan in the bedroom as we eventually wanted to enjoy the mattress feel/support we had experienced at the store.  

Fast forward several days, the smell never disappeared (it continued to get worse and spread across the entire house).  My spouse and two young sons as well as myself started having difficulty breathing (we all tasted chemicals on our tongue and could only get relief by remaining outside the home).  After 5 days (having never being able to even tryout the new bed) we paid another $69.99 to have the mattress picked-up and returned to Mattress Firm (thank goodness they had a 100 night money back guarantee).  Once the mattress was removed, we spread baking soda (product which should absorb odors and then be easily vacuumed up) throughout the entire bedroom (carpet, furniture, support bases which couldn't be returned) in an attempt to remove the chemical odor.  However, we were not successful at removing the chemical odor.  

Since the strong chemical odor remained throughout the entire house (now appearing to be a longer term problem and raising questions without answers), I (having a PhD in Chemistry) started researching the off gas odor and discovered the chemicals used to manufacture and fire retard these polyurethane memory foam mattresses (secret formulations due to US patents, etc) are highly reactive, toxic isocyanates, diols, and other reactive chemical compounds, all of which per MSDSs have very low exposure tolerances and create respiratory issues and skin contact problems at very low concentrations.  From what I could locate on the web, I saw no need to contact Tempurpedic as their only response (as expected due to monetary position and size of business) was to provide a generic statement noting they comply with all rules and regs.  I was at this point extremely "[REDACTED]" to say the least since I now had no apparent recourse (just hoping family's health had not been negatively affected due to the short duration).  

Fast forward another week (mattress removed from home for approx. 1 week), the chemical odor still remains throughout our entire home (on the walls, clothing, furniture, etc).  We have had our carpets/curtain/rugs/cloth furniture steam cleaned (another $320.00 out of pocket cost), continue to run the ozone air purification machine, run window fans 24/7, and have changed all HVAC filters in further attempts to remove the chemical odor.  Unfortunately, the chemical odor appears very resistant to removal and continues to remain along with the respiratory health concerns and chemical taste on our tongues.  In addition, we now have purchased a new fully organic/natural mattress and are awaiting its arrival, but are afraid to bring the new mattress into the home concerned that it could pose the same issue and/or absorb the chemical odor prolonging our chemical exposure. 


Please my family asks that the US government or appropriate US agency progress some type of warning or legislation to address this very apparent toxic chemical poisoning problem before it negatively affect any additional tax paying families.

Product Description: Natural Gas powered 40 gallon water heater
Incident Description:
A little over a month ago, the 3 year old water heater in our house started detonating the natural gas that powers it instead of smooth ignitions when the heater would start a cycle to warm up the water.  At it's worst, it was a loud enough detonation that it sounded like somebody slamming a door on the other side of a larger house.

Our plumber came out, serviced the unit and found that the screen that covered the pilot light / burner assembly literally had holes burned through it and indications of hot spots on the assembly.  Presumably these hot spots were causing the detonation when the water heater would first cycle on.  Almost $400 in labor later, a new assembly was installed and the problem was fixed.  A month, almost to the day afterwards, the gas valve freezes in the shut position.

The water heater was a State Water Heaters Co model GS 6 40UOC T G 200

State Water Heaters was only willing to ship out a replacement gas valve via 7 to 10 day delivery ground shipping.  They seemed completely unconcerned about the earlier safety issues with the gas detonation or the inconvenience and expense they caused us in both cases.  We replaced the water heater with a different brand due to our fears for our safety.  That cost us another $920, after our plumber gave us a discount. 

The water heater is a defective product at best and a potentially very dangerous one at worst.  Gas appliances are supposed to have a smooth, even ignition process, not one where the gas initially detonates with a bang when it ignites.  Had those detonations gotten bigger, it could have potentially destroyed our house.  State Water Heater's indifference to whole situation only added insult to injury.
Answer Explanation: Plumber contacted State Water Heaters.  He described them as apathetic regarding the issues

Product Description: 2.5 gallon plastic gas can with spill proof system.  environmentally friendly
Incident Description:
I have always had concern about the design of the spout on this gas can.  Nearly every time I use it I end up with a mess of gas on either the lawn mower or my hands, and based on the reviews I now see on Amazon for this product I am not alone.  It is difficult to use and error prone, which is disturbing considering it is meant to store and use a dangerous chemical like gasoline.

This can appears to be designed for environmental purposes, so that vapors cannot escape.  As such the can is airtight, and seems to have no method of venting other than manually pressing in the spout to open it.  Because of this airtight nature temperature changes can cause a great deal of pressure build up in the can.  I normally vent the can outside in a safe direction, but even so it seems dangerous when sometimes gas can spray out of the can due to the extreme pressure.  On 6/13/15 I did not take this step, and attempted to fill my lawn mower tank using the way provided in the instructions, which is to unlock the spout, set the catch on the lip of the gas fill hole of the mower, and press down.  Because of the pressure the gas came out extremely quickly, instantly overflowing the tank and getting all over the mower.  I set the can back in my garage next to the wall, and proceeded to clean up the mower.  After getting it clean I thought I should release any little bit of remaining pressure in the can by pulling down on the spout to open it up.  I assumed most of the pressure had been released in the first incident.  Unfortunately there was still a lot of pressure in the can, as well as a piece of curved plastic next to my garage wall.  The spray of gasoline from the can hit the plastic and was redirected back into my face.  After washing and flushing my eyes, face, and basically entire head for about 20 minutes I headed to the ER.  They found a 2mm chemical burn in my left eye and two separate 2mm burns in my right eye, and proceeded to further flushed my eyes using saline.

I believe this can should be recalled.  It is unthinkable that such a dangerous and difficult to use product is on the market, not just for me but scores of other people.  I have been using gas cans to fill lawn mowers for over 30 years and have never had any experience like this.  In the best case a person will occasionally get gas on their hands while using this product, which is bad enough.  People in the area of the can are obviously in danger of being sprayed under certain circumstances.  I even have concerns about the can bursting due to the pressure, as I have at times seen it swell considerably on hot days.
Answer Explanation: keeping defectively designed can for proof

Incident Description: I used a diaper out of a new carton of Pampers on my son.  He had no rash at all when I put it on and after being in it for approximately an hour, I changed it because he had a bowel movement (changed it right away after the bm).  He had a diaper rash so bad it looked like a burn, and it took approximately 3-4 days to fully heal.  I noticed when putting on the diaper that I could feel what seemed like the gel crystals in the bottom - something that I had never felt before, but had never had any problems so assumed it was ok.  I normally use  other (cloth) diapers on my son so I stopped using the disposable and returned to cloth.  A couple of weeks later I had run out of cloth diapers again and used another out of the box of diapers.  The exact thing happened again even after no bm and only being on my son for about 45 minutes.  Yet again, I could feel the crystals when I put them on him.  After this second time I realized there was something wrong with the diapers, and saved one so that I could report back to pampers to let them know the issue.  My husband didn't realize that was why I was keeping the diaper, and used it on my son a few days later and the exact thing happened a third time.  We use these diapers as back-up when we need them (or when we run out of cloth diapers) so it isn't like my son hadn't used them before - we used them quite regularly (including this brand) and this is the first time we've ever had something like this happen.  3 severe rashes after using 3 new diapers.   It was clearly the diapers as it only happened (every time) when we used that specific lot.

Incident Description:
Please note this fiasco started 4/21/2017. It has continued all of 2018 and so far, through October 2019. Ridiculous!! I am 82 years old and on a very limited income. I wish for an end to this and I be left with an insert that works properly and that I feel safe using. I am totally upset by the injustice in this matter. Please note the attached ad. It says a NEW insert. I am tired of money expended, the stress and time. As this has continued for 31 now going on 32 months, there has been so many telephone calls, visits, so much time with County not responding to me and not doing a thing, it is impossible to put down all that occurred. At the end of page 2, I am stating why I made the decision to get the insert. 

This program started with a request from Washington County, Oregon to fireplace dealers for low bids. There were 3 bids from Washington County and for some reason one from McMinnville, OR. which is located in Yamhill County. I was told to go to the one in McMinnville, about 35 miles from me. As I cannot look for streets/numbers while driving. I had to obtain a driver - taking off work, I might add. The three Washington County businesses were much closer and I had no problem later getting to them. 

I have added to the comments made on the information sheets I received. I am listing them as to the paragraph they respond to from the first report I received. Both reports tie together. 

Paragraph #1 
I did not use that shelf for any purpose. That comment was just to indicate size of ledge. Picture of ledge and shelf beginning to come out, approximately 1/4 inch here, enclosed. I cannot push it in myself. I am concerned that as it continues out, this hot shelf can fall, bounce off the hearth, land on the wood floor and cause a fire. I hope the picture enclosed will be sufficient as requested -it is from the top showing surround, bottom and top shelf. 

Paragraph #2 
I am concerned that other parts of the insert might be loose now, especially since the 40o+ pound insert had to be shaken when installed as there were problems getting it level. When arranging for the Environ (from McMinnville Hearth & Barbeque) to be removed, I asked a Washington County employee here at that time if it was going to be used again. He said after checking it out, if it seemed all right, yes, it would be. This couldn't be the problem like those inserts I received, could it, especially when I was receiving a free one? 

Paragraph #3 
I did not just believe the first insert (Environ, installed 6/26/17) caused excessive heat - it DID. I know hot when I feel it I have grown up with fireplaces since I was an infant. The heat (02/04/2018) involved the bricks above the insert, back wall in next room as high as I could reach and the same with the side areas. That had never happened in the 25 years of use with the insert I lost. 

Paragraph #4 
I have spoken to a [REDACTED] tech and employees from Washington County constantly throughout this mess. A County employee told me the tech from [REDACTED] said that he had checked with the [REDACTED] manufacturer and this was normal for the upper shelf to come loose. Doesn't make sense. This County employee said she would call the manufacturer and let me know what that person said. That was June 13, 2019 and I have yet to hear from her. This has been how this has progressed. 

Paragraph #5 
Over this time period, there have been 6 County employees to my house, all of them more than once and 4 of them numerous times. All totaled with the two fireplace companies and the County, I have dealt with more than 25 people. It has continued for 31 going on 32 months with no end in sight. I think the County is waiting for me to give up and just accept what I have. So what if I have another, not good, not new, appliance. Or at my age, they may just be waiting for me to die and I refuse to do either one to accommodate Washington County. 

Paragraph #6 
Yes, these inserts use room air to be able to burn. It took the Environ 60 minutes to an hour and a half for the fans to start working and air to be pulled in and hot air out The [REDACTED] takes 45 minutes to an hour to start heating. There is a constant humming, slightly metallic noise all the time until the fire is done, very distracting. The air is cold when pulled in -I have to use a blanket. I was told by the County inspector there was an optional feature. This optional feature was one I would have definitely wanted. It did a bypass within the chimney to bring outside air into the insert. This feature had to be done before the insert was installed as the area was located on the side of the insert. By the time the inspector came, of course, the insert had been hooked up solidly to the chimney liner and to the top chimney coverings. The only option I had was to have the whole setup torn apart; the insert yanked out of my old existing brick/mortar shell. The wood doesn't thoroughly bum, leaves chunks like charcoal, and yes, it is seasoned wood. I have a moisture meter and do sporadic checks on my wood. 

One very crazy thing. The EPA inserts need to have electricity for the fireplace to work. If power goes out, as it can especially in the cold, one's furnace can't be used nor the wood burning insert. No furnace, no wood stove, no heat!!! 

Incident Date: From bottom of first page, information sheets I received 
This has not been one incident Constant calls, written letters, etc., with both the Environ and the [REDACTED]. After being pushed in by a [REDACTED] tech or other employee or County employee, when used after 34 days the shelf slides back out again. Enclosed is a picture taken by a County employee of the shelf beginning to come out. It has been pushed innumerous times by a County or [REDACTED] employee. It comes apart continually with use. 

Incidentally, the Washington County Commissioner for my district never returned calls I made to him for help and I had voted for him. 

MY REASON 
I believe that pollution does come from fireplaces and we all need to do something about climate change. Washington County has been talking for some time about the pollution of wood burning stoves. I contacted Washington County, Oregon for their offer to trade in for a "NEW" wood stove. I knew it would be difficult for me to purchase and have an insert installed. Assuming we would all need to go to EPA certified stoves eventually, when the notices of this program came out, I felt it would be best for me to do it then if I qualified for a free one. 

Did I pay for it? I paid dearly - I had an insert that burned warmly, easily and I felt safe with its use. I should have waited until it was mandatory and then worked out whatever I could do. I have found many other things that I do to help in off-setting pollution. Also, electricity is expensive. I lost an entire winter use of the fireplace with the Environ overheating in early February and not receiving the [REDACTED] until late in December. I had to use my furnace. 

Currently, I have an insert, [REDACTED] that requires the door to be cracked open in order to get air. After it starts, I shut the door, go to another room for very few minutes, come back, the fire is generally out. It uses kindling like mad. Even after the room air starts to be sucked in by electricity, the fire can go out. (Environ did the same) I want an insert that I feel safe when it is going and easy to use. I really want to be able to feel safe. The moving air is cold -I have to use a blanket 

Tonight 10/28/2019 
Started fire 2:30 p.m., now 5:40 p.m. After 3 hours, (with time for fan to start) then door shut, fire cuts out More kindling needed, door has to be cracked again to restart burning. Then with door cracked pitch or something spit out two sparks to the bottom of the door onto the bottom shelf. 

Oregon Bar apparently has set up half hour consultations for $35. One attorney whose name I was given simply said he "couldn't help me. "That was with no consultation. All he did was quote people from computer who were pleased with their inserts. Would the County have listed any who were not pleased? I have never had the chance to tell what happened to my inserts. 

Can you help me, please? I am stymied by the County no matter what? Apparently, there are no senior, especially senior, senior advocates particularly if low income is involved. 
[REDACTED]

Incident Description: I have a Graco Playard model # 9B08CAT manufactured in 2/2010 and in use since 1/2011 (~16 months).  When using the bassinet portion of the playard for my 4 month old son, he began crying like he was hurt.  A different cry than usual.  I went into the bedroom to check on him and pick him up and he was stuck.  I couldn't physically pick him up.  I then realized his head was stuck under the oval wall part of the bassinet and the 4 panel mattress has bunched up (the 4 panels overlapped each by about 1/2 inch - 1 inch) to create a space at the end of the mattress.  He was stuck face down into the nylon bottom of the bassinet with the mattress pinning his head against the wall and the oval wall part above his head pinning it down into the nylon floor beside (not on top of) the mattress.  I pulled the mattress further away from the wall and was able to maneuver his head out to free him.  I am an emergency physician and saw that he was unhurt but also see the potential for this to fatally injure an infant.  I wanted to report this so that if there other similar reports, a safety recall could be issued to prevent future injuries.  I believe the problem is that the fabric of the mattress has stretched a bit over the 16 months of usage and now allows the 4 boards inside the mattress to overlap a bit which creates space at the edges of the bassinet.  Because the bassinet has walls that shape the space into an oval, the oval wall can trap a baby's head.  My mattress also with 16 months of use has bowed a bit also shortening the panels.  I have only used my playard in line with Graco's recommendations.
Answer Explanation: Graco will send me a new mattress to try to fix the problem.

Product Description: The microwave is an over-the-range type manufactured by Frigidaire / Electrolux.  Model Number MWV150KBA / Serial Number KG44215364 / Manufacture Date October 2014.  This unit color is black.
Incident Description:
I am a fire investigator and was called to investigate a past fire incident concerning an over the range microwave appliance.  The occupant had returned home and noticed a burning plastic smell in the apartment.  They then found a small fire in the microwave, which was not in use at the time.  They described that when they opened the door to the microwave, the issue stopped.  When they shut the door, the microwave made a buzzing or humming sound and started burning again.  They opened the door back up to make it stop and then called maintenance.  They later determined that it was electrical arcing/sparking.  They recalled that the microwave had arced in the past as well.  They stated that the microwave was last used by their babysitter to warm up a bottle approximately 20 minutes before they got home and noticed the smell and fire inside the microwave.  

I visited the apartment to investigate the issue on 6/18/24.  I observed soot and heat damage on the glass turntable in the microwave that had caused several sections of turntable to crack and break off.  The plastic roller that the turntable sets upon had an area that had burned away.  There was soot staining on the bottom of the microwave compartment, and minor soot deposits on the back wall of the cooking compartment.  It appeared that the fire occurred between the glass turntable and the bottom of the cooking compartment.  There was no evidence of any food or other materials in the microwave or in the fire debris in the bottom.  The only materials present were parts of the microwave.  I also found the microwave to be relatively clean and without excessive grease or food remnants.  

The occupant plugged the microwave back in and I observed that it appeared fine when the door was open.  When the door was closed, the microwave made a humming sound and then electrical arcing was observed on the bottom of the cooking compartment near one of the glass shards from the damaged turntable.  The microwave was unplugged and there was no further activity.

(6/30/2021) Flex-a-bed, Inc.: [REDACTED] purchased a twin sized adjustable bed from Flex-A-Bed, Inc. in March of 2007. The bed is now 14 years old. Our beds are sold with a limited lifetime warranty. I have attached a copy of the warranty card that was in production at the time that [REDACTED] purchased the bed in 2007. Relating to the motors, the warranty states the following: 
During the first five years after purchase, the complete motor set may be removed and sent to the factory for reconditioning at no charge. During the 6th through the 15th year after purchase, a charge of $40 will be made. After the 15th year, a charge of $100 will be made. An additional charge will be made if the motors have been disassembled. All parts must be shipped to the factory [REDACTED] Prepaid, and after reconditioning, will be returned [REDACTED] collect. 
In an email dated 6/10/21 that [REDACTED] sent to us at [REDACTED], [REDACTED] stated the he purchased a Flex-A-Bed at our store in Lafayette, GA. I did not plug the bed in until 2020 when I developed severe lower back pain. After meeting [REDACTED] to seek advice about which mattress might relieve my back pain, [REDACTED] insisted I try an adjustable bed. I told him I already owned one, so he suggested I start using it. When I plugged in the bed, I quickly realized that the bed would automatically start to run.  
A few questions arise from the statement [REDACTED] made above. 
1. The bed serial number provided ages the bed back to March 2007. Why was the bed not plugged in for initial use until 14 years later in 2021? 
2. How was the bed stored for those 14 years, what kind of environment was it stored in, and what modifications/repairs had been made to the bed by the owner? 
The motor system that was used on the bed with the serial number provided was utilized in Flex-A-Bed production from 1979 until mid-2007. During those 28 years of production, we never had a motor combust or cause any damage to an occupant or their home. The motor systems in question had a built-in thermal protector link that would automatically expand and cut power to the motor when the link reached an internal temperature of 180 degrees. The link would reset when the temperature reached below 180 degrees again. The smell that [REDACTED] described was most likely the paint on the motor casing that had heated close to the 180 degree mark. When the paint reached temperatures near the safety cutoff point, it was very common for the end-user to smell a burning-like odor. It was very rare for our motors to reach temperatures anywhere near the 180 degree mark, but if they did, a safety mechanism was in place that would make the motor inoperable. 
The parts needed to manufacture the motor system on [REDACTED] bed are no longer available from our vendors and has been that way for many years. Therefore, if a customer has a bed with that motor system, it is necessary to either physically bring the motor to our factory for repair or to ship the motor to our factory via [REDACTED]. [REDACTED] claims that he brought the system to our factory for repair. After searching our records, we have no recorded event or paperwork that shows [REDACTED] brought the motor in for repair and we did not charge [REDACTED] any money for services rendered in 2021 which normally would have been done in a case such as this. However, at times if a customer brings a motor in for repair locally we will on occasion fix the motor free of charge and send the customer on their way. This could have been done for [REDACTED] but again there is no record of it nor do any of our employees recall this being done for [REDACTED]. 
[REDACTED] called our factory several times during May and June requesting that the motor be repaired. Our service personnel informed [REDACTED] that we would be happy to repair the motor but that the motor must either be brought to our factory directly or shipped via [REDACTED]. Our warranty does not cover in-home service labor on a bed that is 14 years old. [REDACTED] was unsatisfied with this response and demanded that we dispatch a repairman to his home to retrieve the motor. Our service coordinator said that she would ask our employees in the factory if any of them were able to go to the customers home to retrieve the motor for a fee but none of them were able to do so. [REDACTED] was very upset that we would not pay to send someone to his home to retrieve and repair the motor. Our communication ended at that point in time when he was informed that we will gladly repair the motor but that he would be required to get the motor to our factory. 
[REDACTED] states in the report that he submitted that our factory personnel have told him repeatedly that we know what the problem is. This is not true because we have not possessed and inspected the motor to be able to diagnose the problem. Flex-A-Bed has to be able to physically inspect the motor to diagnose the problem and as of today, June 28, 2021, we have not received the motor from [REDACTED]. 
Flex-A-Bed has been in business since 1969 and we take every customer complaint very seriously especially when a safety issue arises. Every bed that we manufacture is 100% tested on the factory floor by our trained personnel before it is boxed for shipment. Repair motors such as the one [REDACTED] is speaking of, is repaired, inspected and tested to make sure it is operating to our specifications before it is returned to the customer. If [REDACTED] did indeed bring the motor to our factory earlier this year, I assure you it would not be returned to him with the motor running constantly. If for some reason the motor was not running properly, rest assured we would be more than happy to repair the motor again at no charge but that opportunity has not been afforded to us at this point. 
I will be happy to discuss any of our safety and testing procedures along with any further questions concerning [REDACTED] case with anyone from your office. [REDACTED] Thank you for your time and consideration.

Children this young do not understand how to safely use the toy, and it should be rated much higher than 18 months (at least 3 years in my opinion).  I followed the recommended age set by the manufacturer not realizing how dangerous this toy is.  Had I known, I never would have purchased it.  

The police investigated and confiscated the toy.  I no longer have it in my possession.

Brand: RC Series Feed Pumps Model# RC/25-50
Incident Description:
To whom it may concern,

My Company was recently involved in a law suit where a chemical feed pump overfeed liquid chlorine in to a small commercial spa, severely burning (2) people. In researching the failure we became aware that the mechanism on the chemical feed pump responsible for controlling the intermittent pumping feature has a tendency to fail. When the intermittent pumping feature fails on the feed pump the chemical feed pump continues to uncontrollably feed chemical until the reservoir holding the chemical is empty.  We became aware that the failure has occurred more than 50 times in the last ten years.
My Relation To The (Primary) Victim: My Client, Patient, Student, Etc. (professional relationship)
Answer Explanation: Through litigation
Company Comments:
(11/22/2011) ROLA-CHEM: The following is Rola-Chem's response to the complaint submitted to the CPSC.

What actually happened, to cause high-chlorine levels in the impacted spa, remains unclear because the evidence was thrown away by the pool repairman (whose company filed the complaint with your agency).  He reported that he saw the chlorinator - which was supposed to be running in "timer" mode - running in the "on" position.  As a result, the spa contained very high levels of chlorine.
 
No one knows how that happened.  All anyone can do is speculate.   
 
Rola-Chem is a company which highly values our customers.  Our employees immediately respond if they hear about issues with our products. 
 
Before this litigation, no one had ever returned a single chlorinator to our company with a report that it had been set in "timer" mode but failed in the "on" position (which was the allegation in this case) - let alone "fifty" chlorinators (of which the complaining company allegedly "became aware").  

As a result, Rola-Chem never had the opportunity - before this litigation - to examine an allegedly failed chlorinator to determine what may have caused the alleged problem.  Even in this litigated matter, since the repairman tossed the solid-state switch and the potentiometer, which he had replaced, no one on Rola-Chem's behalf ever had a chance to examine them. 
 
It is impossible to conclude why the litigated chlorinator failed.  Perhaps someone accidentally placed it in the "on" position - fully intending to return it to "timer" mode - then got distracted with something else.  Perhaps the chlorinator mysteriously went from "timer" to "on" mode - but if it did, Rola-Chem would need the evidence to understand why that happened.
 
If the "we-became-aware" failures have actually occurred, our company needs the return of those allegedly failed products so that we, together with independent experts, can study the situation.  

If there is an actual problem in the field, Rola-Chem believes that users of our products would return the failed parts to us so they can be examined and corrective action undertaken immediately. 
 
Anecdotal information - such as: "We became aware that the failure has occurred more than 50 times in the last ten years" - is insufficient to determine if there is a problem.  Our company needs physical evidence, not stories, to determine if there really is an issue with our product.    

We need users of the allegedly failed chlorinators to return the solid-state switches and potentiometers (which are made by other companies, not ours) to conclude whether any allegedly failed component parts of a Rola-Chem chlorinator have issues.  If they have issues, they will be immediately assessed and resolved.

Product Description: Shark (Euro-Pro Holdings LLC) Steam Mop Model S3501
Incident Description:
We purchased a Shark Steam Mop (marketed by Euro-Pro Holdings LLC) in maybe May 2010.  This is a household device to mop floors with hot steam.  There is a steam generating component in the midsection of the handle (and a water tank) and the steam is channeled to a flexible mop head that is covered by a cloth pocket.

There is a one year warranty.

The mop stopped providing steam maybe last time my wife used it.  She didn't mention that to me before I used it today.  When I used it, I plugged it in to turn it on and waited for it to start producing steam.  You can lift and depress the upper handle to initiate the further production of steam (sometimes when there is low water or other conditions, steam production can be inhibited so patience is required).  I did this intermittently, not aggressively, for maybe a minute or two.

The unit was quiet however, meaning it was not producing steam.

Then it exploded and shot steam all over the floor in maybe a three foot jet.  The mop head broke from the handle, although the break point was actually a release or latched joint, so the explosion itself did not damage the unit.  You could describe it as the mop head explosively detaching.  I was very surprised, and because of the heat, force, and pressure involved I was glad that I was not manipulating the mop head when it explosively detached because I easily could have been scalded.

After unplugging and inspecting the unit and looking for a clog in the steam channel, I repeated the procedure once again, but without purposefully generating steam (I did not manipulate the handle).   The mop head explosively detached again after a short time (30 seconds?).

I then let the unit cool and disassembled the steam channel, as I assumed it was clogged.  In fact, on inspection, I saw that the upper steam channel (which is in direct proximity to the steam production unit) was designed as being plastic.  Part of the plastic had bubbled up like Styrofoam, and part of it had collapsed and melted.  In other words, instead of using a material that was unlikely to melt for the very hot upper steam channel, the designer of the mop used cheap plastic that melted around the time the warranty expired, collapsed around the small steam channel, and caused the unit to explode (or the mop head to explosively detach) in normal use.

I called Euro-Pro/Shark to talk to them.  A rep said that the model probably was out of warranty (by maybe a month or two) and that warranty service was therefore unavailable.  When I told him that I planned to report this to the consumer protection authorities, he referred me to another number 1-866-694-6406 that he said would generate a callback within 34 hours, and made some reference to burns or personal injuries.  I told him that I was not interested in compensation for personal injury, because luckily I was not injured.

However, this unit is basically a ticking time bomb in my opinion and should be recalled.  The melting of the plastic steam channel is a very predictable mode of failure, and it is outrageous that the most predictable mode of failure will very predictably cause the mop head to explosively detach.

I took pictures of the melted plastic piece (which is very small),  which are attached.  The pictures were taken after the channel was disassembled into basically four parts (two of which were plastic and had melted).  There is another choke point in the steam channel, but it is metal and I assume that it is a valve of some sort.  A picture of that also is attached.  I am holding onto the steam mop in case you want it, but it is extremely hazardous in this condition and will not function as intended. It just explodes.

Please encourage Euro Pro to recall all of their units that have an upper steam channel composed of plastic, as it is unreasonably susceptible of melting and causing a resulting explosion.
Answer Explanation: I believe that in normal operation the plastic steam channel melted, causing the explosion.  Retaining product for a short period of time, which is not being used, in case you want it.

Product Description: Reebok Easytone Walking Shoes
Incident Description:
On March 22, 2011 I went to Footlocker to purchase a new pair of shoes.  I was looking for good walking shoes as I am on my feet all day at work and do a lot of walking.  They recommended Reebok Easytone athletic shoes.  I tried them on and they felt comfortable on the bottom of my feet.  I purchased these shoes and went home.  I read the information supplied in the booklet they included in the box which explained that the toning part was an "instability cushion" located in the bottom of the shoes that would tone portions of the calf, upper thigh, and buttocks muscles.  I wore the shoes at work on 3/23 and 3/24.  At the end of my shift on 3/24 I noticed a lot of pain and swelling in the inside of my left ankle.  I did not wear the shoes again.  On 3/25 I could not put any weight on my left ankle and notified my doctor.  During my visit we xrayed my foot and nothing was broken.  I showed him the shoes I had worn and he stated that due to the constant instability caused by the "instability cushion" I had aggravated the tendon and possibly tore ligaments in my ankle.  I was given inflammatory medication and my ankle is wrapped in an ace bandage.  I am unable to work until this heals which I am told could take up to 4-6 weeks.  

I feel that these Reebok Easytone shoes are unsafe for consumers and should not be sold.  The "instability cushion" causes harm to the ankle just by walking in the shoes.  There is no mention in the booklet included with the shoes about the stress placed on the ankle.  

Please contact me if you have any questions

Subject: Urgent Appeal for Regulatory Action on the Toxicity Hazards of Aerosol Fire Extinguishers
I am writing to you following the recommendation of [REDACTED] at the U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, to bring to your attention a critical and under-recognized issue regarding the toxicity hazards associated with aerosol fire extinguishers. This concern is particularly relevant to devices certified under NFPA 2010 and UL 2775 standards and produced by leading manufacturers such as FirePro and [REDACTED]. Current regulatory frameworks lack adequate safeguards, leaving a significant gap in toxicological oversight that directly endangers public and occupational safety.
Key Concerns
1. Absence of Mandatory Toxicological Testing  
   Current standards, including NFPA 2010 and UL 2775, do not mandate comprehensive toxicological assessments for aerosol fire extinguishers. This regulatory omission has allowed the approval and widespread deployment of devices without evaluation of their potential health hazards during activation.
2. Substituted Test Results  
   Investigations by the UKs Marine Accident Investigation Branch (MIAB) have documented instances where manufacturers submitted substituted toxicological test data to regulatory authorities. This malpractice perpetuates the use of devices that pose severe risks to human health. Refer to MIAB findings [REDACTED].
3. Lethal Hazards in Non-Fire Scenarios  
   Unintentional activation of aerosol fire extinguishers in confined spaces has been shown to release toxic gases at concentrations exceeding permissible exposure limits for carbon monoxide (CO) by up to 331 times. These incidents have caused fatalities due to asphyxiation, underscoring the immediate danger posed by such devices.
4. Increased Toxicity During Fires 
   When activated during fire events, aerosol extinguishers contribute toxic byproducts indistinguishable from standard combustion gases. This complicates investigations and conceals their role in fatalities, as deaths are often attributed solely to fire-related toxicants.
Proposed Actions
1. Mandatory Toxicological Testing  
   Introduce mandatory toxicological evaluations for aerosol extinguishers in both U.S. and international safety standards. These evaluations must establish stringent limits for toxic gas concentrations during and after discharge to ensure user safety.
2. Investigation of Standards Compliance  
   Conduct a thorough review of the testing data submitted by manufacturers for compliance with existing standards. Implement robust enforcement mechanisms to prevent approval of untested or misrepresented products.

3. Comprehensive Analysis of Incident Data  
   Undertake detailed reviews of fire-related fatalities involving aerosol extinguishers to differentiate their toxicological contributions from standard combustion byproducts. This data will be instrumental in addressing regulatory gaps.
Support and Collaboration
I am prepared to provide detailed documentation, including independent toxicological assessments, incident reports, and recommended testing protocols, to support your efforts in addressing this issue. Collaboration on these measures is essential to ensure the safety of individuals in workplaces, residences, and public spaces.
The Consequences of Inaction
Failure to address this critical safety gap will leave thousands of individuals, including sailors, miners, office workers, and passengers, exposed to preventable risks. Addressing this issue now will not only save lives but also enhance the credibility and effectiveness of fire safety regulations worldwide.
I respectfully urge you to prioritize this matter and welcome the opportunity to discuss how we can work together to implement these critical safety measures. Please do not hesitate to contact me to request additional information.

Product Description: Apple iPhone 3GS
Incident Description:
On Saturday, June 27, 2009, I bought a brand new recently released iPhone 3GS. I had
stood in line outside the Santa Monica Apple computer store and got the best one Apple
offered. There was no crowd in the store and I assumed the line outside was a marketing
gimmick. A Mac enthusiast had told me that, Apples sale people are very knowledgeable
and professional and referred them as iGeniuses. After selling me the iPhone, the iGenius
who sold me the iPhone, asked me to open the box and unwrap the iPhone and asked me
to hand him back the iPhone. I asked him why he doesnt open it himself if he wants it
back, is this part of the buying experience? He said yes. He activated the iPhone and gave
it back. I then purchased a holder and placed the iPhone in it. Before leaving he asked me
to give the iPhone back to him again. He took my iPhone out of its case. He put my
iPhone in his own case, put it in his pocket of his sweat pants, looked at it his pocket,
took it out of his pants, took it out of his case, put it back in my case, and then handed me
back the iPhone, all without my consent. I asked, What are you doing, are you trying to
see what it looks like in your pocket? He said yes. I was tempted and should have asked
for another iPhone.

On Sunday, June 28, I called the AT&T operator with my new iPhone to review some of
the fine print of the contract. I was on the iPhone for what I would guess would be over
15 minutes. I was particularly focused on the conversation due to some very strange
terms that Apple included in the fine print. Their bizarre terms included a wait time of up
to two years at Apples discretion for a replacement if I lost or damaged the iPhone, no
possibility to insure the iPhone, and an upgrade fee of up to $700 if I wanted to upgrade
before two years.

While focused on the conversation on the iPhone with the operator, I suddenly realized I
was in intense pain where the iPhone was in contact with my face. I quickly pulled the
iPhone away from my face. I found that the iPhone had gotten so hot that I could not hold
it back close to my face. The right side of my face and the iPhone screen was wet from
sweat where the iPhone had touched. The wet area felt hot, numb and was red. I had to
finish the conversation holding the iPhone several inches from my face. I do not know
what caused the superheating. My initial guesses were defective batteries,
electromagnetic waves (from phone antenna, blue tooth, GPS and WiFi which were all on
at the same time), chemical reaction from chemicals on the phone and my face, and
tampering by the iGenius from when he put my iPhone in his possibly contaminated case
and pocket.

I immediately took the iPhone to the store where the rep said it was probably the battery
and offered me another iPhone. I believe he was aware of the problem. I told him that my
face still felt numb and warm and that I did not want to risk it again. I also stated the
terms were unacceptable due to the terms that stated at Apples discretion, I could wait up
to two years to get a replacement if I lost or damaged the iPhone, and the iPhone was
uninsurable. The iPhone was checked for damage, no damage was found and a refund
was given.

The following day, Monday, June 29, my face still felt warm and numb. Other people
initially pointed out to me that the right side of my face was swollen. A Mac enthusiast
told me there is a lot of information on-line about this problem. I researched the matter
on-line, found that this was not a unique situation, and realized Apple must be aware of
the problem. I called the Apple store manager, [REDACTED] , and told him I
believed the iPhone had injured my face. I do not recall his exact words, but believe he
refereed to my injury as an unpleasant experience. I said to him not unpleasant
experience, your !@#$& iPhone burned my face and if I ever heard a product burned
someone, I would pull it off the shelf and have it checked. However, he stated he had no
authority to do that and only the corporate office could make such a decision. I also
called AT&T and talked to [REDACTED] , who said to go get medical aid.
On Tuesday, June 30, the next morning, I went to my family doctor and uncle ([REDACTED]  
who checked my face and ear. He said I needed to have a Neurologist
and/or Ear Nose and Throat (ENT) specialist look at it. He tried getting an appointment
for me with one of his associates but could not get a timely appointment. He said I should
go to the emergency room now, request to be seen by a Neurologist or ENT, and referred
me to UCLA or Saint Johns in Santa Monica.

That same day, I went to Saint Johns emergency room, told them a doctor sent me there
and asked to see an ENT or Neurologist. Initially, a physicians assistant evaluated me
and said this could be Bells Paulsy or Shingles. I asked her if she had read my file from
admitting. She said she had not because people in admitting have poor handwriting. I said
I was there because I believed my iPhone had overheated and had injured the right side of
my face and ear. I have never had Bells Paulsy or Shingles and the symptoms were local
to where the iPhone had been in contact. She said that iPhones do not get hot enough to
cause this kind of problem. I was kept waiting for 2 more hours. I asked to leave at that
point. A doctor who overheard my request said, I have been overlooking the physicians
assistant that has been treating you and will put in your file that you are leaving without
our consent. I protested and said but I have been sent here by a doctor to be checked by
an ENT or a Neurologist. She looked surprised when I said a doctor had sent me with the
request to see specialists, and then said we do not have any available right now, but we
have to make sure that you have not had a stroke or a brain tumor. I was then given a
CAT scan of my brain, told good news, you do not have a brain tumor or stroke and
sent home with several referrals to ENTs and Neurologists, given a prescription for antiinflammatory
medication and told if my condition worsens come back. I found I had
trouble with my bearings on the way out and continued to have trouble with direction for
two more months after the incident.

I was very upset that evening and made an on-line complaint to the California Attorney
General. A week later, [REDACTED], from the California Department of Justice
responded, saying the US Consumer Product Safety Commission in Washington is in a
much better position to render assistance in this matter.

On Wendsday, July 1, I called the Neurologists and ENTs the emergency room had
referred me to, but could not get an appointment for one or two months with any of them.
The symptoms had gotten worst.

On Thursday, July 2, the right side of my face had swollen more. The swelling had
increased to the area around and including where the iPhone had been in contact with my
face and throat. I called my family doctor again and he said go back to the emergency
room and tell them that my doctor said to ask you to do it right. I went back with my
request. The head nurse reviewed my case. This time an ENT doctor checked the
swelling and ordered x-rays to make sure the swelling was not obstructing my airway.
The doctor said, we could try a few things now, but potential complications are too high
and recommended waiting it out. The head nurse came to me afterwards and said call
back the doctors they had referred me to and tell them that the emergency room physician
had requested you be seen as soon as possible. I was again sent home with a prescription
anti-inflammatory. I called the doctors again and the earliest appointment I could get was
with a Neurologist, Doctor , [REDACTED],  on July 9th. I also got an appointment
with an ENT, Doctor , [REDACTED], on July 17, 2009.
Doctor , [REDACTED],  examined me on Thursday July 9th, and ordered an MRI. The MRI was
done on Sunday, July 12. On July 16, the neurologist called, advised that internally
everything looked okay, and scheduled a follow up.

On July 17, 2009, about 20 days after the incident, the ENT did an evaluation and
scheduled a hearing test and noted that I still had swelling on the right side of my face.
He said we could inject steroids or wait it out. I asked him, if it was possible that my
symptoms were unrelated to the iPhone incident and he said it was unlikely to be caused
by anything else. I chose to wait it out and get healthy as possible. A subsequent test and
evaluation by the ENT, six months later, showed there was no significant hearing change
from the first test, but said it may take a while for the feeling in my face to get back to
normal. He said a year is a relatively short time for this type of injury.
While waiting for my face to heal, I experienced several issues and complications that
required attention related to this matter. , [REDACTED], , DO (Doctor of Osteopathic
Medicine) started treating me on Sept 9, 2009. Various methods were tried including
getting off old meds that I was on for years. At this date, although my secondary
symptoms have gotten better, the primary problem, unusual sensation in my face,
remains.

I shared my iPhone experience with several people. Most Mac lovers were very
disappointed with Apple, some did not believe me, and some attacked my honesty,
intelligence, education, financial stability, and character. For the record, I am a computer
systems developer. I have been self-employed for over twenty years. I am the CEO of
[REDACTED]. I have subcontracted as a systems
developer for Lockheed, Microsoft Consulting Services, and AT&T in the past, and have
personally influenced the decisions of the CEO of Microsoft. At this time I have a perfect
credit score of 990 as reported by three credit reporting agencies. I have a an AA degree
in Chemical Engineering with a pre-med emphasis, a BS in computer Science and an
MBA, and taught computer technology as a college instructor at the age of 24. I
developed and marketed medical imaging systems that communicated diagnosis and
treatment information with digital images over 14 years ago. I have had a Series 7 license
in the past for investment banking purposes. Part of my business now revolves around
integrating the Mac and PC environments using thin clients, virtual machines, and cloud
computing technology. I also develop hybrid telephone call routing and recording
systems that route calls to voice over IP, landlines, cell phones, PCs (Linux & Windows)
and Mac computers. I actively try not to offend Mac users.

Another Mac enthusiast who was very upset about what I had said about the Mac iPhone
tried to discredit me by pointing several people to this article on the Apple support web
site http://support.apple.com/kb/HT2101. This article has had several revisions. The last
revision is dated April 15, 2010. The first time I saw it, there was a photograph showing a
full iPhone screen with Temperture at the top in large letters. Below that, an

Incident Description:
I purchased a Nest Hello video doorbell approximately 3 years ago.

After searching on-line, I found out there is a lithium ion battery in it that is not documented.  It's sealed in to the product with heavy tape, and not able to be inspected.

Google, Nest is one of their product lines, will not repair a Nest doorbell when it is out of warranty.  

Since the product was not repairable by Google, I ordered a new battery from a reputable supplier, and opened the doorbell.   

The battery in it was not only defective, but was swollen, like the ones about to catch fire.   I saved the battery in a safe place (bucket of sand, outside.)  

Not having a way to inspect a potentially hazardous battery either physically, or via software and not notifying customers of this dangerous situation is the core of my complaint.

In the event of a fire, the doorbell is physically attached to the outside of a house, with low voltage wires penetrating the wall to the inside of the building.  This could  lead to an extremely hazardous situation for the customer since smoke detectors would not detect the initial onset of fire.

Customers might also not be able to address this situation because of:

 1: Not being aware there is a dangerous battery in the product.
 2: Not being able to see the problem since the battery is sealed inside the product.
 3: Not being notified via software that there is a problem with the battery.
 4: Google will not repair the Nest Hello doorbell when it is out of warranty.  This refusal to repair it extends to replacing the battery.

I avoided a fire by being proactive and fixing a product that the manufacturer will not support after warranty.  Others might not be so lucky.

Product Description: Chicago 14" Electric Chainsaw Model 67255
Incident Description:
Product: Chicago 14" Electric Chain Saw. Model 67255. Distributed by Harbor Freight Tools

This is the second saw I had. The first I had to exchange. There is a basic design flaw and the company doesn't want to acknowledge it. Thank God I haven't injured myself yet. 
Here is the problem: There is a front handle with guard (good); There is a lockout switch which slides forward. Below there is a trigger switch which slides forward. This combination is unsafe. The trigger switch should slide up or depress. This is the natural motion. When you push down on the front handle to cut, that removes pressure from the power switch and the saw stops as you try to cut. Product Description: Revell light duty aluminum handle knife with blade assortment
Incident Description:
On November 11, 2014, I purchased a Revell light duty aluminum handle knife with blade assortment from Michaels.  Prior to purchasing , I hadnt realized that no sheath was included. I opened the package at my dining table, discovered the missing sheath, turned and walked about 2 feet to my kitchen counter to retrieve an old [REDACTED] knife sheath from my sewing kit. When I went to put the sheath on the Revell knife I discovered the blade was missing. There was a large canvas shopping tote and a backpack hanging from the chair where I opened the package as well as carpet all around. I did an extensive search in a 2 foot radius in which Id opened the package including in the backpack and shopping tote but I couldnt find the blade. I assumed Id tipped the knife over the recycling bin at the corner of the cabinet where my sewing kit resides and the blade had fallen in there. The recycling bin was full so it wasnt feasible or safe to search through it for the blade.  

On December 4, 2014, I took the tote that had been hanging on the dining room chair grocery shopping. While taking the tote downstairs later that evening to put the groceries away, I felt something poking me in the thigh just below my hip. I reached my left hand down to move the bag off my leg thinking Id inadvertently picked up a pine needle. When I pushed the tote off my leg, I immediately felt hotness and dripping from my hand.  Upon inspection there was a 2 inch long gash from base to head across the proximal phalanx of my left middle finger. The gash was deep enough that it necessitated stitches.  Luckily the blade didnt cut deep enough to cut the tendons as it would have severed them since it went from right to left across the proximal phalange which would have necessitated surgery to reattach.  As the incident occurred late at night, I couldnt just visit my doctor or even an Urgent Care for stitches; I had to go to the emergency room.  The bill for that was $1633.27 with an OOP cost of $805.28, though the cost could have been exponentially higher had the blade severed the tendons or hit bone.

I consider it very lucky that the blade didnt present itself earlier in the day while the tote was being loaded with groceries or while my kids helped me bring them in from the car.  While Im not happy I was cut, I am very happy that it was me and not any of the other people who could have been hurt, especially my kids.

Fortunately, I was not looking through the glass door like I was doing just moments ago.  The front glass door blew open and there was smoke throughout the kitchen. There were small pieces of the white insulators in several places in the kitchen, up to about 4 feet away from the toaster oven.

This Black & Decker toaster oven was new and not tampered with or damaged in any way as far as I know.  I have looked on the internet and find at least a few other people who reported the exact same experience (explosion of the heating elements, white powder everywhere) and coincidentally was the same model:  TRO355.

I have had an older but very similar Black & Decker toaster oven that I used without any problems for over 10 years.  But this TRO355 was extremely dangerous and we are lucky that my spouse or I or my children were not injured by this incident.

Incident Description: I purchased a package heat pump unit Model 13HPP42AP-3A on 11/11/14 unit serial number 1614K06686. Unit has been serviced regularly. The control wires for the unit were wired tightly over an exposed metal edge with no stand offs or grommets to prevent wire wear. After 7 years of regular use in a 2-adult household, we have discovered a possible design flaw that allows the lower hinge pin to become unscrewed during normal use, ultimately resulting in the heavy door abruptly falling to the floor.  As a direct consequence, I incurred $143.44 in unreimbursed damages.  When contacted, the manufacturer (Amana) was not interested in inspecting the damage, offering instead to provide a service call at my expense.  The issuer of an extended warranty service (GE Service Protection Plus ) declared that the policy did not cover such events.   But more importantly, this event could have caused serious injury to small children or pets, had they been in the area.


DETAILS

Purchase:  On Jan 17, 2004, we bought the subject refrigerator/freezer from HH Gregg, at a cost of $2046.57, including delivery and installation.  Delivery and Installation appeared to come off without a hitch.  [When called about the accident in 2011, HH Gregg stated that they no longer carry Amana products.]

Accident:  On October 4, 2011, when the top door was opened wide (with hand on door to control its movement), to fully access the various drawers in the body, it suddenly and unexpectedly fell from its hinges onto the floor, breaking 3 of the plastic bins in the door, and destroying some of the contents housed in those bins.  I was stunned by the event, and simply stared at the door and mess on the floor for several seconds.  

Upon gathering my wits, I noticed that the bottom hinge pin was also on the floor with the door, having come unscrewed from the hinge mount on the refrigerator.  With difficulty, I was able to screw the pin back into the lower mount, the screw threads being undamaged, and re-mount the door.   The refrigeration function appears to be performing satisfactorily at this time.

I now routinely inspect the screw mounted lower hinge pin for any evidence of it unscrewing from its mount.  

Apparent cause:  I can only conclude that the lower pin had become unscrewed gradually during the time I owned the refrigerator and finally dislodged from its final friction position when the door was opened wide on that date.   I found the pin laying on the floor about 6 inches from the pin hole in the door, and there was no damage to the screw threads.  I picked it up, noted its likely function, and screwed it back into the hinge mount on the body of the refrigerator.  I then re-mounted the door, minus its contents.

However, had small children or pets been present in the vicinity, they could have been seriously injured when the door fell off its hinges, since the event was sudden and without warning.  Adults could have also been injured, most likely with broken bones in the feet.  Note that the door was full width and quite heavy.  

Damage and costs:  The door has a slight dent on the lower left corner in the vicinity of the hinge hole.  This appears to be largely cosmetic, since once remounted, the door appears to function normally on the restored lower pin.  Three bins were broken and had to be replaced at an unreimbursed cost to me of $ 98.09.  A number of small jars of food items were shattered and had to be replaced at an unreimbursed cost to me of $45.35.   I waited till now to report this, because the replacement bins took this long to arrive.
