Product Description: Samsung Top Loading Washer Model No. WA400PJHDWR/AA
Product Type: Washing Machines, Other or Not Specified (140)
Incident Description:
In mid-2012, we bought a new SAMSUNG top loading washer, model # WA400PJHDWR/AA (Ser. No. Y69Q5AEC703298R) from Lowes in Gainesville, FL for $666.85  Two weeks ago, while washing a load of clothes, we heard a loud clanging sound during the spin cycle, followed by a louder BANGING sound, after which water starting pouring out all over the floor of our utility room and adjoining family room.

We tilted the washer and saw that the drain pump assembly had broken loose from the bottom of the washing machine tub and had detached itself and the accompanying drain hose and was just dangling in mid-air.  The washing machine was now unusable.

I learned from a Lowes call center rep that there were many reports of this same problem with the WA400 model SAMSUNG washers, and that SAMSUNG had issued a RECALL for Lowes-owned store assets (washers still in stock at any Lowes store or warehouse).  However, SAMSUNG did not opt to issue a recall to the general public for the same problem, even though the Lowes rep was aware of 246 cases at that time (mine being #247), and that there were 155,000 affected washers. Also, some consumers had experienced "flooding damage" depending no what part of the cycle the machine was in and where it was located (luckily ours was downstairs and on ceramic tile and at the end of the spin cycle, but in some cases, washers were located upstairs or near hardwood flooring and there was significant flooding damage. Lowes did ask if this was the case for me.) 

So, it was a known defect, known by SAMSUNG and now Lowes.  Since the SAMSUNG washer only has a 1 year warranty, I learned I would be responsible for all repair costs, but not the parts. Armed with this information, I contacted Samsung Customer Service and filed a complaint, asking WHY they had not issued a RECALL of these known defective WA400 washers.  They DENIED that there were 155,000 defective washers, as I had learned from Lowes, or that there was a significant problem, but they offered to pay for the repair cost as a one time courtesy, which I accepted.

The washer was repaired today by the Samsung rep.   A whole new drain pump assembly, including the pump, bracket, hose and wiring harness were installed.  The new pump assembly does not attach to the bottom of the washing machine tub, as the original OEM part did.   I got a look at the SAMSUNG Service Bulletin that the technician had in his  possession, and it was number ASC20131127001 and it listed models WA400, WA422, and WA456 as all being affected by this problem.  So, this reassures me that the quantity of washers affected is quite large.

I have seen several complaints posted online about this same problem.  348 complaints on [REDACTED], and several on [REDACTED] and on LOWES.COM.  All say the same thing - that the drain pump breaks off and floods their home and they are stuck with the repair bill and potential damage to their home.   Electrocution is a possibility as well, as the wiring harness can also come loose when the pump breaks off, so if the washer were to flood an area and an unsuspecting homeowner were to step into the puddle created by the washer, he could possibly get electrocuted from 120 VAC.

I also found online reference to another SAMSUNG service bulletin ASC20130222001 dated June 6, 2013 that says the same thing as the one my technician had in hand.  I found this reference onlin here: [REDACTED].

I posted multiple times on the Samsung Home Appliance [REDACTED] page that they need to issue an IMMEDIATE RECALL of all of these affected units (models WA400, WA422, and WA456), as this problem is potentially hazardous to the property of the homeowner and to life safety.   However, Samsung seems to be handling this on a case-by-case basis.   I did read enough of the service bulletin, and learned from the appliance repair company, that this problem affects the 3 Samsung top loading washers models listed above, manufactured from Jan. 2012 - Dec. 2012.  The design was changed the 2nd week of Dec. 2012, I believe.  Our washer, like thousands of others was manufactured in July 2012, and purchased on Sept. 1 2012.  It is 17 months old.

PLEASE REVIEW THIS SITUATION AND CONTACT SAMSUNG.  My washer is now repaired, but the problem here is that there are THOUSANDS of other newer SAMSUNG washers out there that will very likely fall apart from regular normal use and can flood and damage the consumer's home.  Also, many consumers start a load of wash and then leave to go run errands (as we have done).  We were lucky - we were at home when ours broke apart and started flooding the floor.... Others might not be so lucky.

Ironically, Samsung's corporate model is this: "At Samsung, we follow a simple business philosophy: to devote our talent and technology to creating superior products and services that contribute to a better global society."   Where their washers are concerned, they have fallen far short of this mark!

I had the Master Forge Grill, MFA350CNP, for less than a year and used it on a regular basis.  I turned it on to heat prior to grilling. You call Lowe's Corp Office, they have you work with the local store, then local store sends you to the parts #.  With this being a Lowe's brand, my initial thought is Lowe's corporate would be handling this situation.  

I had to replace some siding because of the heat from the fire was very intense.  My concern is there could be a global issue with this grill.  Lowe's is still selling it.  I'm thinking their thought is since the regulator has been replaced in future grills, it is ok to sell.

I did learn I do need to return that information card so in case there is an issue, the company can contact me regarding recalls.

I eagerly await your support and advice.  The device model is MALV-600.

(8/5/2025) World Kitchen, LLC: This is a response on behalf of Anchor Hocking d/b/a World Kitchen to CPSC consumer Report ID: 20250714-F35FD-2147329596, regarding a glass measuring cup, which the consumer mis-identified as being a Pyrex measuring cup, manufactured by Anchor Hocking. Based upon Anchor Hockings review of the proposed records and discussions with the consumer, Anchor Hocking responds as follows:  

I. ANCHOR HOCKINGS 16 C.F.R. 1102.12 COMMENTS ON THE REPORTED CONSUMER COMPLAINT.

A.	Identification and Inspection of the Products at Issue Not Performed 

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect or otherwise view the product at issue in this claim. Identification was made based on the picture provided and description by the consumer. 

Because the measuring cup could not be provided, Anchor Hocking cannot do an inspection as to any potential defect, for common misuse, retailer mishandling, or other cause of the failure. Without an opportunity to review the facts and products involved in the records disclosed, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.

B.	Compliance with Industry Standard

Anchoring Hockings glassware is manufactured in compliance with the applicable industry standard set forth in Chapter 24 of the Cookware Manufacturing Association Engineering Standards for Cookware and Bakeware.

C.	Consumer or Retailer Misuse

In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier and/or retailer mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide. Examples of this type of mishandling are:  hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; retailer mishandling including improper stacking or storage; or using in a too-hot oven. Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance either retailer or consumer misuse caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

After discussing the age and use of this product, consumer misuse may have contributed to the alleged failure. The glass was several years old and showed signs of use including scratches. Consumer was instructed on glassware safety and urged to review the manual with the replacement product sent, as well as handling instructions on Anchors website. 

D.	Tempered Glass Bakeware

According to the consumer, they were using an Anchor Hocking measuring cup to mix pancake ingredients when it suddenly exploded. There is an explanation for this method of failure. Anchor Hockings glassware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening. Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury. The method of failure is actually a safety feature rather than evidence of a defect. Therefore, the consumers report of the product exploding is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass, rather than evidence of a defect.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for oven bakeware state the following warnings:

Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns. Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Glass bakeware is not without limitations. While it is a healthier alternative to other types of bakeware, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break. Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking. Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin. Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority. Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority. Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals.  Anchor Hocking is proud that it has never had any of its products recalled by the Consumer Product Safety Commission.

Product Description: Gas Clothes dryer
Incident Description:
I purchased this dryer new from Sears in February 2010.  Shortly thereafter I smelled gas coming from the drum and vent.  Sears came and changed the valve. 

This year the smell has become more frequent and consistent.  Around September 2017 I called Sears for repair (I purchased an extended warranty). I was told that I had to call the gas company before they could come out.  The gas company determined that my vents are clear, the gas lines are in good condition and there were not leaks and the gas smell was coming from the dryer.  I called Sears and they scheduled a repair visit.  Approx. 2 weeks later the repairman came and changed the valve and left.  I ran the dryer an hour later and the gas filled the drum and vent again.  I called for the repairman to return but they scheduled a visit for approx. 2 weeks later again.  

I went ahead and called for the gas company to come out and check the dryer again and they determined it was the dryer and the dryer was on recall.

The Sears repairman came and smelled the gas and ordered new parts from where the gas goes into the dryer to the valve.  3 boxes of parts.  Approx. 2 weeks later he arrived again with an older more seasoned repairman who thought it unnecessary to change all the parts.  He changed some parts and left with the ones he didn't use.  He ran a cycle and didn't detect gas and left.  I also informed him that the gas company said the machine was under a recall.  He was unaware of the recall. The recall recommended a valve change which was done on the first visit.

Approx. a week later about November 11, 2017 I  ran the machine on a 40 minute timed cycle on medium heat and after 30 minutes opened the dyer door and was hit with the strong smell of gas.  My clothes smelled like gas too!

I called for a repairman again and Sears said they will not send someone out if there is a gas leak.  I had to explain again that the smell is there only when the machine is running and the gas company had been out twice already and determined it was coming from the dryer.  I had to insist they schedule a repairman visit.  Another 6 days from now is the date!
Company Comments: (11/22/2017) Sears Holdings Management Corporation: Sears Holdings takes product safety issues very seriously.  We investigate each CPSC database incident report.  We encourage our customers to provide additional information about incidents to our Customer Care Network, by calling 800-479-6351.

Product Description: DeLonghi BCO330T, Serial Number 72825
Incident Description:
On February 7th, 2018 at approximately 3:30 PM PST, I was operating an Espresso/Coffee Machine (DeLonghi BCO330T, Serial Number 72825).

I firstly began using the machine by adding water in the top reservoir of the unit, waiting about three minutes for the water to heat up, then I added almond milk to a frothing cup and heated up the milk with the unit's steam wand. 

Shortly after, I grabbed the espresso portafilter and added coffee using the measuring spoon included with the unit, enough to fill it at half capacity or for two shots of espresso coffee.

I began by priming the brew head to clean it. I then inserted the portafilter into the brew head, ensuring that the filter basket was properly inserted into the portafilter and that it it was flush, as I normally do when I operate the machine. I twisted the handle counter clockwise into the machine and ensured the handle was pointing to the arrow on the machine, so it lined up properly. 

I began the espresso brewing process by turning the switch on the side of the machine upwards and espresso began to brew and fall into a glass cup that was provided in the box for use with brewing espresso. 

As it was brewing, the unit had already poured enough coffee for one shot of espresso, and being accustomed to the machine, I knew it would take about a minute or two to finish brewing the full two shots of espresso, so I walked less than five feet away from the machine to another side of the kitchen and nearly two seconds after I walked away I could hear pressure build up in the machine, then suddenly heard a boom similar to a grenade exploding.

I stood there realizing and shaking by what seemed to be an explosion. I understood that I was lucky to have walked away for a moment as I could have been killed or seriously injured by the explosion's debris (the portafilter that flew from the blast of pressure, the hundreds of pieces of glass from the glass cup as well as the burning hot espresso grounds and coffee) which flew all over the room, the dining room, and the living room. 

I began by trying to clean up the mess and cut my finger with the broken shards of glass, so I consulted a cleaning lady and had her come clean up the debris which flew all over the room and previously prepared food and other kitchen items. 

I am writing this so appropriate measures can be taken to prevent this from happening to anyone else. I was left with a scene that looked like it came out of a Hollywood movie. Moments after the incident happened I contacted DeLonghi's customer service and spoke with a woman named [REDACTED] from Coffee Machine support and not only was my story not believed, but [REDACTED] asked me twice to plug in the machine again and attempt to brew a new batch of espresso, while she was on a video conference call with me although my repeated attempts to tell her that I was not comfortable with going through the experience again as I was almost seriously injured.

These lanyards are designed to convince mothers that the newborn stomach size is only 5-7 mL to prevent them from supplementing newborns who are crying inconsolably for milk when there is not enough.  The most recent scientific data shows that in fact, the newborn stomach size is 20 mL using ultrasound and autopsy.  These non-factual visual aids are leading to accidental newborn starvation and its complications, namely severe dehydration, hypernatremia, hypoglycemia and excessive jaundice which are all known causes of brain injury and permanent disability.  

Newborn stomach volume: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pubmed/23662739

Brain injury caused by insufficient milk intake in breastfed newborns: https://drive.google.com/file/d/0B0_MbXCqYazzVkMtejF3Y2tDLVk/view

My son's story:
My son was born 8 pounds and 11 ounces after a healthy pregnancy and normal uneventful vaginal delivery.  He was placed directly on my chest and was nursed immediately.  He was nursed on demand for 20-30 minutes every 3 hours.  Each day of our stay in the hospital, he was seen by the pediatrician as well as the lactation consultant who noted that he had a perfect latch.  He produced the expected number of wet and dirty diapers.  He was noted to be jaundiced by the second day of life and had a transcutaneous bilirubin of 8.9.  We were discharged at 48 hours at 5% weight loss with next-day follow-up.  We were told by the lactation consultant before discharge that he would be hungry and we were instructed to just keep putting him on the breast.  Upon getting home, he became fussy and I nursed him longer and longer into the night.  He cried even after nursing and latched back on immediately.  He did not sleep.  By the next morning, he stopped crying and was quiet.  We saw our pediatrician at around 68 hours of life (end of day 3).  Despite producing the expected number of wet and dirty diapers, he had lost 1 pound 5 ounces, about 15% of his birth weight. At the time, we were not aware of and were not told the percentage lost, and having been up all night long trying to feed a hungry baby, we were too exhausted to figure out that this was an incredible amount of weight loss.  He was jaundiced but no bilirubin was checked.  Our pediatrician told us that we had the option of either feeding formula or waiting for my milk to come in at day 4 or 5 of life.  Wanting badly to succeed in breastfeeding him, we went another day unsuccessfully breastfeeding and went to a lactation consultant the next day who weighed his feeding and discovered that he was getting absolutely no milk.  When I pumped and manually expressed, I realized I produced nothing. I imagined the four days of torture he experienced and how 2 days of near-continuous breastfeeding encouraged by breastfeeding manuals was a sign of this. We fed him formula after that visit and he finally fell asleep. Three hours later, we found him unresponsive. We forced milk into his mouth, which made him more alert, but then he seized. Despite that, he was found on the fourth day of life lethargic and unable to feed.  He had lost 10% of his birth weight and had a low glucose of 20 mg/dL (normal > 47 mg/dL).  This child was given IV glucose after which he developed a seizure.  They obtained a brain MRI which showed extensive areas of injury to almost the entire brain.  In addition to this child, 10 other healthy term newborns were identified to have developed hypoglycemia from insufficient breastfeeding as well. Information I found at trademarkia.com says that PetEdge did indeed register the trademark Cambridge Aquatics. The packaging and instructions say the aquarium comes with a two-year limited warranty.

Incident Description: I purchased a Brunton propane stove a couple years ago and the gas hose leaked from the over-pressure valve. Primus, the parent company sent me a replacement stove, a Primus Profile and hose. I was about to use the stove 2 days ago in below freezing temperatures in [REDACTED]. When I screwed the propane cylinder onto the hose, the over-pressure valve failed and a jet of propane came shooting out - same problem as with the first stove. It's pretty clear that the hose assembly has a sacrificial part in the over-pressure valve and that this part fatigues and eventually fails. Under normal use, the valve freezes due to the expanding propane gas, and my guess is that these freeze-thaw cycles are what fatigue the part and lead to failure. If someone were to leave the hose attached to the cylinder while they were camping, the valve could fail and fill a car or camper with propane. In addition, if the valve fails while cooking, the jet of propane could easily reach the flame of the stove about 2 feet away. I have the second hose that failed if you need to examine it

After cleaning out the washer thoroughly however, this kept happening to new loads of wash.  I ran the Pure Cycle at least 6 times in 24 hours to try to clean it and the dirt/mold just keep coming out and collecting in the basin.  I also wiped out/cleaned/scrubbed the detergent pull outs and everything else I could get to inside the washer.  Since none of this was helping the problem, I contacted Samsung support looking for suggestions, or to have it repaired.  I never heard back from them.  In an attempt to problem solve this myself, I came upon the Samsung Community online and found a long thread (38 pages!) of people having the same problem as myself.  It was then that I realized this was a mold problem, not dirt!  Quite disturbing!!!  My son and husband have had terrible "allergies" lately and my son recently had to start using a preventative inhaler.  I'm sure having his clothes/sheets/towels/everything washed in mold for who knows how long contributed to that problem!  After finding the community, and since I still hadn't heard a word from Samsung, and couldn't get ahold of them I took the bottom of the basin out and everything was caked in mold and build up (see pictures)!  We thoroughly scrubbed everything off that we could get to under the basin, and in the hose and soaked it all in bleach, but I cannot be sure it's not hiding somewhere else that we couldn't see or reach.  This seems to only be a temporary fix, as it will likely build up again over time since you can hear the water sitting under the drum.  We have always used the proper HE detergent on this machine and it is very disappointing that after only a few years we will need to purchase another new washing machine.  We spent a lot of money on this machine and it's going to have to be trash, unless Samsung can fix it!

	2.	That the CPSC review whether the products labeling, warnings, and instructions are adequate to prevent harm in residential settings.
	3.	That the CPSC consider regulatory or enforcement actions to protect consumers from hazardous products labeled for industrial use.

I can provide documentation, medical records, and photos if needed. Please let me know how best to submit them.

Thank you for your time and attention to this matter. I look forward to your response.

Sincerely,

Product Description: Sharp R420LK Microwave Oven
Incident Description:
I purchased a Sharp R420LK microwave oven from Amazon in May 2010 to replace a malfunctioning Sharp microwave oven that I had for over 5 years.
The 420 model oven is made with a mica waveguide cover on the inner surface of the oven that covers the microwave generator. This cover is the major weak point of this oven.
There is a warning on page 8 of the oven's manual that states: Keep the waveguide cover clean. Food residue can cause arcing and/or fires.
At some point when the family was using the oven, some food spatter landed on the waveguide cover and was not noticed by anyone.  Subsequent uses of the oven caused the spot of food spatter to burn a hole in the waveguide cover so that the next use of the oven resulted in much sparking in the oven.
I took the oven to a Sharp authorized servicing facility on 1/3/11 and it took Sharp two months to tell me that they would replace that oven with a refurbished same model.  I picked up the refurbished model on March 1, 2011.
Last night, I heated up two frozen Teriyaki Chicken Breasts for dinner in an open Pyrex dish without any cover.  Evidently, during the cooking cycle, a spatter landed on the waveguide cover unbeknown to us.  Later, my daughter placed a snack pack of popcorn in the oven to cook it & the oven started shooting electricla discharges inside the oven - sort of like seeing discharges of lightning occur.  The cooking was stopped & a spatter was noticed on the waveguide cover plate.  It was cleaned and then the oven performed normally.

I have owned various makes of microwave ovens for 35 years.  The original lasted for 15 years before it was replaced.  Later models also worked for several years before being replaced.  This Sharp unit (R420LK) is the first one, and the only brand, that I have found to have a mica waveguide cover.  I have never had any problems with arcing or waveguide covers in all my previous experiences with microwave ovens.  I have used microwave ovens at various worksites that had not been cleaned in awhile and they did not do any arcing inside the oven.

I believe that the mica cover that Sharp uses make the oven a definite safety hazard unless the oven is kept very clean to remove any food spatters that might land on the cover.  They also use the same material on other model waveguide covers.  This is the last Sharp microwave oven I will ever purchase because of the use of an inferior material inside the oven as a cover over the waveguide.
Answer Explanation: Sharp replaced the original with a refurbished same model

(5/16/2011) SHARP ELECTRONICS CORPORATION: Arcing in the cooking cavity is not a safety hazard as the arcing is confined to the cavity and immediately stops when power is turned off or the microwave door is opened.  It is the owners responsibility to keep the oven cavity clean and remove food splatters from the mica waveguide cover to prevent damage and cavity arcing.  Mica is a proven and reliable material for the waveguide cover and is used by many microwave oven manufacturers.  Users should follow the instructions in the model R420L owners manual.

As stated on page 8 of the manual, Keep waveguide cover clean.  Food residue can cause arcing and/or fires. 

Also on page 21 of the owners manual notes, Waveguide Cover  The waveguide cover is made from mica so it requires special care.  Keep the waveguide cover clean to assure good performance. Once we actually left the house without realizing the cooktop was on and returned to find the cooktop bright red and so hot that the overhead vent fan turned on in response to the heat. In reviewing information online and in speaking with Samsung, it is clear that this is a known issue that has caused many other consumers similar problems and safety concern.  I received a call from Samsung on October 10, 2018 in response to a live chat and an email in which I expressed concerns about the unsafe functioning of this range.  The Samsung representative acknowledged this is a known problem.  Her only suggestion was that we use child-proof door handle covers on our stove knobs.  Given the sensitivity of the knobs, the use of the child-proof covers does not prevent the knobs from being activated.

We no longer feel that this range is a safe appliance for our home.  We feel that Samsung needs to take action to prevent a tragedy in their customers' homes.

The reason I am writing this message is to provide my comments/concerns regarding a new Kitchen Aid appliance. Within a few days of purchase, I utilized the oven portion of the range.  To my amazement, not only did the stainless steel door become extremely hot to the touch, but at a high temperature (450 degrees) the stove top became warm to touch and the front of the stove top was almost as hot as the oven door.   The oven door was sufficiently hot to possibly cause burning of a persons hand.  Thinking that it might be just a fluke because the range was brand new, I put off calling the repair man for about four weeks.

The higher the temperature; the hotter the door would become.   Also, the vents that are located on the oven door to vent the heat from the oven could cause the area around the door handle to become hot.  He checked with his office to determine if similar concerns had been received.  After discussion with his office, he indicated that the heating of the door was a normal operation of the range.   I indicated to him that I felt the door was much hotter than the quoted temperature. We turned the oven to a temperature of 375 degrees.  After do so, I still felt that the door was extremely too hot to the touch.  The repair man noted the hot temperature of the door but was unable to provide a solution.  

I feel that the issue concerning the oven door temperature is an unsafe condition.  This problem has not occurred with any of the previous ranges that we have own.  I feel the situation could be dangerous considering how hot the door becomes when the oven is being utilized.  A burn could occur especially with small children if contact with the door is for more than a few seconds .

I consider this issue sufficiently serious enough to be considered for investigation. Also, I feel that the location of the oven vents is a contributing factor to the heat of the door when in use. Also, how much installation  (if any) is utilized in the door to keep the temperature down?

(4/25/2011) Anchor Hocking, LLC: Anchor Hockings comments regarding Report No: 20110412-B2F90-2147480256

The report to the CPSC involved a 20 cm x 20 cm glass baking dish, manufactured by Anchor Hocking.  The consumer reported that on April 12, 2011, she had been using the dish to bake chicken at 400 degrees for 20 minutes, when she heard the dish explode.  The consumer submitted a photograph showing what appears to be a glass dish that had shattered into many small pieces.  The consumer reported that there were no injuries.

Anchor Hocking has not had the opportunity to inspect the product at issue in this report.  Often, similar products manufactured by other entities are improperly identified as Anchor Hocking products.  Without having the opportunity to inspect the glass baking dish, Anchor Hocking is unable to determine whether the product involved in this incident is, in fact, an Anchor Hocking product.

In addition, because the glass baking dish has not been provided, Anchor Hocking cannot do an inspection as to the cause of the failure.  Without an opportunity to review the facts and products involved in the report, it is impossible to determine the cause of the alleged problem.  In Anchor Hockings experience, consumer misuse, failure to follow the manufacturers instructions, and supplier mishandling are the causes of the overwhelming majority of glass product failures industry-wide.  Examples of this type of mishandling are: hitting the glass on a counter or hard surface causing a chip to break off; using improper cleaning materials or utensils; using on a stovetop; placing a hot dish on a wet or cold surface; adding liquid to a hot dish; or using in a too-hot oven.  Anchor Hocking believes there is a chance misuse or mishandling caused or contributed to the alleged failure of the product.

According to the consumer, the glass baking dish shattered into a number of pieces.  There is an explanation for this method of failure.  Anchor Hockings glass bakeware is subjected to a manufacturing process known as tempering or heat strengthening.  Tempering is designed to strengthen glass against thermal shock and in the event of a failure to cause the products to fail safely by shattering in many smaller pieces that are unlikely to cause serious injury.  The consumers report of a product shattering into many small pieces is actually an indication the product failed as it is designed to with tempered glass.

To warn the consumer of this potential, the care and use instructions for the oven bakeware state the following warning:  Failure to follow these warnings may cause the product to suddenly fracture into many small pieces, which could result in property damage or serious personal injury from cuts or burns.  Scratches from certain cleaning materials and utensils can weaken bakeware causing unexpected breakage when exposed to sudden temperature change.

Tempered soda-lime-silicate is stronger and more durable, breaks into relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shards when it does break, and is a more environmentally-friendly product.  Tempered or heat-strengthened bakeware is similar, although not identical, to tempering of other glass products where safety is a concern such as automobile windows, sliding glass doors, shower doors, etc.  The priority is to eliminate a severe cutting hazard if a break occurs.  The alternative form of glass bakeware is made with borosilicate, which is significantly weaker against mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) and when it does break, it breaks into larger pieces of very sharp glass creating a significant risk of severe cuts, punctures, etc.  Another failure mode is thermal shock, which results from a significant and immediate temperature change.  Consistent scientific testing for decades has established that tempered soda-lime-silicate and borosilicate glass perform, at least, equivalent in thermal shock resistance.  Indeed, Anchors testing, when the decision was made to change from borosilicate to tempered soda-lime-silicate in the 1980s, demonstrated a 40% improvement in thermal shock resistance for Anchors tempered soda-lime-silicate glass compared to annealed borosilicate silicate glass bakeware.  

Glass bakeware is not without limitations.  While it is a healthier alternative to metal bakeware because no hazardous materials leach into the food, and cooks often prefer it because it helps retain moisture, like all glass, it can break.  Manufacturers of glass bakeware, including Anchor, have studied and evaluated the safety of glass bakeware while considering the rigors of cooking.  Mechanical breakage (i.e., dropping or hitting hard or sharp objects) is the most frequent failure mode by a significant margin.  Accordingly, making the bakeware stronger and more durable against mechanical breakage is a priority.  Likewise, having the bakeware break in a safer manneri.e., relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges and shardsis a priority.  Tempered soda-lime-silicate glass achieves these goals.  

Surprisingly, however, even with the obvious and known limitations that glass can break, the number of injuries associated with the use of glass bakeware is remarkably small.  Approximately 700 million pieces of U.S.-manufactured tempered soda-lime-silicate glass bakeware have been sold in the U.S. in the last 10 years.  Each piece of bakeware is used multiple times per year, yet the National Electronic Injury Surveillance Survey (NEISS), which is used by product safety experts to assess the risk of consumer products, shows that there have been zero to three unsubstantiated claims per year of glass bakeware shattering or exploding.  Glass bakeware is an extraordinarily safe product when used in accordance with safety and usage instructions.

Product Description: Fitness Gear Inversion Table
Brand: Fitness Gear (produced for Dick's Sporting Goods)
Incident Description:
On September 23, 2012 I purchased a Fitness Gear Inversion Table, Style STE00059, UPC 886081164509.  I used it twice a day inverting it maybe 90/100 degrees until October 31, 2012.  On October 31, I decided to do the 180 degree invert and perform the exercises they show in their video.

I had hung there about 1to 1-1/2 minutes before twisting to one side.  When I did I felt the table slip and I grabbed for the pull-up rails.  Next thing I know, I'm falling onto my head with my body crashing down full force onto the hardwood floor.

I was taken to the Emergency Room and after CTs and x-rays told I had concussion and whiplash.  I followed-up with my family physician 2 days later and he told me I had mild concussion with the soft tissue up and down my spine torn loose from the spinous muscle, and in the cervical area, the spinous muscle is torn lose from the spine.  I have multiple contusions and strained muscles and both my doctor and ER physician say I'm lucky to be alive or a quadriplegic.

I had no idea what caused the failure, but this week I decided to look at it.  I now believe it is due to faulty product design.  The only thing that holds the foot mechanism on is an adjustment pin which lets the mechanism slide to adjust to your leg size.  The only thing that holds the pin in is a spring and gravity.  When I inverted to 180 degrees and the table felt like it slipped, I stiffened out when I grabbed the rails.  When my feet tensed, I think it dislodged the pin held in by gravity and the tiny spring allowing the entire foot mechanism to fall out of the table.  

I believe, if the foot adjustment bar had had a bolt to hold it in, although it may have slipped, I would have still been able to hold myself on the table and return to an upright position. 

This is a design hazard and needs to be recalled and a warning issued so no one else has to suffer the way I am, and will be for months to come (if not years).
Company Comments: (12/17/2012) Dick's Sporting Goods, Inc.: Dicks Sporting Goods is committed to providing our customers with high quality and safe products. We are communicating with this customer to gather additional information about the incident.

I purchased a Electrolux electric slide-in range; model number EW30IS65JSA, serial number NF10928958 stove on  April 12, 2011.  This appliance broke for the second time in three years due to a spillover and a poor stove design.  Recently on several occasions my daughter and I got shocked when touching the stove and the overhead microwave.  On August 22, 2014 I had a home inspector visit my house and I explained that my daughter and I have gotten shocked.  He inspected the microwave to see if it was grounded and it was.  On August 24, 2014 I was putting a plate of food in the microwave to reheat and my arm was touching the microwave while my right hip was leaning against the Electrolux stove.   I received a big shock that went through my left arm and caused me to drop my cell phone
 
Because of this, I contacted a licensed electrical contractor/electrical inspector and he examined the microwave and the stove on August 30, 2014.  He determined that the microwave was indeed grounded.  However, upon testing/inspecting the stove he found that between the exterior of the stove and the microwave exterior there was 125 volts AC present.  Upon further investigation he said that the stove case was energized with this referenced voltage.  He considered this an electrocution hazard and he turned off the circuit breaker which turns off the power to the stove. This action eliminated the voltage on the exterior of the stove.  The electrician recommended that I contact Electrolux immediately and have a representative come out to examine and correct this dangerous situation. Please contact me to set up an appointment.  Thank you.

Product Description: Bad Boy Buggy ATV
Incident Description:
Record of Events Related to the Purchase and Use of 
2010 Bad Boy Classic ATV 

September 8, 2011


1.	Purchase of Bad Boy Buggy Vehicle:

The Bad Boy Buggy ATV was purchased by mother-in-law, [REDACTED] in September of 2010.  [REDACTED] desired an all-terrain vehicle that had a low ecological impact and could be used to negotiate her 175 acre parcel of woods and fields on [REDACTED] in the town of Middlefield, New York.  The Bad Boy Buggy was recommended to her by a neighborhood friend and by the dealer for the company, a Mr. [REDACTED] of Clay New York as a vehicle she could use to transport tools and supplies throughout her property.  Mr. [REDACTED] who owns the 4ward Sales Company dealership came to her property with a demonstration vehicle in early September of 2010. At that time he drove the vehicle on the land with [REDACTED] and I and we talked with him about its suitability for its intended purposes, including travel on rough logging roads with steep inclines.  He said that the vehicle was made for just this type of use and so should work well for us. He also gave me an introductory lesson on how to use the vehicle including the operation of its directional switching and the electrically activated braking system. 

[REDACTED] and Mr. [REDACTED] negotiated a deal on a 2010 demonstrator model that had been used by another family in the area as a service replacement.  Mr. [REDACTED] said that he would take the vehicle back to his shop and clean and service it so that it could be delivered in as new condition and would be fully warranted by the company.

The vehicle (Bad Boy Buggy Classic, VIN# [REDACTED]) was purchased by [REDACTED] for $11,775.52 from 4ward Sales on September 15th and delivered to her [REDACTED] of property.  The vehicle was kept in a shed specially purchased and wired for the vehicle on her property.  During the Fall and Winter of 2010 and 2011 the vehicle was used only 3-4 times due to inclement weather followed by the winter snows. In the Spring and Summer of 2011 the Buggy was used somewhat more frequently with a total of about a dozen usages all on [REDACTED]s property and for short distances on [REDACTED] by members of her family (mostly myself) for recreation.  

During the entire ownership period the only service on the vehicle was that I removed the right rear tire to add sealant to fix a flat.  Other than that it was entirely as it was received from Mr. [REDACTED] in September of 2010.



2.	The ATV Accident of August 21st, 2011:

On the evening of August 21st my family consisting of my wife, [REDACTED] (53), my daughter [REDACTED] (17), son [REDACTED] (14) and myself [REDACTED] (53) were invited to [REDACTED]'s Upper Lean-To on her property for a picnic with her, her friend Dr. [REDACTED] and my brother and sister-in-law [REDACTED] and [REDACTED].  We were scheduled to travel to South Korea the next day and this was a farewell picnic for the family. The Upper Lean-To is situated on the southern side of [REDACTED] on a steep clearing with a view of the Village of Cooperstown and Otsego Lake in the distance.  That evening we were invited by [REDACTED] to use the ATV to get to the Lean-To and my son [REDACTED] drove the vehicle up to the site.  The trip was uneventful and we parked behind my brother-in-laws SUV on a flat area and enjoyed our picnic.

At about 7:15pm that evening we decide that it was time to go, my daughter decided that she would like to try driving the ATV down to the parking area.  Others were seated as follows, [REDACTED] was in the right rear position, [REDACTED] in the left rear seat position and I sat in the passenger seat.  Although the vehicle was equipped  with seat belts (available only on special request) none of us were wearing them that night. I reviewed the vehicles operations with [REDACTED], including putting the vehicle drive switch in the forward position and the use of the electric brakes. She put the ATV in forward and moved it around my brother-in-laws SUV and began the descent down the hill. I immediately noticed that the ATV was picking up speed in an unsafe manner and told her to let her foot off of the accelerator and put the brake on.  She looked at me and said that she was already doing that and told me that her foot was on the brake, I looked over at her and confirmed that both of her feet were holding the brake pedal to the floor.  I could feel some resistance coming from the mechanical braking system, but at no time could I feel the electric braking system engage. After a few seconds I could feel the small resistance of the mechanical brake give way and the vehicle pick up a lot of speed.  We traveled very quickly down the upper part of the hill and struck a tree head on.  My wife, daughter and son were thrown from the vehicle by the force of the impact.  I hit the windshield, which was hitting the tree and then managed to stumble out of the ATV and then lay on the ground. The total distance travelled was approximately 325 feet from the place where we got into the ATV to where we struck the tree.  If we did not strike that tree we would have continued down the hill (approximately as steep as a downhill ski slope), with much more dire consequences. 

My in-laws called 911 for emergency help and I and my family, stayed in the positions we had fallen on the ground until the EMS crew from the Cooperstown Fire Department arrived and removed us to Bassett Hospital in Cooperstown, NY to be treated in the Emergency Room. Also responding to the incident, besides the Cooperstown Fire Department were the New York State Police and the Hartwick and Milford, New York Fire Department EMS squads. 
3.	Injuries Resulting from the Accident: 

[REDACTED]: I fractured my face in four places including a tripod fracture of the cheekbone and a smaller fracture of the upper jaw.  I stayed in the hospital overnight for treatment and then received plastic surgery at Bassett Hospital to repair my broken cheekbone.  I have residual numbness over the right side of my face and continue to experience intermittent pain as a result of my injuries.  I also have some scarring from the injuries and from the surgery. 

[REDACTED]: Was treated and released from Bassett Hospital for a fractured ankle in three places and bruising and fracture blisters on her lower left leg and chest. She also experienced bruising to the face and pain in her chest that may be related to a rib fracture. She is out of work for at least six weeks and continues to experience pain in her ankle while in use and at rest and to a lesser degree in her chest.

[REDACTED]: Was treated and released from Bassett Hospital for a knee injury that required her at first to use an air cast and then support bandages. She continues to experience leg pain in both legs as a result of the injuries.

[REDACTED]: Received minor injuries including cuts and scrapes that required minimal treatment in the Emergency Room. 

	

Prepared by:


[REDACTED]

Product Description: Raptor SD zero turn mower manufactured by Hustler (Turf Equipment).

Incident Description: I own a Hustler brand of zero turn mower, a Raptor SD.  The design of the fuel tank is such that once initially filled, after a minute or so, the tank is no longer full to the top as the fuel has migrated to an air pocket at the top of the tank and started filling it.  You can repeat this process one or two times, adding additional fuel and then the tank is actually 100% full.  However, the evaporative emission system employed on this mower will then siphon out a large amount of fuel out of the fuel tank and dump all of this fuel on the floor beneath the mower through the vent on the system.  It is a large amount of fuel.  It is fortunate that I do not have a gas hot water heater in my garage as the fumes from this large amount of fuel would certainly have ignited inside the closed garage. Dumping of the fuel is not readily noticed after filling the tank, but apparently starts some minutes later, after leaving the area.  This needs a design remedy asap before a fire does happen with one of these mowers.
Answer Explanation: Sent manufacturer similar e-mail w/o pictures

Product Description:
Magna Latch

The Magna Latch has two sections.  One section is mounted on a fixed pool fence pole.  It has a magnetic bolt and a knob to pull up the bolt.  The other section is mounted on the gate.  It has a platform with a recess.  Inside the recess is a magnet.  When the gate closes, the magnet on the gate section pulls the magnetic bolt into the recess.  This should hold the gate closed.  However, if the two sections are not aligned, then the gate appears latched, but in fact it is not.

The Magna Latch as a whole is about 1-2 feet tall, 1 inch wide, and 2-3 inches deep.  It is black.
Incident Description:
Our house is in Las Vegas, Nevada.  Around January 9, 2017, we installed a removable mesh pool fence with a Magna Latch for the gates.  This was to keep our young son and daughter from entering the pool.  In the early evening of June 20, 2017, friends visited.  Their children played in the pool with our children.  After a while, our daughter and her pool buddy left the pool because our daughter said that she was finished swimming.  However, at some point she went back to the pool and was able to open the gate.  She suffered a near drowning, and she passed away on June 29, 2017 from  injuries resulting from brain anoxia.

June 20, 2017, was a record hot day in Las Vegas.  A couple of days later, an investigation by the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department showed that the Magna Latch was not closing correctly.  The aluminum fence poles had bowed, which pulled the parts of the Magna Latch out of alignment.  The Magna Latch looked like it was closed, but it was not.  Subsequent inspections by experts have confirmed that the Magna Latch is not closing correctly.

Our family is completed devastated by the incident and the passing away of our very young daughter.
Answer Explanation: The fence fabricator purchased the Magna Latch and installed it on the fence and gate poles

I have a photo of what he found that I am hoping I will be able to attach to this report somewhere. The appliance is now unplugged - I called HotPoint to report what the electrician had found and was given the number (800) 386-1215 and told to call Monday morning to report this.

Further internet searches have uncovered similar problems people had with HotPoint RB757 model ranges, but I couldn't find anything with my model number RB787.  I don't know if it is because of it's age? But it sounds to be the same problem people were having with RB757 being a fire hazard.

Incident Description:
About two months ago I installed several hard wired smoke alarms in my house.  Within two days of the installation, we had our first false alarm.  Since then we have a false alarm at least 5 to 10 times per month.  It is ALWAYS at night, between the hours of 11pm and 5am, usually at 2 or 3 am.

These are not battery chirps.  Often times one alarm will sound one blast, and then no more.  Sometimes an alarm will sound several blasts, but they are random in timing.  Other times it will be a full alarm, which then sets off all the other alarms.

The frequency of the alarms seem to have no pattern.  Sometimes they will sound multiple false alarms in one night, then go several days or a week with no false alarms.  The false alarms originate from different alarms, sometimes our bed room, sometimes the kids' bedroom.

I installed the alarms exactly as the instructions said to.  The alarms are at the proper height.  They are not near any bathroom or the kitchen.  The HVAC vents are on the other side of the room so there are no wind currents.  The attic is well insulated with an R value of 45.  The alarms are far away from all sources of EMF or RFI.

This is a very dangerous issue.  Frequent false alarms are like the alarms "crying wolf".  If they alarm for a real fire they will likely be ignored, creating extreme risk to life.  The false alarms are also likely to cause the removal of the alarm, leaving people at a much higher risk of death from fire.

Upon researching the exact make and model of alarm I purchased, I found an amazing amount of people having the same problem.  The alarm has a rating of 1.2 out of 5 stars on Home Depot's website, and EVERY review talks about false alarm issues.

This is a very serious issue.  I feel it is only a matter of time before a serious injury or fatality happens because people are disabling or ignoring these alarms.  This product, especially since it is a safety product, needs to have some sort of corrective action taken.  It is a safety product required by law, that may actually increase risk.

Incident Description:
I am writing to advise you of a serious hazard uncovered with a Maytag "advanced cooking system super capacity plus gas convection oven / range that could have resulted in a house explosion."

My wife was baking a cake and while the oven was on we both proceeded to do some gardening outside. Awhile later my wife went back into the house to check on the cake. She immediately rushed out to tell me the house was filled with gas. I immediately cancelled the oven concerned that even that activity could cause a spark that would ignite the gas. The central air conditioner was on and the gas odor permeated the entire house from the basement to the second floor. I know the oven did initially ignite as the cake ultimately was half baked.

Following opening windows and doors, I called our gas provider. It was Saturday and they sent a service technician out on an emergency call. He electronically sniffed out the area and determined that the gas was coming from the stove (oven). I explained to him that recently, when the oven was first turned on that we were hearing a puff at ignition but never smelled any gas. I was shocked when he told me that based upon my description and the age of the stove, he knew exactly what was wrong and that he had experienced this many times before. He advised me that the ignitor, with age, develops resistance and doesnt always get hot enough to ignite the burner or if the burner does ignite, it sometimes only partially ignites the burner allowing it to leak gas. He measured the current to the ignitor and confirmed that it was too resistive and the current was too low to function reliably. He replaced the ignitor ($160.50) and everything was fine from that point on. Obviously, we are still concerned.

My wife was always fearful of using the ovens timed delay to bake for this very reason. I always thought the oven had a safety mechanism such as my gas dryer that requires a heat sensor to trip before the gas valve would open. Fortunately, my wife never felt comfortable with using the timed delay and I am grateful that she did not. I could only imagine what would have happened if we were out of the house for several hours with the oven leaking especially since we have both a gas furnace and a gas hot water heater.

When the stove was fairly new, I expressed concerns with the burner ignitor. I experienced a situation whereby one burner ignitor failed. Since all the ignitor spark simultaneously, the gas from the burner with the failed ignitor traveled to one of the other burner ignitor causing a little explosion. 

I wrote Matag and was basically told that unfortunately parts are made by humans and therefore cannot be perfect

Considering the risk associated with this failure, I feel this response is inadequate and should be recalled.

Product Description: GE Profile Dishwasher: Model: PDW9280N00SS, Serial Number TM922574B.
Incident Description:
I have a GE Profile Dishwasher: Model: PDW9280N00SS, Serial Number TM922574B.

We woke up around 4 a.m. on 2/10/18 to the smell of smoke and smoke alarm set off.  We came downstairs to find smoke billowing out of our dishwasher.  When we opened the dishwasher we discovered that all plastic parts of the dishwasher had melted, such as the arms at the bottom, the wheels and most of the racks.  Some of the plastic was smoldering and smoking.  The melted parts had dripped all over the vessels in the dishwasher.  It was so hot that it felt like the interior of a broiler or hotter and even with oven mitts, handling the dishes was impossible.  We switched off the circuit and waited for it to cool.  When it did, all the plastic had congealed destroying the entire contents of the dishwasher.  Some of the plastic had burnt, hence the smell.  All the plastic parts of the dishwasher had partially or completely melted.  It took nearly a week for us to get the smell out of the house, despite us leaving all the  externally venting exhaust fans on continuously and leaving some of the doors open, until it became unbearably cold.

We are now without a dishwasher and have lost an entire night's load, which includes our glasses, cups, plates, silverware, cookware and several serving ware, which are now destroyed.  We are going to have to repurchase all of them and a new dishwasher.  More importantly, this was a major fire hazard and had I not woken up and switched off the dishwasher we may have had a major fire.  Our children's bedroom was directly above the dishwasher and we shudder to think what might have happened.

We since contacted GE and were directed to their Monogram Preferred / Special Programs and Recalls.  They sent a technician out who said that (a) the dishwasher is unsalvageable; and (b) we were very lucky that the cabinets around the dishwasher did not catch fire.  However, they want us to pay for a new dishwasher and they have so far not reimbursed us for the destroyed vessels and damage.
Answer Explanation: We contacted their customer service and were directed to the Monogram Preferred / Special Programs and Recalls, case number [REDACTED]

This label is very misleading for consumers. We demand that all glass shower manufacturers should be required to notify their consumers of this possible danger so that consumers can take proper precautions. It should also be a requirement to be notified of this possible danger when purchasing or becoming a tenant of any property with glass shower enclosures.

Product Description: Scepter brand 5 gallon plastic gasoline container
Incident Description: This is about a 5 gallon gas can.  I noticed that every time the weather warmed up my garage would fill with gasoline fumes.  Upon checking, I found wet gasoline on the outside of the container and on the surface on which it sat.  Fortunately, no fire occurred.  The design includes a breather tube that extends from the cap into the can.  Even with the level of gasoline in the can below the full mark, the breather tube is below the fluid level.  When the temperature warms, the expansion of the gasoline and air in the can forces the liquid up the breather tube to the cap and nozzle area where it leaks out due to pressure in the can.  In the picture you can see the wet gasoline on the outside of the can as a shiny area below the filler cap.  Tightening the cap does not prevent the leak.  Also, the can is very poorly designed for handling while transferring fuel from the can.  One hand is required to lift the can.  One hand is required to hold open the mechanism to pour gasoline.  But since the handle for lifting does not extend around the side of the can to be able to tilt the can for pouring, ANOTHER hand is needed to tilt the can somehow.  Most humans have only two hands, making the job of lifting, tilting and opening the can all at the same time very awkward, if not impossible.  This product is clearly poorly designed and dangerous.

The consumer has no injuries to report. The consumer believes this product poses a safety hazard.

Product Description: Samsung refrigerator RSG257AARS/XAA 24 cu side by side counter depth with in-door ice and water.
Incident Description:
We bought a brand new Samsung refrigerator RSG257AARS/XAA in August 2011 as part of a total kitchen remodel.  On 12/16/12 we came home after being out for several hours to a flooded kitchen.  Water was actively pouring from the front door ice dispenser chute, as if a faucet was on.  We immediately turned off the power to the fridge and this stopped the water from pouring out, we also then turned off the water supply.  When we opened the freezer door a wave of water escaped.  Ultimately the water that pouted out in those few hours did incredible damage to our home.  Our insurance spent $12,000  to replace the kitchen floor, the floor in adjacent rooms, the ceiling and 2 walls in the finished basement below the kitchen. This is not including the initial tear out of wet materials and mold abatement work that had to be done.  It is now February and we are still working on the repair work.
